alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A1:
The World to be Rid of One Rascal.
SAN FRANCISCO, May 28.—The Supreme Court has affirmed the decision of the lower court in condemning to death Alexander Goldenson for the murder of a little school girl, Mamie Kelly. Goldenson was at that time 19 years old, and was studying art. He had gone to several entertainments with Mamie, but finally her mother forbade her to go with him. Goldenson met her on the street as she was returning from school with her companions, drew a pistol and shot her dead. The girl was only fifteen years old and bore a good reputation. The crime was so atrocious that a crowd pursued Goldenson in his flight to the police station, where he secured a refuge, and on the following night a mob of several thousand tried to break into the County Jail and lynch the murderer. They had no leader, however, and the police were soon summoned and drove them away. Goldenson was tried promptly and convicted of murder in the first degree, with the penalty of hanging. His main defense was hereditary insanity, and the ground for appeal was that the Court had not allowed him time to secure insanity evidence from Russia, where Goldenson came from. The present decision ends his legal fight and he will soon hang.
alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A2:
THE GOLDENSON CASE.
The action of Governor Waterman in declining to interpise Executive clemency between the law and the offender in the case of Alexander Goldenson, will meet with public approval. The prerogative of Executive clemency
the prerogative of Executive clemency is the refusal to exercise it in cases like that under consideration, where the crime is unrelieved by a single ray of light which would soften its asperity and justify the hope that the perpetrator was not at heart a murderer of the first degree.
alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A4:
GOLDENSEN IS GAME.
A San Francisco Murderer Who Will Swing To-Morrow.
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 12.—The sheriff is overrun by crowds who want to witness the Goldensen hanging next Friday. Four hundred and fifty invitations have been issued. Among those who called for tickets was a well dressed woman from Australia, who said she did not want to miss the execution, as it would be a rare psychological study. When told that women were not admitted to hangings, she asked if she could not get a pass should she dress in men's clothes. Goldensen begins to weaken, but is braced up on stimulants. He prepared a long indictment of the sheriff, which he was prevailed upon not to print. He wants to speak for half an hour on the gallows, but this will not be permitted. He threatens to die cursing Sheriff McMann, and he says these curses will have their effect as the sheriff will speedily follow him to the grave. Goldensen's lawyers will attempt to-morrow to have the sheriff arrested for contempt, for failure to bring Goldensen before a jury impaneled to test his sanity. If the sheriff is arrested, he will delegate his duties at the gallows to the coroner. There will be a disagreeable scene at the hanging, as Goldensen is ugly and bears venomous hatred toward the sheriff.
alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A5:
Mattie Kelly's Murderer Hanged.
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 14.—Alexander Goldensen, who shot and killed a fourteen-year-old school girl named Mattie Kelly, on Nov. 10, 1886, was hanged in the county jail here, a few minutes after noon to-day. No hanging since the days of the vigilantes committee has excited greater interest on the Pacific Coast. His crime came near causing a riot, and two ineffectual attempts were made to lynch him by assaulting the city jail, but in each instance serious disorder was prevented by the police. Notwithstanding the popular feeling against the young murderer, the legal fight in his behalf was prolonged for nearly two years. The murderer's last night was passed in drinking, card-playing and blasphemy. The only known cause for the shooting of his victim was her refusal to accept his attentions. Goldensen was eighteen years old when he committed the murder, and was a person of vicious habits.

TO HEAVEN VIA THE GIBBET.

COLUMBIA, S. C., Sept. 14.—"Dock' Dargan, a negro boy, 19 years old, was hanged in the jail at Bennettsville to-day for the murder, in April last, of William E. Cox, Jr., a white boy of about the same age. He met his death calmly, and declared that he was going to heaven. He died without a struggle, his neck being broken.
alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A10:
LEGALLY CHOKED.
Murderer Goldensen Expiates His Crime on the Gallows.
Special to the Globe.
Crime on the Gallows.
Special to the Globe.
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 14.—Alexander Goldensen was hanged in the city jail a few minutes after noon to-day for the murder, on Nov. 10, 1886, of little Mamie Kelly, a schoolgirl fourteen years of age, who had rejected his attentions. Goldensen, who was but twenty years old, passed last night in drinking, playing cards and singing songs, and met his fate to-day with the bravado which he has all along shown. The case has excited more interest on the coast than any murder that has occurred for years. Two attempts were made to lynch Goldensen during the two years which have elapsed since the murder, but in both cases the police succeeded in beating off the mob. A determined and able legal fight has been made for the prisoner, and it was only yesterday that all hope was abandoned.
alexander-goldensen-san-francisco.A16:
Alexander Goldenson.
Alex. Goldenson was hanged at San Francisco on Friday, Sept. 14th, for the murder of Mamie Kelly, a school girl 14 years of her husband. The murder occurred on the afternoon of November 10, 1886. Mamie Kelly was returning from school to the home of her grandmother, Mrs. Dora Sweeney, 22 Hayes street, chatting pleasantly with a companion, when, at the corner of Polk and McAllister streets, she was confronted by Goldenson, who was lying in wait for her at that place. He placed a pistol close to her head, fired and killed her instantly. The assassin then fled, followed by an angry mob of men who, if they had caught him, would have saved the State the expense of a trial and the Sheriff the trouble of hanging him. After committing the dastardly crime he added insult to injury by defaming the character of his victim, but the autopsy held on the remains proved Goldenson to be a liar, as well as a murderer. GOLDENSON'S BRAIN.
The Coroner Sued for the Deceased's Mental Machinery.
The Coroner Sued for the Deceased's Mental Machinery.
SAN FRANCISCO, October 31.—The parents of Alex Goldenson, who was recently hanged for the murder of Mamie Kelly, have commenced suit against Coroner Stanton to recover possession of the brain of deceased. After an autopsy was held the Coroner retained possession of the brain in order to refute any claim as so Goldenson's insanity that might be made in the future.

News Summary.
A fight took place between Russians and Americans near Tripp, Dakota. yesterday morning, in which the Americans were driven off. Two brothers named Johnson were wounded, one fatally, and four Russians are known to have been wounded. The fight was caused by an American farmer taking a goose in lieu of two chickens missed from a dozen he had bought at a public sale.

It is reported that a riot occurred on Tuesday morning, at Sackett's Mill, in Stafford county, Virginia, between whites and colored, growing out of a political dispute. A white man, named Bennett Hiflin, was killed, and a colored man was "badly mutilated." Many others were wounded.

A house in the eastern part of Rockingham County, Virginia, in which a number of colored people were having a party, was blown up by dynamite on Wednesday night. Several of the inmates are reported to have been fatally injured.

Michael O'Gars, aged 13 years, killed his 11-year-old brother, while hunting near Flemingsburg. Kentucky, on Wednesday. In attempting to shoot a rabbit Michael tripped and fell, the contents of both barrels being lodged in his brother's head.

White Caps in Hopedale, Ohio, gave Dr. John Parkhill, a leading physician, a terrible thrashing on Christmas night. His errand boy had been intoxicated, and the White Caps accused Parkhill of drugging him.

Michael Keattling, a messenger in the War Department in Washington, fell over the balusters on the fourth floor of the building on Thursday and was killed. The fall was about 80 feet. Keatting was intoxicated at the time.

A coal train ran into a passenger train on the Pine Creek Railroad, near Williamsport, Pa., on Thursday morning. The engine and several cars were wrecked and burned, and two men were injured.

John Hines, who was burned at the wrecking of the hall at East Prospect, Pa., on Christmas night, died on Wednesday night. The injured numbered 45, several of whom, it is feared, will die.

A farmer named Emory, living near Westfield, Dakota, had a quarrel with a cowboy about wages on Wednesday and was shot dead. A posse is pursuing the cowboy.

James Green, a prominent citizen of Wolcott, New York, cut his wife's throat yesterday and then cut his own. They will both die. Domestic trouble was the cause.

Michael Conley, 68 years o'd, of Conshohocken, while visiting his son in Philadelphia, was choked to death yesterday by a piece of meat lodging in his throat.

Snow fell in Iowa, Wisconsin and Dakota on Wednesday. Railroads in the vicinity of Waverly, Iowa, were badly blocked, but trains were running.

The postoffice at Sunbury, Penna., was robbed last night. The thieves got 76 cents. The office at Northumberland was also entered and 24 cents secured.
amos-moore-mcgaheysville-1888-12-26.A3:
BLOWN UP WITH A BOMB.
Dynamite Breaks Up a Negro Dance in the Old Dominion, and Fatally Injures Three Persons.
Fatally Injures Three Persons.
HARRISONBURG, Va., Dec. 28. — A dynamite cartridge, placed under the corner of a house near McGaheysville, in this county, Wednesday night, in which a party of negroes were having a dance, exploded and almost totally destroyed the building, and fatally injured Amos Moore and two women. A terrible loss of life would have happened if an alarm had not been given by a man who saw the cartridge, and recognized the danger. All but three escaped from the building before the explosion took place. Moore and the two women, who had not time to escape, were thrown with terrible force through the building. They cannot recover. Threats of lynching are freely indulged in.

amos-moore-mcgaheysville-1888-12-26.A11:
STREAKS OF LIGHTNING.
Mrs. and Miss Kate Power were killed yesterday in Chicago while crossing the R. I. track near 47th street.

Chinaman Loue Sing was hanged at San Francisco on the 28th for murdering his uncle.

Greater portion of Deloraine, Manitoba, was destroyed by fire Friday morning.

Presents to the value of $10,000 were distributed to the poor children of St. Louis on Christmas—all accumulated from ten cent subscription. J. J. Jennings editors of Post-Dispatch, originator of the scheme, was presented with a very costly gold watch by the citizens.

Prado, the murderer of Marie Aguetant, his mistress, was guillotined at Paris Friday morning. He protested his innocence to the last.

The Carter house, near McGansville, Va., in which a party of negroes were enjoying a dance, was blown to atoms by dynamite on Wednesday night. Amos Moore and two women were fatally injured.

A meeting of the National Wool-Grower's Association has been call for the 10th of January at Washington.
amos-moore-mcgaheysville-1888-12-26.A12:
POINTED PARAGRAPHS. Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.
Spicy Manner.

A tobacco association has been formed at Louisville, Ky.

Mrs. Merritt Owens, of Cincinnati, was assaulted and robbed while shopping.

J. A. Flinn was assaulted by the pastor of the Christian church at Columbus, O.

The residence of William Howard Neff, of Cincinnati, was destroyed by fire fire Friday.

Sylvester Smith, wanted for forgery and horse stealing, was captured at Wabash, Ind.

Martin Sullivan has been pardoned in Massachusetts after twenty-seven years' imprisonment.

Samuel G. Harbaugh, formerly state librarian of Ohio, died at Hagerstown, Md., on the 27th inst.

A report is current at New York that Chauncey M. Depew will be Gen. Harrison's secretary of state.

There is some talk at Columbus of Hon. Henry L. Morey as the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio.

The preliminary steps toward the formation of a wrapping-paper trust have been taken at Indianapolis.

Otto Lang's grocery at Frankfort, Ky., was robbed of $20 in money and a lot of goods Thursday night.

A colored man named Isaac Carey was murdered by his brother, in the Freedman's hospital at Washington.

The first convention of colored Catholic societies in the United States will be opened at Washington, January 3.

The loss of life by the Kate Adams disaster has been reduced, by a careful count, to nineteen or twenty persons.

Benjamin Ferguson was shot and killed, at Menter, Ind., by Francis Palmer. They quarreled over a trivial matter.

Christian Kalmbach, an Omaha saloonist, was assaulted by thieves as he was closing his place, and probably fatally injured.

C. C. Astwood, for six years past the United States consul at San Domingo, has been dismissed in disgrace from his position.

The explosion of a dynamite cartridge under a house near McGaheysville, Va., where a dance was in progress, fatally injured three persons.

Pete Morris, residing near Jellico, Tenn., attempted to kill an old man named Higdon, near Cumberland Gap. Higdon's daughter, Martha, fatally shot Morris.

Adam Chesrown, a witness in the Chesrown case at Ashland, O., was cross-examined for six hours by John McSweeney. Chesrown is now a raving maniac.

The annual banquet of the Massachusetts Tariff Reform league took place at Boston on the 18th inst. Secretary of the Treasury Fairchild was the principal guest.

Southern Republicans whose names are prominently mentioned for cabinet positions are Hendersen. of Missouri; Goff, of West Virginia, and Agnus, of Maryland.

Ex-Secretary Teller called on Gen. Harrison Friday. He was non-committal on the object of his visit. It is said, however, that he took occasion to pitch into Blaine.

Gen. G. B. Williams, on behalf of the Washington inaugural committee, had a conference Friday with Vice President-elect Morton, regarding inaugural ceremonies.

There are thirteen moonshiners in prison at Frankfort, Ky., and quite a number more en route, to be tried at the next term of the United States court, which begins January 7.

Henry Ashoff was jostled by three well-dressed men in a hat store at St. Louis, and afterward discovered that he had been robbed of $300. One of the men was arrested.

William E. McDermott, of Grant county, Indiana, has been arrested in Missouri, on a requisition, charged with the seduction of Miss May Holmes, the daughter of a Dunkard preacher.

Webb Brandon, wife murderer, was hanged at Winnipeg. He displayed great fortitude. The parting between him and his three children was affecting in the extreme. He killed his wife while drunk.

The printers, cigarmakers, carpenters, coal miners, boiler-makers, blacksmiths and plumbers of Danville, Ill., are holding meetings preparatory to the formation of the Danville Federation of Trades.

beaswell-beaswell-1888-08-26.A1:
NEWS SUMMARY.
Philadelphia Maniac on the Rampage-A Train Knocks Maggie Funzie 30 feet-Fall of a Derrick.
Dr Charles Sutleif entered the Sherman House, in Chicago, on Sunday, and brandished a knife, declaring that several men were following him. He chased the imaginary pursuers about the corridor for a time, and was then taken into custody. He is a graduate of a Philadelphia college, where his parents still reside.

As a picnic party were crossing a trestle on the Chicago and Northwestern Railway, near Janesville, Wisconsin, on Sunday evening, a freight train came along and knocked Miss Maggie Punzle to the rocks, 30 feet below. She was killed. The others escaped by crawling out on the end of the ties.

While a car was being raised to the track of the Michigan Central Railroad, at East Saginaw, Michigan, on Sunday, the derrick used for the purpose fell over into a crowd of sightseers. Two brothers named Collier were killed and several persons were badly injured.

The striking brakemen on the Wisconsin Central Railroad are reported to be causing much trouble in trying to prevent the running of trains. The first freight train since Saturday was sent out from Ashland under police protection yesterday. Two of the strikers were arrested.

William F. Clark, alias Colt, who has been arrested in New York for forgery, has, it has been discovered, been operating quite extensively. His forgeries will aggregate about $10,000, and his victims were large business firms.

At Williamstown, New York, on Sunday night, three farmers surprised a burglar while wrecking a safe. He dashed through a window and was shot and dangerously wounded in the side. He refuses to disclose his identity.

Up to date there have been about 115 cases of typhoid malaria in Bristol, Rhode Island, and about 12 deaths. The cause of the epidemic is said to be due to impure milk and water and a defective sewage system.

A negro was lynched near Rockmart, Georgia, on Sunday night. The body was discovered by the flagman of a train near a high trestle. No particulars of the affair are known.

The weavers of the woollen mill of the Harris Woollen Company, in Woonsocket, Rhode Island, went on a strike yesterday against heavy fines imposed by a new overseer.

A stock train ran into a herd of cattle near Fort Buford, Dakota, on Sunday. Seventeen cars of stock were ditched, killing thirty-five head. Two train hands were injured.

Charles A Doran, a clerk in a hardware store in Detroit, Michigan, was yesterday struck on the head by a box of hinges which fell down the hatchway, and fatally injured.

Thomas Lewis, a switchman, in Louisville, Kentucky, had his foot caught in a frog on Sunday night, and before he could release it was struck and killed by a locomotive.

The Republican State Convention of New York will meet in Saratoga to day. It is expected that ex-Senator Warner Miller will be nominated for Governor by acclamation.

Josef Dredzynski, a Polish lumber shover in Chicago, was fatally shot on Sunday by an unknown man who made his escape.

Robert and Ralph Mulvane, brothers, were fatally injured by the fall of a plasterers' scaffold at Canton, Ohio, yesterday.

As Michael F. Daly was about to open his butcher shop in Boston yesterday, he was fatally stabbed by an unknown colored man.

Adam Sherer was killed in Chattanooga, Tennessee, yesterday by a runaway team.

Afterward, when reproached for his conduct, the negro said that "he didn't care what they thought about it."

Saturday night between 11 and 12 o'clock a noise was heard on the trestle about 100 yards from the station, and the telegraph operator and night watchman went out to see what was the matter.

CALLED TO A HALT.

When they reached the end of the trestle they were met by several parties, who told them they could not go any farther, saying: "This is our business, and will be attended to all right."

An Exciting Contest Expected in the State next Tuesday.
Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR.

CHARLOTTE, N. C., Nov. 3.—Never in the history of North Carolina was politics known to be heated to such an extent as at present. In all parts of the state the greatest excitement prevails and the contest promises to be very close.

In this section the political craze is astonishing. Republicans have had federal supervisors of election appointed for many Western counties, including this (McKlemburg County). Many of these supervisors are negroes, and

WILL BE ARMED AT THE POLLS.

Tuesday. This has been the means of creating great indignaion among white voters and to add to the excitement Chairman Eames, of the state republican committee, has issued a circular saying he has employed Pinkerton detectives to be at every voting precinct in the state and declares that the republicans have a majority.

AND WILL CARRY THE STATE or fill Albany prison with North Carolina democrats. Many negroes in this section have openly declared their intention of voting with the democracy, and when one thus announces himself he is served with letters of warning ornamented with a coffin, and signed "Republican Ex. Committee."

black-charlotte-1888-11-02.A3:
GREAT EXCITEMENT.
NORTH CAROLINA DEMOCRATS WORKED UP TO FEVER-HEAT.
Negro Supervisors of Election—Pinkerton Detectives—Attempt to Lynch a Democratic Negro.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
HVLHETR. N. 41. November 3 —

CHARLOTTE, N. C., November 3.—The greatest excitement ever known in political circles prevails in this section. The Democrats are aroused as never before, and not a few are terribly indignant at the manner in which the Republicans are trying to play the bulldoze game upon them. Negro supervisors of election have been appointed at the instance of O. H. Dockery. Republican candidate for Governor, in this and many other western counties. It is also said there are Pinkerton detectives in this section watching the Democrats. Much indignation is manifested by all white citizens and their blood is hot. Rumors say the Republicans have been warned by their leaders to be ready for any emergency, and they have accordingly armed themselves. Many have illegally registered here to vote, and if they make the attempt they will be quickly nabbed and jailed. Reports from along the South Carolina line say the negroes there are registering in both States, expecting to cast a double vote. Many arrests will be made.

Last night a crowd of negroes caught a colored Democrat named Black and plead with him to return to the Republican fold. He refused, and they bound him hand and foot, then placed a rope about his neck, and were casting about for a limb to swing him up to when other parties came to his rescue. Some of the mob have been arrested.
black-charlotte-1888-11-02.A4:
THE SAMOAN KING DEPOSED. TAMESEE OVERTHROWN BY FRIENDS OF THE EXILED MALIETON.
Affairs in the Samoan Islands, which at different times within the last two years have threatened to get the United States and Germany into a snarl, have taken another interesting turn. There has been a revolution, a battle has been fought, a king has been deposed, and the interests of American merchants have been placed in jeopardy. Letters received yesterday from William S. Coppers of the United States steamship Adams have placed THE SUN in possession of an account of these events. The Adams was there at the time.

The Samoan Islands constitute one of the most important groups in the Pacific Ocean. The harbor of Pango-Pango is the key position of the Samoan group and also of Central Polynesia, and is valuable as the chief stronghold for the protection of commerce in South Pacific waters. The islands are in the path of vessels from San Francisco to Auckland, from Panama to Sydney, and from Valparaiso to China and Japan. They lie outside the track of hurricanes, and this helps to make them the most valuable islands in the South Pacific. Half way between Honolulu and Auckland, Pango-Pango is an accessible coaling and supply station for steamers, and with the Pacific mail steamers making it a port for coaling it would necessarily become the chief commercial place in that part of Polynesia. That is the view held by the Germans, the English, and the Americans, all of whom are interested in controlling the affairs of the islands.

The United States made a treaty with Maunga, the chief man of the Samoan tribes, in 1872. By that agreement the harbor of Pango-Pango was ceded to the United States, the condition being that the Government at Washington should become the Samoan protector. The general opinion of the natives was that it was best to have the favor of this Government rather than get into the grasp of Germany or England. The Germans had been making strenuous efforts to get the islands for themselves. The natives wanted firearms very badly, but the Germans would sell them none except for land. By this means the Germans acquired hundreds of thousands of acres. But they were unpopular with the Samoans, and when the port of Pango-Pango was given to the United States the Germans showed their irritation so plainly that the natives disliked them still more. Bismarck was fostering the interests of the German Commercial Company of the South Seas, and from 1872 on for a number of years the interference of Germany in Samoan affairs was constant and radical. Last year things came to a crisis. Malietoa was King and was friendly to American intorests. The Germans didn't like him. They had had a man-of-war there, and in August they brought a squadron. The German Consul and the German Commodore immediately began war upon Malietoa, and raised the German flag over the Malietoa Government house. There was riot and bloodshed, in spite of the joint protest of the American and English Consuls. The Germans at last, with the help of the followers of an insurgent chief, Tamesese, deposed Malietoa. Then Tamesese became King. Germany's seizure of Malietoa's sovereignty angered both the United States and the British Governments, and though the subject has been discussed by several powers there has been nothing final done to deprive the Germans of the foothold they have gained.

Te reign of Tamesese and the domination of the Germans have kept the islands in a turmoil ever since the events of 1887. The adherents of the deposed Malietoa never acknowledged Tamesese as King, and last August they gathered their strength to revolt against the new government. A body of the Malietoans came in contact with some Tamesesens at the end of August near Apia, the capital city. The fight lasted an hour, and there were four or five killed on both sides. After that the Malietoans gained in numbers and armament. They supplied themselves with efficient rifles, and built forts, which officers from the foreign war vessels in the harbor declared to be impregnable to attack from their opponents. Besides the chief fort of Foleula, there were several small works. The Malietoans received recruits daily. Their women joined them in preparing for battle. When the followers of the deposed King numbered nearly 5,000 they told the representatives of the foreign powers that they were going in to lick Tamesese and his supporters. They told Capt. Leary, the commander of the man-of-war Adams, the United States vessel stationed there to protect American interests, that they would die before they would give in to Tamesese. Capt. Leary said he was not going to interfere in native quarrels, but he warned them that in no event would he tolerate the sacrifice of life among the foreign residents. If that should happen he would have to make reprisals. The natives assured the Captain that if any of their people attempted to injure foreign residents or their property the offenders should be beheaded. Then the Malietoans got ready for the final conflict. The Germans had carried off Malietoa the year before in a ship and put him on a far-away spot in the Pacific, much as the English banished Napoleon to St. Helena. Malietoa's friends were therefore unable to make him King again. They found another man. Their choice was Mataafa. They elected him at their fort of Faleula. That made a Government in full opposition to Tamesese, the King favoring the hated Germans.

On Wednesday, Sept. 12, a party of 500 of the Malietoans attacked the Tamesesens in a fort at Matautu, near Apia. Some of the bullets hit the vessels in the harbor, and one of the crew of the German war ship Adler was wounded in the mouth. The crash of musketry was constant. The onslaught had begun at 12:50 in the afternoon, and from then until 2 P. M. it raged fiercely. A full came then, but the attack had spread to other forts, and the fight was soon as furious as ever. The soldiers of Tamesese were driven into the sea, some being shot down in the water and many taking refuge on reefs. Meanwhile the Tamesese party had sent for help, and when they had been driven to the reefs the reinforcements came in boats from Mulinu Point. Sharp firing followed between the boats at sea and the party on shore. It lasted fifteen minutes, but the distance was too great for the carrying powers of the guns, and little damage was done. The Tamesese troops rallied at 3 o'clock, but they were outnumbered and had to retire. Desultory firing continued until a little before 8 o'clock, when the Malietoa-Mataafa party advanced on a strong fort to the east of the battle area of the afternoon. This attack was made by moonlight. The besiegers captured the fort after a plucky defence of an hour. The garrison of the fort contrived to escape to their villages inland.

This finished the fight. It was a victory for the Malietoa-Mataafa party. Their opponents fled in utter rout. The victors did not follow, and after remaining on the battlefield until morning they marched in triumph into Apia. The foreign residents were out to see them. No acts of violence were committed. The followers of Tamesese, who had remained in town, withdrew to Mulinu Point, the headquarters of Tamesese. A company of marines from the German war ships went there, too.

The newly proclaimed King Mataafa followed up his victory by sending a despatch to the German Consul and the Captain of the German war ship asking them to remove the marines from Mulinu Point, and also to haul down Tamesese's flag, then flying at the Point. The two war ships in the harbor—the German and the American—maintained perfect neutrality during the fight. The only foreigner who was killed was Capt. Bissett of the schooner Vindex. He was walking to the British Consul's office while the battle was going on, and was hit by a stray bullet.

black-charlotte-1888-11-02.A5:
AT WHITE HEAT.
The Pot Boiling in Mecklenburg County.
Special to Wil. Messenger.

County.
Special to Wil. Messenger.
CHARLOTTE, N. C., Nov. 3.—Never in the history of Mecklenburg county was politics so heated as at the present time. Not only is politics the sole topic of discussion in this city, but throughout the county is all the talk. "Soap" from the Morton horde followed by threatening and most outrageous circular letters from Chairman J. B. Eaves, of the State Republican Executive Committee, has set the political pot boiling. But this is not all. Dockery has had Federal supervisors of election appointed for a number of the Western counties, including this, (Mecklenburg), many of these supervisors being negroes, who will stand armed at the polls to boss the voting. The excitement has run to highest pitch and every Democratic voter is fully aroused and will do his full duty until the fight is over. Republican "boodle" is being freely scattered here and the party is making the most desperate efforts to capture the county. A number of negroes will vote the Democratic ticket, and all who thus announce their intention are served with "Letters of warning" signed by the Republican Executive Committee. These letters are embelished with a coffin, and warn Democratic negroes that they must come back to the Republican fold or die before November 6th. A negro named Sid Black, was taken up by a crowd of nearly 100 armed men near here last night, and told he must come back to the Republicans or die. Black had announced himself a Democrat and stood firm in the face of the motly crowd, thirsty for his blood, who bound him hand and foot, put a rope about his neck, and was preparing to carry him away to swing. when he was rescued by other parties. Some of the mob has been arrested. Many negroes have registered here to vote illegally, and if they present themselves at the polls Tuesday will be nabbed and jailed. It is generally understood that nearly all the Republicans are arming themselves, and intend to use every possible means to dulldoze and frighten the Democrats, out in this section they will not be bulldozed by either threats, bullets or blood. Paties supposed to be Republican emissaries have been seen here but they lie exceedingly low. The white men in this section have had enough abuse heaped upon them by Republicans, and now to go further is not safe by any means. Many think this heated excitement will give the Democracy a larger majority in this section, than ever before. It has made this issue squarely, white men and negroes. C. P. Lockery has been swinging around here lately, but fails to make any converts to radicalism. The Democrats will have a grand torchlight procession here Monday night and "Zeb" Vance and Atkins will speak.

blevens-globe-1888-04-18.A1:
Lynchers Folled.
GLOBE, Ariz, April 13.—An attempt was made this morning about 1 o'clock by six masked men to break open the county jail, for the purpose, it is supposed, of taking out the two prisoners, Burnes and Blevens, and lynching them. The mob, after waking and holding up the night jailer, had taken off one lock and were working on the other, when the prisoners' cries gave the alarm, and the mob made their escape.
blevens-globe-1888-04-18.A2:
AN ATTEMPTED JAIL DELIVERY.
An unsuccessful attempt was made Friday morning, at 2:30 o'clock, by six masked men, to either lynch or release prisoners in the county jail—it is not known which. Hugh Blevins, night watchman, was called to the door of the outer corridor and upon asking "Is that you, George?" (meaning the Sheriff, George Shute) someone outside replied, "Yes, let me in." Mr. Blevins opened the door, when six masked men, armed with Winchesters, entered, forced Mr. Blevins into the inner corridor and placed a guard over him. The others then turned their attention to the cage, which they attempted to open and succeeded in taking off one of the locks. The second lock, however, they found more troublesome, and before they could accomplish their purpose, the prisoners had raised such a cry that the jail breakers were frightened off and left post haste. There are several theories afloat as to the object of the visit, all of which, however, are mere suppositions. Burns and Blevins, prisoners, claim to have recognized three or four of the visitors, who, they assert, intended lynching them.
blevens-globe-1888-04-18.A3:
TERRITORIAL ITEMS.
Figs are ripening upon the trees in many portions of Florence and vicinity.

Phoenix has three candidates for delegate to the Republican National Convention.

Winslow wants a lawyer, a physician, a minister, a bank and a jail. So says the News.

Yuma county shipped $25,000 in gold dust by Wells, Fargo's Express last year. A pretty good showing, considering the few men engaged in placering.—Sentinel.

It is stated that the Copper Queen folks at Bisbee, propose to build a railroad from Fairbanks to their town, and that operations will be commenced very soon and the road finished before next fall.

Chas. John Zimmerman, formerly of Woodland, California, an engineer in the railroad yards, was shot and instantly killed at Nogales last week by John Sherman, a barkeeper. The men had been quarreling.

In a fight resulting from a tiswin drunk, on Tuesday night last, two San Carlos Indians, (one belonging to Capt. Jack's band and one to Casador's) were killed. The murderer's were arrested and lodged in the guard house at San Carlos.

J. C. Herndon, Morris Goldwater and Bert Foster, of Prescott; L. W. Blinn, of Cochise, A. C. Baker, of Phoenix, P. J. Bolan, of Graham, and L. C. Hughes, of the Tucson Star, are named as possible delegates to the National Democratic Convention.
The Pasadena Mining Company has forty to fifty men at work on their gold mines in Carga Muchacho district. The mines supply twenty-five tons of ore to the mill at El Rio and is paying handsomely. J. F. Cupid is the Superintendent and W. Smith is in charge of the mill.—Sentinel.

In Globe on the morning of the 13th inst. an attempt was made by six masked men to break open the county jail, for the purpose of taking out the two prisoners, Barnes and Blevens, and lynching them. The mob was scared off by the cries of the prisoners.

At Tombstone last Friday Geo. Daves shot Pietra Emmonds and then committed suicide. Daves fired three shots at the young woman, one of which took effect in her shoulder, causing a serious and perhaps fatal wound. The cause of the tragedy was jealousy.

Juan Castinado, a young Mexican about twenty-eight years of age, killed himself at Clifton on the 9th inst. by shooting himself in the head with a Colt's 45 revolver. His afflianced had deserted him and in desperation he went to where she lived and ended his life.

Mr. and Mrs. J. A. Bright and their two children were poisoned yesterday morning, presumably by eating musty oat meal. They were all very sick for several hours, but were better when we went to press and believed by Dr. Porter to be out of danger.—Wilcox Stockman.

At the preliminary examination in Justice Meyer’s court of John Sherman, who shot and killed J. C. Zimmerman, better known as “Black Jack,” Justice Meyers rendered a verdict of justifiable homicide. Hereford & Lovell appeared for the defense. No testimony other than that adduced at the Coroner’s inquest was presented.—Tucson Citizen.

Albert Smith, a Casa Grande negro, stole one of Jim Woods’ horses a few days ago and left the place. Mr. Woods swore out a warrant for his arrest and took the train with L. Blomberg for Tucson and returned by next train with his man. He also recovered a portion of the money supposed to have been stolen from his safe a few weeks ago, amounting to between $200 and $300.—Enterprise.

Prof. Douglas, General Manager of the Copper Queen Mining Company, recently made a speech to the miners of Bisbee, in which he stated that wages would be $3.50 per day, that no work would be done in the mine on Sunday, and that there would be no regular pay day. The men could draw their money when they wanted it, or could let it remain with the company, as they pleased. This was done to discourage gambling.—Epitaph.
A Mexican seventy years of age named Jose Portillo, killed Juan Sanches on Monday, at Tuscon, by severing his head from his body. There had been a slight grudge between the parties. Sanches was visiting a house last evening where the old man was visiting with a friend, eating supper. As Sanches was about to seat himself his slayer sprang to his feet, seized the cleaver and with a single blow severed the head from the body. It is alleged that old Portillo is insane.

A gentleman recently from Prescott Junction brings the information that the Atlantic & Pacific Railroad Company has concluded to establish a division at Prescott Junction, and have already commenced the erection of the necessary buildings to be used for eating house, round house, etc. This will make the division headquarters of the Atlantic & Pacific in this Territory at Winslow, Prescott
blevens-globe-1888-04-18.A5:
ESCAPE OF A CONVICT.
Sheriff George Shute and deputy Sam Bullock, accompanied by Probate Judge E. H. Cook, left Globe on Wednesday last, with the prisoners Harry Blevins, Thomas Burns and Raphael Arvizu. Blevins and Burns were taken to Phoenix for trial, having obtained a change of venue to Maricopa county. Arvizu was to have gone to Yuma to serve a three years sentence in the Territorial prison for horse stealing. Upon reaching River-side, however, Arvizu "played roots" on the guard by feigning a necessity to retire to the brush in the immediate neighborhood of the station. He was permitted to retire and having reached the chapparel he vanished from sight, and upon being looked for by his late custodian, his tracks were the only visible signs discovered of his late presence. He, however, was seen by a person near the river, who gave the alarm, but the searchers believing that the halloo was an admonition to an unruly burro, no attention was paid to the outcry. The shackles had been removed from Arvizu's limbs, he having complained that they hurt his ankles; and consequently he was in a condition for expeditious traveling, and availing himself of his untrammeled stride he braved the river, and upon reaching an island was seen no more. The Sheriff was feeding his horses when Arvizu left the room.

Deputy Sheriff Frank M. Hammon learned from the driver of the Globe and Riverside buckboard, that Arvizu the Mexican prisoner, who made his escape there on Wednesday, was shackled when he left the room and managed in some way to free his limbs after reaching the brush, as he was not shackled when he swam the river.
blevens-globe-1888-04-18.A6: Sheriff Geo. E. Shute returned from Phoenix yesterday. He states that Blevins and Burns were acquitted on the charge of conspiracy. Burns who has about six weeks of a sentence imposed at the last term of court in Globe, yet to serve, was left in the custody of the Maricopa officials. as it was cheaper than to bring him back here.

dandy-hook-woodward-1888-05-17.A2:
Democratic Caucus BATON ROUGE, May 19.—The democratic caucus, after one ballot for junior, United States senator, adjourned till Tuesday. The vote was: White 37, Jones 35, Eustis 31, Blanchard 15.
Plot Against King Milan Thwarted. BELGRADE, May 19.—The police have seized documents revealing the widespread nature of the recently thwarted conspiracy. It was intended by the plotters to arrest King Milan and the leading public men of the capitol and install Prince Koragoergevick, on the throne, and also to promote a revolt in Bosnia. The conspiracy is attributed to Russian influence.

Horse Thieves Promptly Lynched.

WOODWARD, I. T., May 19.—A party of vigilants overtook and captured four men driving a herd of stolen ponies, in No Man's land, Thursday night. Two of the prisoners were noted criminals, known as Chetewood and Dandy Hook, and perhaps deserved their fate, but the other two protested their innocence, claiming that they were but employed to assist in taking care of the horses. Their story, however, was hooted, and all four were promptly lynched. The brothers of Chetewood, who belong to a band of notorious outlaws, have declared vengeance and say they will not leave the country until they have avenged his death. On the other hand vigilants have warned them to leave at once.

WILL Be Able to Take a Journey.

BERLIN, May 19.—The Emperor Frederick remained in the park from 5 to 7:30 o'clock yesterday evening, dividing his time between resting in the tent, and driving about in a pony carriage. The evening consultation of the doctors was held in the tent. On leaving the park, the emperor walked up the steps of the schloss, supporting himself by the balustrade. He was also able to visit the chapel. If the improvement of the past few days continues, he will go to Pottsdam after Prince Henry's wedding, and to Hamburg early in July. Prof. Viracho's formal report declares that the examination of the sputan discloses nothing of a cancerous nature.

Fame and Fashion Fill the Galleries.

WASHINGTON, May 19.—Long before the house met this morning every seat in the galleries was occupied. The fluttering of fans and bright costumes were heard and seen in great numbers, there being a few seats in the diplomatic gallery and front row of the executive gallery, reserved for the president and his family. At every door was a large knot of spectators, peering over the shoulders and under arms to get a chance at the floor upon which the long debate on the tariff bill was to be closed by Reed, of Maine, and Speaker Carlisle. The buzz of expectancy and hum of conversation were stilled for a moment while the chaplain offered prayer, only to break out afresh, when the clerk proceeded to read the journal. When the reading of that dreary document had been completed, the house went into committee of the whole, on the tariff bill. Baker, of Illinois, was first recognized. He said that yesterday, at the moment when he was out of the hall, words were spoken by a gentleman from Kentucky (Mr. Breckenridge) reflecting on his honor, reflecting upon the honor of his constituents. He then sent to the clerk's desk, and had read the remarks of Mr. Breckenridge reflecting upon the manner in which the defeat of W. R. Morrison in the 18th Illinois district had been accomplished.

Four Men, Driving a Herd of Stolen Ponies in No-Man's Land, Killed.

WOODWARD, I. T., May 19.—A party of vigilantes overtook and captured four men driving a herd of stolen ponies in No-Man's-Land Thursday night. Two of the prisoners were noted criminals, known as Chetwood and Dandy Hook, and perhaps deserved their fate, but the other two protested their innocence, claiming that they were employed to assist in taking care of the horses. Their story, however, was hooted at, and all four were promptly lynched. The brothers of Chetwood, who belong to a band of notorious outlaws, have declared vengeance and say they will not leave the country until they have avenged his death. On the other hand the vigilantes have warned them to leave at once.

Woodward, I. T., May 19.—A party of vigilantes captured four men driving a herd of stolen ponies, in No Man's Land on Thursday night, and lynched the whole party. Two of them were noted outlaws, known as Chitwood and Dandy Hook. Brothers of Chitwood have declared vengeance.

hem was one of the notorious Chitwood boys, who have been robbing, thieving and murdering for years in the neutral strip and in southern Kansas. It is doubtful if even the Benders were more cold-blooded or their crimes greater. One of the others lynched was a notorious criminal for whom, it is said, numerous rewards have been offered by Kansas authorities. He went under the name of "Dandy" Hook, but had a score of aliases. The other two were strangers in the strip and declined to give their names. They protested their innocence to the last, and there is no reasonable certainty that they were guilty. Stolen horses were found in their possession, but they claimed to have got them honestly. All were hanged on the charge of horse-stealing.

Heavy frosts were reported in Illinois, Iowa, Indiana and Michigan on the 15th.

FIVE HUNDRED of the Detroit Dry Dock Company's ship carpenters struck on the 15th because the company refused to discharge a man who did not belong to the union.

NOTES FROM BLACK'S.

BLACK's, January 30.—We are now having very cold and clear weather.

Nearly all the merchants of our town have hung out their red flags. They are selling out at cost. Most of them will buy a new spring stock.

The town authorities are having the streets repaired, a work much needed, as some of them are in very bad condition.

Mr. Joseph Black, who attends to the signal station, keeps us informed daily as to the weather.

Since the election the citizens seem to be satisfied and are giving the school their hearty support. They will use every effort to make the graded school a success.

A few days ago one of the drivers employed at Borders & Cline's livery stable, alighted from a buggy within a mile of town. When the horses found that no one had charge of them, they made a dash for home, going at a frightful speed through the streets. Several attempts were made to stop them, but without avail. When they reached the stables they ran over a buggy, breaking it to pieces.

David Bruce, who murdered W. R. Wilson, at Russellville, Alabama, a few weeks ago, was taken from jail last Friday night and lynched. The Supreme Court of Missouri has decided that the local option law of that State is constitutional. This establishes prohibition in thirty-four of the fifty-one counties, and eleven of the sixteen towns and cities that have voted on the question. George Edwards, a farmer, was shot and killed last Friday at Guyton, Ga., by a trap gun set in a store for burglars. He entered at one door, while the storekeeper was opening the other, in doing which the gun was discharged. Jim S. Semmes, who murdered Deputy Sheriff Outrey, near Tuscaloosa, Ala., was taken to Birmingham on Saturday, and placed in jail out of fear of the mob at Tuscaloosa. The Massachusetts Democratic executive committee unanimously endorses President Cleveland's tariff message. Near Amite City, La. last Saturday night, Ben. Edwards, colored, was lynched for brutally assaulting a white woman. In the city of Mexico the average winter temperature is 58 in the early morning, 68 at noon, and 55 at midnight. King John, of Abyssinia, claims to be a descendant of the Queen of Sheba. C., were taken from Plymouth jail, lashed to trees and riddled with bullets about one mile from town. BIRMINGHAM, Ala., June 27.—All yesterday and today it has been the talk throughout the city that an attempt would likely be made by a mob of his own race to lynch Doc Carnegie, the negro who was arrested and jailed Sunday for murdering his wife. But little credence has been given these conjectures, but tonight reports have been coming in from the negro quarters on the outskirts of the town that arrangements were really under way to march on the jail and take Carnegie at midnight. The police force is now on guard at the jail and all the deputy sheriffs have been summoned.

Jr., Lucein Odom and Eugene Coxe were on their way to McDaniel's mill to go in bathing. When near the East end of the dam they were met by a colored boy named Dock Dargan (a son of the well-known Essex Dargan) armed with a double-barreled shotgun. A few hurried words passed between Wm. E. Coxe, Jr., and Dargan, when Dargan raised his gun and fired, the ball entering the left breast and causing death immediately. Dargan then ran off, going in the direction of his home. He was arrested Sunday morning and lodged in jail. Rumors of lynching are heard, but the Sheriff will protect the prisoner until court meets in June. The deceased was in his twentieth year, and was the son of Mr. W. E. Coxe. Dargan had previously had a difficulty with one of the Coxe boys, and his mother brought out the same gun to him to shoot young Coxe. On Monday night some parties went to the house of Essex Dargan, father of the murderer, and fired into his house, it is supposed, purposely to kill the father, but instead killed an innocent three-year-old child.—Bennettsville Democrat.

MOUNT CARMEL, PA. May 6.—Between 10 and 11 o'clock last night a terrible accident occurred on the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad, between this place and Locust Gap. Freight train No 67, consisting of seventy-five cars, bound for Williamsport, became disconnected by the breaking of a coupling, and the engine and three cars ran half a mile before the crew discovered that the train was divided. The first section awaited the arrival of the second at the foet of a heavy grade, and the two brakemen losing control of the second section, it dashed into the first section, causing an explosion in the third car, which was loaded with Dupont powder. At the scene of the accident the railroad runs along a steep hill, at the bottom of which stood two rows of houses occupied by the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company's employees. On the hillside stood a little cottage occupied by John Quinn and his family of four children, two boys and two girls. The force of the explosion wrecked the buildings, seventeen in all, and the stoves set fire to the ruins. Quinn and his two little girls were burned to ashes. The two boys escaped with burns. Simon Kerwick's family consisted of Mary and Willie Cavanagh, adopted children, aged respectively 8 and 14 years, David Kerwick aged 8, Alice Kerwick aged 5 and his wife and a new born babe. Mr. Kerwick carried his wife from the burning building, but the children were burned to death. Thirty persons were injured. In all twelve cars were destroyed and seventeen houses, with their furniture. All the windows in the Locust Gap churches and schools were broken and the doors blown off. In Mount Carmel large store windows were broken. The loss is estimated at $75,000. Wrecking crews have the road open again for travel.

LAKE CITY, S. C., May 5.—Mr. J. Nolen Sauls, who lives about seven miles west of here, died suddenly, on Tuesday, of heart disease. He was a good, quiet, orderly citizen and a farmer of good standing. Mrs. C. C. Revel, his sister, who lives in Darlington, came to see him a few days before his death, and on Wednesday night sat up with the rest of the family until about midnight, when she retired. She did not get up as early as usual next morning, but no one thought strange of it until her baby was heard crying. Some of the family immediately went to see what was the matter, found the little fellow sitting by his mother weeping, and to their great surprise found her laying on her face in the cold and chilly embrace of death. As soon as the fact of her death was known Trial Justice H. P. Baldwing, of Scranton, immediately empanelled a jury of inquest, and found that she came to her death from heart disease.

CHARLOTTE, May 3.—Lizzie Ingle, a young white woman, was burning corn stalks in the field of J. F. Kerns, in Long Creek township, yesterday, when her clothes caught fire, and before assistance could reach her was so badly burned that she died in a few hours. A colored man arrived first, tore off the burning clothing, and went for help. Mr. Kerns, arriving twenty minutes later, found Miss Ingle standing erect, alone, burned almost to a crisp. The accident occurred at 3 P. M., and she died at 10 P. M. The deceased was 21 years old, and had recently moved to the neighborhood. She bore her sufferings without a murmur. The scene and circumstances are represented as pitiable in the extreme. The young woman bore a splendid character, and her fate is greatly deplored.

WALHALLA, S. C., May 5.—On yesterday morning Mrs. Clara Addis, an old lady about 69 years old, who was spending a few days with her son, near this place, was accidently burned to death. The family was in the field at work and no one was about the house to render her any assistance or to give the alarm. One of the family returned to the house about 9 o'clock and found her in the yard dead with all her clothes burned off.

LAURENS, May 5.—John Hill, a farmer, sixty-five years old, living near Clinton, in this county, committed suicide by hanging himself this morning. Hill was naturally weak minded and had lately lost his eyesight.

VIRGINIA CITY, NEV., May 4.—Jno. L. Black and Samuel L. SOUTHERN GOSSIP.
BOILED DOWN FACTS AND FAN- CIES INTERESTINGLY STATED.
The Atlanta Commonwealth is the name of Georgia's new prohibition paper.

The Times-Union newspaper, of Jacksonville, Fla., is a thing of the past, being absorbed into the News-Herald.

The United States fleet has left Pensacola and gone to New Orleans. It is likely the vessels will be sent to Cuba, as troubles are serious on the Island.

An immense crevasse has occurred in the west bank of the bayou at Lafouche Crossing, La., but it is thought there will be no serious damage to the crops.

Grave robbers are putting in their nefarious work at Athens, Ga. An attempt to steal the body of Simon Marks, a wealthy Hebrew, was frustrated.

The Tennessee Druggists' Association met in Chattanooga. Resolutions were adopted advocating the organization of a state pharmaceutical association.

John Barrett, an Atlanta, Ga., negro, was arrested for burglary by three detectives, and although handcuffed and closely guarded, dropped down a thirty-foot railroad embankment and made good his escape.

Col. Rule, of the Knoxville, Tenn., Daily Journal, newly elected commander of the department of Tennessee and Georgia, G. A. R., will deliver the memorial oration at the National Cemetery, at Marietta, Ga., May 30th.

At the target practice of the Lee Light infantry, at Opelika, Ala., Private John Simmons was struck in the forehead by a large piece of iron from a defective gun that burst while he was in the act of loading his piece.

Dock Dargar, a negro, killed a white boy named Coxe, of Bennettsville, S. C. The negro was jailed and an effort was made to lynch him but failed. At the house of Dargar's father, a row ensued and a child three years old was killed.

Quite a strike is in progress at the Pratt mines, at Birmingham, Ala. The company proposed to reduce wages five cents a ton and the miners resisted. The matter will be discussed by the board in a day or two. A strike is also on at the Wheeling mines.

A peanut trust has been formed in Norfolk, Va., embracing firms engaged in the peanut trade in St. Louis, Cincinnati, New York, Norfolk, Petersburg and Smithfield, Va., in fact, the entire peanut interest in the country, with the exception of three small factories.

Miss Annie Tillman, of Anson county, N. C., was sent to school at Greensboro, in the care of James McLaughlin, who was en route to the Union Theological school in Virginia. It was a case of love at first sight, and the couple stopped off at Charlotte and got married. The young lady is wealthy.

One of the most pleasant gatherings ever held in Atlanta, Ga., was the gathering of the Sunday-School children at Piedmont Park for a first of May celebration. Beautiful prizes were awarded for best recitations, etc. Nearly all the ministers and many prominent citizens took part in addressing the little ones.

A special tax levy on each dollar of taxable property in Chattanooga, Tenn., is the latest sensation furnished by the city council. An ordinance to that effect has been introduced and passed its first reading. The tax payers are indignant, and the exposure of extravagant expenditures is looked for.

John Robertson, deputy United States marshal, went to the room of Eugene Byer, of Enterprise, Ala., another deputy marshal, at a hotel there and renewed an old difficulty. Both men drew revolvers and began shooting. Lights were extinguished and Robertson was shot through the right lung and will die. Byers was not injured.

They captured three stills and arrested five moonshiners. One of the stills was located in Cleburne county and two in Clay. Fayette Hazel, Tom Jones, William Johnson, William Wigginton and George Albright were captured.

This and That.
A Brutal Murder.—Death brings sadness always. But there are times when his relentless hand crushes almost beyond a possibility of recovery the broken heart. Such was the case on Saturday, the 30th of April, 1888, when the gentle, lovely and pious Willie N. Coxe was brutally murdered by the hands of a young negro boy, in open daylight, in the public road, near McDaniel's Pond, in Marlboro County, S. C. Willie was a youth of twenty Summers; had gone to Bennettsville and enrolled his name as one of the military company at that place; subscribed for the first time for himself for one of the County papers—of which the first number or copy contained his sad death. He was a youth of noble aspirations, having determined to obtain an education if possible, and had just received a catalogue of College. He joined the Methodist Church at Ebenezer in the Summer of 1882, under the ministry of Rev. John C. Kilgo, and lived up to his profession so closely as to win the saying of those who knew him as "the best boy among us." He met the negro while on his way home from Bennettsville, and there was hardly time after meeting for the usual salutation when the negro fired his gun, killing Willie instantly. As the murderer is in custody of the proper authorities, I forbid further comment by my pen. Thank God for Willie's life; and, though shot down without a moment's warning, we have a good hope that he was prepared to meet his God in peace. GEO. M. BOYD. Blenheim, S. C., May 7, 1888.

Florence District Conference.—This body, composed of thirty-nine preachers—itinerant and local—and seventy-eight lay delegates, will meet in the Methodist church at Kingstree on Wednesday, the 30th inst., at a quarter past 8 o'clock P. M. After religious services the Conference will be organized. Rev. J. K. McCain will preach the Conference sermon on Thursday, at 11. The first business session will be held on Thursday morning, at 9 o'clock. It is hoped that all the members, clerical and lay, will be present at the beginning, and remain to the close. The reports from the charges will embrace: The spiritual condition of the Church, the work of the Sunday schools, missions, the financial systems in operation in the several Circuits and stations, and the condition of church buildings and parsonages. The preachers in charge will see that their respective Quarterly Conference Journals are in the Conference room on Thursday morning. Reduced fare on the several railroads leading to Kingstree. It is hoped that Bishop Duncan will preside, and that Wofford College, Columbia Female College and THE SOUTHERN CHRISTIAN ADVOCATE will be represented. The list of subscribers to THE ADVOCATE in this District is steadily growing, and we will confidently expect you, Mr. Editor, to represent its claims on that occasion to the universal patronage of our people hereabout. Preachers in charge will please not omit to carry to the Conference the full amount assessed for Bishops on their respective charges.

Wm. C. Power, P. E.

WIRE GAUZE FOR COTTON BALES.—A letter was received at the cotton exchange yesterday from Tennessee to the effect that a new kind of wrapper for baled cotton was about to be placed upon the market. The new envelope consists of a fine wire gauze, which has been, it is claimed, subjected to all kinds of tests, including hooks and compressions, and it has proved equal to jute bagging in every respect. A great advantage claimed for it is that it is almost or quite fire-proof. The correspondent states that he has built fires under a bale of cotton encased in this wrapper and heaped live coals of fire on top of it, without even scorching the cotton. The price of the new material is at present about the same as that charged for jute bagging under ordinary competition, but it is thought it might be made considerable lower by a large demand. The matter attracted a great deal of attention at the cotton exchange yesterday, and much favorable comment was heard. The board of managers will take under consideration at its next meeting the advisability of accepting cotton when incased in this new envelope. Nothing definite can be done, howeyer, until the buyers of Bremen and Liverpool consent to accept the new wrapping.—[New York Times, 14th.

THE GALLOWS.—Alexander Goldensen, who shot and killed a fourteen-year-old school girl, named Mamie Kelly, on November 10, 1886, was hanged in the county jail yard at San Francisco, Cal., at noon last Friday. No hanging since the days of the vigilant committee has excited greater interest on the Pacific coast. His crime came near causing a riot and two attempts were made to lynch him by assaulting the city jail, but in each instance serious disorder was prevented by the police. Notwithstanding the popular indignation against young Goldensen, the legal fight in his behalf was prolonged for nearly two years. The murderer's last night was passed in drinking, card-playing and blasphemy. The only known cause for his shooting his victim was her refusal to accept his attentions. Goldensen was 18 years old when he committed the murder and was a person of vicious habits.

Dock Dargan, colored, who killed Will C. Cox, a white youth aged about 18 years, was hanged at Bennettsville, this State, on Friday morning. The murder was committed on the 28th of last April. The condemned man ascended the gallows at eighteen minutes to 11 o'clock and remained perfectly calm. On being asked by the sheriff if he had anything to say, he replied that he had nothing to say except that he wanted to be hanged at once. His neck was not broken. He died from strangulation within twenty minutes and his body was cut down at 11.28.

LOCAL NEWS. ANOTHER MOB. They take Ell Davey from the Traits and kill Him. He was Charged with House Burning.
The 4 o'clock train, Thursday morning, was halted between Woodland Mills and State Line by a squad of disguised men, and a prisoner. Eli Davey, charged with burning the tobacco barn of Mr. Louis Browder, and who was being conveyed to the county jail at this place, in the custody of Constable Winstead, taken therefrom, and killed.

Davey was a colored man, and charged as above stated with burning Mr. Browder's tobacco barn, which was burned on the 5th of March. His examining trial was held before Esquire Bonz, in Fulton, on Wednesday, and the evidence though circumstantial was strong, and the court held him to answer before the next term of the Circuit Court, and failing to give the required bond, ($500), he was committed to the county jail.

It is said that after the examining trial, in which he plead not guilty, that Davey confessed his guilt.

In Fulton, after the trial, open threats of lynching the prisoner was made, and made to such an extent that County Attorney Murrell, made an earnest appeal in behalf of the prisoner, begging that the law be permitted to take its course. Constable Winstead, apprehending danger, announced that the prisoner would be kept in the city lock-up Wednesday night and carried to Hickman the next morning, the idea being that the mob would form, raid the lock-up at night, but that in the meantime the officers would carry the prisoner by the night train to the county jail, and thus the lynching be averted. In some way the lynchers got hold of the program, and intercepted the Constable and his prisoner as above stated. About a dozen masked men entered the train, armed with shotguns and pistols, and there appeared to be about as many more on the outside. Constable Winstead plead for his prisoner and the law, and did all he could reasonably be expected to do for his protection, and when the prisoner was forced from the train, he went off with them, and was still pleading with the mob when the train pushed off.

Besides the burning of Browder's barn, with about $600 worth of tobacco in it, there have been two other houses recently burned in that portion of the county, supposed by many to be the work of an incendiary, the house of Mr. Liep, and the house of Mr. Wm. Campbell, and in the latter an unfortunate son of Mr. Campbell was burned alive. Hence, the community was wrought up to a high feeling against the offender. We do not know that the prisoner was accused of the last named fires, but the air is full of implications in regard to them.

—Gus. Bass, the old celored citizen who fled from Hickman, in tight, the day the news was received of Cleveland's election, has returned. The old fellow was possessed of the idea that Cleveland proposed to kill all the old negroes and sell the young ones back into slavery. We suppose he now realizes how egregiously designing politicians deceived the colored people. At any rate he comes back, Cleveland hasn't had any of the old negroes killed, nor any of the young ones sold, and, to all appearances, the race are getting along about as well under Democratic rule as they did under the Republicans.

—Fulton County Democratic Committee is without a Chairman. The members of the Committee ought to meet and recommend some one for the position. The Kentucky Democracy must make things hum all along the line the coming presidential campaign, and bring our State majority back to the old-time figures—50,000. Democrats have stayed at home on election day, and negroes multiplied, until these Republican fellows are getting disagreeably close up to the top round of the ladder. The last State election made Democrats mad, and this year they are going to vote.

A steam laundry was not located at Mayfield, because water could not be had in sufficient quantities; and the Mayfield Monitor thus comforts its people: "All right, me darlint, just wait until our artesian well is completed, until the canal connecting the Mississippi and Tennessee rivers is constructed, until Paducah and the Ohio river are removed to Mayfield, until the great government fish-pond is located here, until the bowlegged steamship canal is extended from Nicaragua to our city, then we will flash you a cablegram to "Come along, me Ducky.""

A vigilance committee has organized in Dresden, composed of twenty-two determined citizens, to suppress the "jug line" that has been carried on for some time between Martin and that place. Posters have been stuck up in conspicuous places announcing that parties caught smuggling whisky in such a manner will be tarred and feathered and given thirty-nine lashes.

A Negro Barn Burner Hanged Up by a Mob.

UNION CITY, Tenn., March 16.—Yesterday morning Eli Davie, a negro barn burner, was found a short distance from the depot at Woodland Mills ornamenting the limb of an oak tree. The facts as gathered from W. J. Winstead, an officer who was carrying the negro to jail at Hickman, Ky., are as follows: Tuesday night, March 6, the barn of Lewis Browder, a prominent and wealthy farmer, who lives about six miles from Fulton, Ky., was destroyed by fire with all its contents, consisting of nearly 1,000 pounds of tobacco, and machinery amounting to fully $3,000. The excitement in the county was very great, and immediately a reward was offered by the authorities for the apprehension of the fiend. On Tuesday Davie was arrested, while hiding in a straw stack, by four other negroes, and carried to Fulton, where he had a trial, and was sent to jail in default of bail. W. J. Winstead, who was ordered to carry the prisoner to jail, reached Woodland Mills, in this county, this morning about 2:30 o'clock. When the train stopped six masked men boarded it and demanded the prisoner. The officer drew his pistol and told the men they could not take him. He was caught from behind by a man who had entered the rear door, and the mob took the negro and carried him to a tree about 300 yards from the depot and hung him. An inquest was held this morning, and the jury found a verdict that an unknown negro had been found, and that he came to his death at the hands of unknown parties. The negro confessed that he burned the barn, but said it was accidental. The hanging occurred in Obion county, but the Kentucky boys did the job.

Death of a Schoolmate of General Grant.

RIPLEY, O., March 29.—William Maddox, an old pioneer of this place, died this morning of softening of the brain. He was born in Adams county in 1821. — The Presbyterians of the United States will hold in May a centennial celebration in honor of the completion of the first century of the Church's existence in this country. When the Church was organized in America it had 16 Presbyteries, 177 ministers, 419 churches, and 10,000 members, while to-day it has 389 Presbyteries, 8,328 ministers, 11,212 churches and 750,000 members.

— George N. Hawes died at Millersburg, Ky., last Thursday. During the cholera scourge of 1849 young Hawes had a violent attack of cholera and to all appearances died. He was placed in his coffin, but during the funeral services he recovered consciousness and arose. Since that time he has lived a recluse. He remained in an upstairs room for over five years, and was never known to speak to any one during that time.

A colored man named Hamilton was arrested in Savannah four years ago charged with the murder of the Haertel family. The evidence against him was strong but not sufficient for conviction and he was released. He was employed in the work of tearing down the old jail, and on Saturday, while he was digging at the foundation directly under the cell he occupied while under arrest, the bank caved in on him and a timber fell on him and broke his neck.

A Nogales, Arizona, dispatch says: The recent seismic disturbances and subterranean noises along the Pacific slope in Mexico, have terrified those who remember the earthquake of last May. The people are moving out of the dangerous localities by hundreds. Ever since the first severe shock, on May 3, 1887, the noises and tremblings have continued with increasing violence. The indications of the coming of a serious earthquake or of the bursting forth of a volcano are shown by the peculiar moisture of the earth and the appearance of hot springs which usually precede such disturbances.

A Memphis dispatch of Thursday says: News received here to-day from the Sledge and Mason plantations, a few miles below Australia landing, tells of a killing and lynching which occurred there on Saturday last. Robert Taylor, a white man, shot and killed a negro who attempted to strike him. Another negro, who became involved in a game of cards and cut with a razor a very popular negro, was lynched by men of his own race. They put a rope around his neck and dragged him a hundred yards or so through a creek and up on a levee, where they swung him to a tree.

Prof. John M. Langston, of Virginia, has joined ex-Senator Bruce and Fred Douglass (all negroes) in opposing the scheme to bring about a negro exodus to South America. He thinks the proposed exodus is a fraud from first to last, and that there is no need for it. The negro, he says, is advancing slowly and surely in this country, and cannot better himself by any other country. Langston was for seven years Minister to Hayti, where he saw enough to convince him that negroes are not yet prepared to live in communities by themselves where they have to manage their own political affairs.

On Tuesday of last week, Charles E. Cross, the president, and Samuel C. White, the cashier, of the State National Bank of Raleigh, N. C., absconded, taking a large amount of the funds of the bank with them. They were speedily traced to Toronto, Canada, where they were shadowed until the affairs of the bank were examined; and it being soon ascertained that they had committed extensive forgeries, indictments were obtained against them and they will be extradited and tried in the Wake superior court for that crime. When arrested in Toronto they had with them about $24,000 in cash. It is said their forgeries will reach over $50,000.

Last Friday closed the sixth week of the trial at Brandon, Miss., of Col. Hamilton for the murder of the young Prohibition editor Gambrell. The sensation that day was caused by the Court ordering the sheriff to search every person applying to be admitted into the court room Saturday morning, saying that if any pistols or other deadly weapons were found that he would visit the severest punishment in his power. Since the trial began it has been a notorious fact that the partisans of both sides had pistols in their pockets, and since the trouble between the opposing lawyers, a few days ago, in which the Sheriff prevented blows, a row has been imminent.

The prohibition people of North Carolina have decided to assert themselves during the campaign of this year, and have issued a call for a State convention to be held in Greensborough on May 16 next. The call states the business of the convention to be the election of twenty-six delegates and as many alternates to attend the National Prohibition Convention to be held at Indianapolis June 6, the selection of eleven candidates for Presidential electors, the nomination of a full set of candidates for State offices, the election of a State executive committee, and the full and complete organization of the State.

In an address recently delivered by Major E. A Burke, of the New Orleans Times-Democrat, facts are produced which indicate that the losses in recent years of Southern farmers in the value of their farms have been attended by a large transfer of capital to manufacturing enterprises of various kinds. The number of factories in the South in 1887, according to Major Burke, was 54,176, as against 34,563 in 1880. Capital in factories increased in the period indicated from $179,366,000 to $371,285,000, and the product from $315,024,794 to $529,- 835,000. Despite the fall in prices of farm products there has been an increase of the amount produced, the figures for 1887 being $745,050,696, as against $612,278,318 in 1880.

WILD DOINGS IN THE SOUTH.
The Bloody Work of a Band of Black Ku-Klux.
By the steamer Kate Adams news of some rather wild doings in Bolivar county, Miss., last week has been received, that, owing to the remoteness of the river from the telegraph and railroad mail service, has failed to reach here sooner. It seems that about the middle of last week the negroes on the plantation just south of Australia landing, in Bolivar county, had a grand bail. This bail was enriched with that usual accompaniment of colored fandangoes, which ended in a fracas among the crap shooters. One burly rutilan, in his eager haste to pink his successful opponent with a leaden bullet fired wide of his mark, and lodged the fatal missile in the body of a bystander, causing his instant death. Of course this broke up the game of craps, but did not complete the tragedy. The shooter was arrested and confined in a neighboring saloon, under guard of a negro officer, to await an opportunity of removing to the jail at the county seat, some twenty miles. It so happened, however, that the slain darky was a very popular man among his race, and his enraged partisans lost no time in organizing a mob to ku-khlux the murderer. But when the time came to use the rope their hearts failed them, and the mob retired, with many mutterings, for the night. On the next night, however, they had gained confidence from numbers and reflection and proceeded to lynch the victim of their displeasure in the most approved style.

Procuring a good rope, they surrounded the saloon, and compelled the surrender of the trembling prisoner, which was done without resistance by the officer. Fastening the rope firmly around one foot, they threw the shackled negro to the ground, and gathering the rope in winning hands, dragged the struggling wretch on his back across the levee and to a convenient tree several hundred yards away, where, amid brutal curses and jeers, they quickly drew him up in mid-air by a rope around his neck and left him hanging. The mob then quietly dispersed to their homes. As in this case both ku klux and victim were Republicans, the hanging will hardly be heralded by the Northern press to the country as a Southern outrage, though the result is the same, viz: The Republicans have been deprived of a voter, and when the authorities have settled with the lynchers it will probably have lost several more. —Memphis Avalanche.

gallup-gallup-1888-02.A1: Mrs. Lieutenant Glassford brings word of a deed of violence committed at Gallup, New Mexico, while the train was there, on which she was a passenger.
