gus-williams-bagdad-1888-09-03.A1: On Monday morning last the Coroner was informed that a colored man by the name of Gus Williams, who came here sometime ago from about Washington, La., was dead near Grout's shingle mill in Bagdad. A. J. Perkins, Jr., M. D., in his official capacity as Coroner, proceeded at once to the spot and viewed the body, and the jury summonsed in the case rendered a verdict to the effect that he came to his death by a pistol or gunshot wound in the hands of unknown parties. The particulars in the above killing, as near as could be obtained by an Echo reporter, are about as follows: The fact became known on Sunday evening that a rape had been committed on a little white girl in Bagdad, and quite a number of citizens met for the purpose if possible of ascertaining who was the guilty party. Everything pointed to Gus Williams as the guilty party, and he was accordingly arrested, confessed his guilt and the crowd started to jail with him when he was fired upon by some one unknown with the above results.
gus-williams-bagdad-1888-09-03.A2:
A Brutal Crime and Swift Retribution.
On Saturday last Bagdad, in this parish, was the scene where one of the most heinous crimes known, was committed by a burly negro on a little white girl six years of age.

Gus Saddler, a negro, about 19 years of age, hailing a few months ago from St. Landry parish, made a criminal assault on a little white girl at Bagdad on Saturday, and threatened to kill her if she told any one. Sunday; however, the pain becoming unbearable, she told the particulars to her parents. The report spread and in a few hours many of the citizens of West Lake Charles and Bagdad assembled and arrested the negro, tied him hard and, putting a rope about his neck, pretended they were going to hang him, for the purpose of making him confess, which he did fully. As they were about to start to turn him over to the sheriff, some unknown party shot him through the head, causing death instantly.

Dr. Perkins, coroner of the parish, was called and viewed the body on Monday, and on Tuesday a coroner's jury was impanelled, and, after examining sixteen witnesses, the jury's verdict was; "death caused by a shot through the head by an unknown party." The body was turned over to the negro's relatives who sent it to St. Landry. The child; at last accounts, was doing well. These are the facts that our reporter was able to ascertain.

NORTH CAROLINA NEWS.
There are 1,062 Farmers' Alliances in the State.

The next Pharmaceutical Association will be held in Durham.

Mr. W. A. Guthrie, of Durham, has accepted the Republican nomination for Supreme Court Judge, vice Judge Russell declined.

The State Farmers' Alliance met at Raleigh last Tuesday at 12 o'clock in Metropolitan Hall, and was called to order by President S. B. Alexander.

In Granville county on the 31st of July, Eliza Ann Adcock died from poison administered by her husband and his brother's wife. It is a black affair. The perpetrators of the crime are in Oxford jail, making in all fifteen in Oxford jail to be tried for their lives at the next term of Granville court, says an exchange.

Charlotte Chronicle: Mr. Pride, secretary of the fair association, yesterday received a telegram from Sergeant-at-Arms W. P. Cannady, stating that Senator John H. Gease, of Iowa, and Senator B. W. Perks, of Kansas, had accepted the invitation and would be at Mount Holly next week to deliver protection speeches.

Raleigh Signal: Our venerable fellow-citizen, Col Paul Cameron, has given an order to Mr. Geo. B. Hiss, the stirring and energetic manager for the firm of Van Gunden & Young in this city, to grade off the side walk and build a stone wall, with dressed stone coping, the entire length of the Hillsboro street boundary of the St. Mary's School property. If all our wealthy citizens would follow the Colonel's example Raleigh's beauty will be better appreciated.

Morganton Star: We are glad to be able to quote from good authority that Col. Chas. Price has signified his intention to support Hon Daniel G. Fowle for Governor. We look upon this as a ten stroke for Judge Fowle and the Democratic party. Col. Price is considered one of the brightest lights, intellectually, in the State, and could have received the nomination at the last Republican Convention for Governor if he had suffered his name to be run. He is assistant counsel for the R. & D. Railroad, and is one of the best lawyers in the State.

Durham Plant: J. S. Lockhart and C. B. Green, who went to Washington to invite speakers to the Durham Exposition, report that they received every assistance at the hands of Senators Vance and Ransom, who manifested a disposition to do anything in their power for the success of the occasion. Messrs. Lockhart and Green received assurances that our Senators will attend the Exposition and were encouraged to hope that Gov. J. B. Gordon, of Georgia, Senator John W. Daniels, of Virginia, and Hon. S. S. Cox, of New York, will also come.

Raleigh News Observer: Chairman Whitaker received intelligence yesterday that Mr. Sanderlin had been taken very ill and had been forced to discontinue the canvass and go home. His malady is of such a serious nature that it is feared he will not be able to resume his appointments for several days. The announcement is received with general regret everywhere, and there is great disappointment among numbers at various points who have been looking forward to hearing Mr. Sand derlin. By his jovial bearing and irresistible charm of manner he has captivated all wherever he has been. His return into the harness will be hailed with pleasure everywhere.

Old John Robinson, the show man, died in Cincinnati the other day. He was aged 82. His property was valued at from three to four million dollars.

The Vance Guards are arranging for a grand military ball one night next week. It is intended to make it a pleasant and successful affair in every way.

There has been an excess of rain during the past two weeks. The crop outlook was gloomy enough before, but now it is worse. The rain has damaged tobacco more than the drought did, some farmers tell us.

"The cup of sin is sparkling at the top but there is death at the bottom." The same may be said of the cup of wine, if indulged in too freely—and the habit of drinking once begun, who knows where it will end?

Miss Alberta Gallatin is by all odds the best performer in her line in the country. She put an admirable amount of bright airiness into her part, and was graceful and fascinating.—Boston Advertiser.

Secure your tickets for Romeo and Juliet, at Burwell Hall Saturday evening.

This is from the New Orleans Picayune: "Among the candidates in North Carolina is a Fowle for Governor, a Holt for Lieutenant Governor, a Finger for Superintendent of Education and a Bunn for Congress. If Fowle gets Holt with a Finger he will take the Bunn."

Wake Forest College has opened with the largest attendance ever had at the beginning of the season. One hundred and seventy students is the number enrolled. Several others have gone in since. The Baptists have just cause to be proud of such an institution of learning.

The ladies are first and foremost in every good work, and the Oxford Orphan's Friend throws out the following timely hint to them. It says:

The ladies of North Carolina will please bear in mind that the cold winter is coming on and that we have 240 children to make comfortable. Just one day's work for us now will do you and us good. Try it and see.

Barnes, Stainback & Co's new store in the Young Block is really one of the handsomest mercantile establishments in town. The room is well lighted and their stock is shown off to good effect day or night. They have it stocked with one of the largest and handsomest assortments of clothing, hats, shoes, neckwear, gents' furnishings, etc., in Henderson.

Help us spread the Gold Leaf. Say a word to your neighbor in behalf of the paper and get him to subscribe. There are many more improvements we wish to make, but can only go forward as our patrons enable us. The Gold Leaf is yet short of what we wish it to be, but a little assistance from its friends in the way of influencing others to become patrons will help us to go forward.

The Adcocks (Henry C. and Jennie C.), charged with poisoning the wife of Henry in Granville county last month, passed through here yesterday in charge of an officer for Raleigh. The case has been removed from Granville and will be tried at Vance court in October. It was thought best to remove them to Raleigh for safe keeping in the mean time. Our people re-great that this case is to be tried here.

Miss Alberta Gallatin plays her roles charmingly and is a perfect picture of refined womanhood. The lovers of good plays, well acted, should not miss the chance of seeing her. —Memphis Appeal.

Miss Gallatin will appear at Burwell Hall Saturday evening in the beautiful Shakespearean character of Juliet. Our citizens should not fail to see her. Reserved seat tickets 75 cents; at Harris' drug store.

The excessive rains it is thought will prove very damaging to crops. Tobacco has been much injured, cotton is rotting in the bolls, is badly soiled and otherwise damaged, and peas are sprouting in the hulls in some cases. The winds have blown corn down and torn tobacco leaves to some extent. Altogether the outlook for the average farmer has been made far more gloomy during the past ten days.

Miss Alberta Gallatin carried off the honors of the evening. Her acting stood out in bold relief; she had animation, grace, freedom and a fascinating manner, combined with a musical voice and pretty face, which captivated her audience and earned her much applause. —Brooklyn Union.

Romeo and Juliet, the first one of Shakespeare's plays ever put upon the boards in Henderson, will be presented by this company Saturday night. Secure your tickets.

Justice S. H. Allen claims that two Novelty Force Pumps loaned from the Gold Leaf office on the night of the fire, saved the rear end of the Cheatham building on Main street (Harris' drugstore) from burning. Standing inside, behind the walls, persons using the pumps could throw water just where it was needed to keep the flames from reaching the woodwork on the windows and eaves of the house. Every property owner should have one of these little pumps. They cost only $2.50.

A Lively Fight in Elizabethtown— Damage to Cotton—Murder Trials, &c.
Trials, &c.

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

SALEGH. N. C. September 12 — I

Damage to Cotton—Murder Trials, &c.

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

RALEIGH, N. C., September 12.—Last night at Elizabethtown, Bladen county, there was a fight in which Editor R. S. White, of the Beacon newspaper, Alexander McDonald, Donald A. McDonald, and Edward McDonald were engaged. White was set upon and badly beaten. He shot Alexander McDonald, inflicting a wound which is considered fatal, and he also shot Donald McDonald in the arm. The cause of the trouble was the publication by White in his paper of an article making severe comments on Alexander McDonald, who is register of deeds of Bladen county. McDonald is a Republican and is a candidate for reelection. Donald and Edward McDonald are his sons.

DAMAGE TO COTTON.

It is learned here to-day that wet weather has had unusual effect in discoloring cotton in unopened bolls. Bolls were broken open and the cotton inside was found yellow. If this is extensive the loss will be very great indeed. It was the subject of considerable comment here to-day.

THE JOINT CANVASS.

Judge Fowle to-day authorized his representative, R. H. Battle, to say that in continuing the joint canvass he would go to any of the counties in which neither Dockery nor he had spoken. Battle is Fowle's referee, while T. R. Purnell is Dockery's. It is expected that arrangements will be made for thus continuing the joint canvass.

News was received to-day that the county bridge at Haw river had been swept away by the freshet, and that the county bridge at Belden's, on Haw river, was wrecked.

THE STATE NATIONAL BANK.

Receiver Dowd, of the State National Bank, said to-day that he had not yet collected any money towards the payment of the second dividend on the bank. It will require a fight to collect every dollar now. It takes $80,000 to pay a 20 per cent, dividend like the one already paid. He expects to get another dividend of some size, but thinks that will be about all. He says he may be able to get 30 per cent, more. His first idea was that the bank would pay fifty cents on the dollar, but he now thinks forty cents is about the figure.

All damage done on the Richmond and Danville railway by the floods is all repaired, and trains are to-day running regularly. Through mails are still out of gear somewhat.

Final arrangements were made to-day for the tobacco exposition at Durham. The success of the affair is assured.

SUDDEN DEATH AND MURDER.

John H. Johnson was drowned in Goose creek, Pamalico county, day before yesterday by falling from his schooner.

Anna Ellis and William Ellis murdered their father, Allen Ellis, in Sampson county. Very meagre accounts of the affair have been received.

The Telephone Exchange will be at once established at Durham.

J. L. Watkins and R. H. Wright have purchased the Durham Woollen-Mills and will operate them.

FIRE AT YANCEYVILLE.

A fire, possibly of incendiary origin, at Yanceyville Sunday night burned the stores of J. W. Vaughan, Florence Harrison & Co., and George O. Wilson & Co., causing a loss of $18,000, with $8,000 insurance.

John B. Eaves, chairman of the Republican State Executive Committee, came here to-day and held a conference with Republicans here on the campaign.

TO BE TRIED FOR THEIR LIVES.

The Superior Court of Granville county is in session. It is the most remarkable term ever held, for no less than twelve persons are to be tried for their lives—five being women, one a white woman. Two are charged with arson and ten with murder. The Adcock poisoning case is of special interest. Henry Adcock and Jennie C. Adcock are charged with poisoning Henry's wife. The Adcocks concerned in this matter appear to be dissolute and degraded people. Dr. H. B. Battle, State chemist, left for Oxford to-day, upon a subpoena as a witness in this poisoning case. Dr. Eugene Grissom, superintendent of the insane asylum here, is also an expert in a case of a negro man charged with murder. It is alleged that the man is insane.

SAVED FROM LYNCHERS.

Henry Adcock and Jennie Adcock were brought here securely tied to night and quietly taken to jail by the coroner of Granville county. They were received by Deputy-Sheriff Johns and were at once locked up. They are a very tough-looking pair. The woman is ugly and delicate. They are committed upon an order for transfer signed by Judge Shipp, which states that threats were freely made to lynch them if they were allowed to remain in Oxford jail. The orders are that the prisoners such be securely guarded. They have made oath that they cannot get justice in Granville county, and so their case is removed to Vance county. It will be tried at Henderson October 15th. It is learned that if the mob which lynched three negross last week had had a little more time it would also have lynched the Adcocks. Judge Shipp's orders are that the prisoners be securely guarded. Threats are freely made at Oxford that they will not be permitted to live in Granville county, and there is quite a sensation over the matter.

Mr. James B. Warren, manager at Duke's factory, has bought the handsome residence of Mr. J. A. Long, on Caswell Hill.

The report from Durham county in the weather crop Bulletin is in these words: "We continue to hear nothing but discouraging reports from all kinds of crops. Farmers are just beginning to cure their tobacco, and report but poor success."

Hon. John Robinson, Commissioner, in his review of the crop reports for the several counties for Aug. 1st, says, in general, the average condition of crops is not so good as on 1st of July except for cotton and grasses. The prospects, however, are very encouraging.

The following report is made from Durham to the weekly Weather Crop Bulletin: "Much damage is reported from the heavy rains of the past week. Farmers were stopped in the curing of their tobacco by the rains, and now they say it is growing green again and cannot ripen before frost."

—The Republicans of Durham township held a meeting Saturday afternoon, at Mangum's Hall for the purpose of electing delegates to a county convention to be held in this place on the 29th, D. C. Mangum called the meeting to order and made a tariff speech. T. H. Burgess was elected chairman. Three delegates were appointed.

—Capt. T. L. Peay in the citizens meeting: "I will meet my committee any where, at any time, day or night." That is the proper spirit with which to go into the work of the Exposition. The Captain is on the right line.
Now, fellow-citizens and ladies of Durham, let us work for the success of this Durham enterprise—the Exposition in October.

—We have tickets, State and national, that it would be an honor for any man to work for, and that mean the very best thing in a substantial way for the people of the whole country. Now let us proceed to roll up our sleeves and secure their election. Let us, in the meantime, not forget home and use our exertions to elect the county ticket. Work is the watchword. The enemy is active. We cannot afford to be othe wise.

—Henry and Jennie Adcock, charged with the murder of the wife of Henry Adcock's wife, were last night removed from the Oxford jail to Raleigh for safe keeping. The crew against the Adcocks was o have come up for trial at Oxford to-day where court is at present in session, Judge W. M. Shipp presiding. Judge Ship knowing that the feeling was very high and that there was imminent danger to the prisoners gave an order for their removal there to be kept till the tall term of Vance Superior Court which convenes on the third Monday in October. The case will then be tried there instead of Granville.

OLD NORTH STATE.
TERRIBLE ACCIDENT-A MAN'S ARM TORN OFF.
Sudden Death-Improving-Heavy Frost- A Burglar's Strange Weapon-Shot by a Woman.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
RALEIGH, N. C., October 15.—The weekly weather crop bulletin of the State Weather Service, which covers the last week, says that the rainfall in all districts was above the average, affecting the crops—cotton especially—unfavorably. The harvesting of crops and wheat-sowing were delayed by the excessive rains. The temperature was below the average. Frosts were generally reported, with little damage. The next issue of the bulletin will be the last this season.

There are now 241 pupils at Oxford Orphan Asylum. Collections will be taken in all parts of the State on Thanksgiving-day for their benefit. Money is greatly needed.

The commanding officer of the Salvation Army in the United States arrived at Elizabeth City to-day, and this evening special services were held there.

In Hertford county a negro man had his arm torn from the shoulder by a cotton-gin on Friday. He died Saturday of his terrible injury.

Rufus Edmonson, a leading farmer of Wayne county, died Saturday night suddenly of paralysis.

Colonel Thomas M. Holt, the Democratic candidate for Lieutenant-Governor, was able to be out in a carriage this morning for the first time. He is yet very weak, and it does not look as if he would be able to take any active part in the campaign.

Governor Scales will not be able to be here to open the State Fair. This information was received by the secretary to-day. The Governor will devote himself to the canvass in the Fifth district, and will hardly be here before the election.

There was the heaviest frost of the season in this section to-day. It did little damage except to cotton. Nearly all tobacco worth cutting is housed.

At Falls of Neuse, this county, yesterday, a negro woman shot and it is supposed wounded mortally a white man named Strickland.

Steps are being taken to establish a male college at Asheville under the auspices of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South.

In Montgomery county J. C. Roper, a venerable farmer, was awakened from sleep in his house by repeated blows on the head. He found that a burglar was attempting to beat out his brains with a stone. A faithful negro servant came on the scene and frightened the burglar away. Roper is painfully hurt.

The case of Baltzer & Toole, of New York, against the State of North Carolina, involving some $160,000 and which was to have been argued in the State Supreme Court this week, has been by consent continued until next term.

The fair at Fayetteville will be held in the middle of November. Postmaster-General Stephenson has accepted an invitation to deliver the annual address.

Captain S. B. Alexander, Lieutenant-Governor Stedman, and Judge Fowle are now all actively engaged in the campaign. They are doing work in different sections.

There will be many events this week. Two fairs will be held. One is the State Fair here, and the other that at Elizabeth City.

The State Board of Pharmacy meets in this city day after to-morrow for the purpose of examining applicants for license as druggists.

To-day Henry C. Adcock and Jennie C. Adcock were taken from jail here to Henderson to be tried for their lives in Vance county Superior Court. They are charged with poisoning Eliza Ann Adcock, Henry's wife, to get her out of their way. This crime was committed in Granville county. Lynchers were after them. They swore they could not get justice in Granville and so got their case moved to Vance. They were immediately upon taking this step brought here for safekeeping. For the first week or more they were in hourly terror of lynching. Jennie Adcock is Henry's paramour. They are ignorant and degraded people. Both are white.

The appeal of Cross and White will be argued in the Supreme Court this week, perhaps Thursday or Friday. It is purely upon a question of jurisdiction, the defendants claiming that they cannot be tried in the State courts, but only in the Federal courts, for any offence within the scope of extradition laws.

Some days ago a man named Calvin Bivins, near Goldsboro', split the skull of his son-in-law, named Ingram, with a blow of a hatchet. Ingram has died. He had attacked Bivins, and the latter in defending himself inflicted the fatal wound.

Calvin Sherrod (colored), who lives in Wayne county, lost his house by fire Saturday. Two of his children, who were locked in the building, were burned to death. It is a habit of negroes to go to work and lock their little children in the house. The result is an average of fifty fires and about as many deaths every year.

During the last year about $44,500 was raised for benevolent purposes, about $9,000 more than during the year previous. There are 51 vacant churches in the synod, of which the greater number are in Concord Presbytery. Fourteen churches have been built during the year. There are 53 manses valued at over $112,000.

The United States District Court at Newberne has adjourned. S. F. Nable, who attempted to kill Revenue-Officer Wood, gets a sentence of a year in the penitentiary at Columbus, Ohio. The same sentence is imposed upon James E. Abbott for knowingly receiving a check stolen from the Newberne post-office.

DARING BURGLAR.

A daring attempt was made by a burglar upon the house of J. R. Beaman, in Sampson county. He was absent from home. His wife heard a noise and went into the hallway to discover its cause. In a second a well-dressed white man sprang from behind the door and caught her with both hands around her neck. He demanded the key to her husband's store. Mrs. Beaman had a lamp in her hands. She retained her hold on this and also retained her presence of mind and defied the burglar. She called for neighbors who lived near. The burglar became frightened and threw her violently against the side of the hallway and fled. Mrs. Beaman sprang to her room and seized a shotgun and fired twice at the burglar. At this moment her family returned, and then, woman-like, she fainted four times.

Yesterday a large party of negroes left the Ashbyville section for Southern California to make it their home.

The trial of Henry and Jennie Adcock, for poisoning, has been postponed until the February term of Vance Superior Court. In the mean while they will be kept in jail here.

Sam Jones, at the conclusion of his meetings at Durham, will go to Trinity College and preach.

Enterprising citizens of Greensboro' have raised $4,000 as a gift to Graham College on condition that it is located there.

It has been decided by Democrats to make the campaign red-hot in Western North Carolina from now until the day of election.

It is noticeable that in the past fortnight the Third-party people have become more aggressive and stronger in their claims. Once they were content to say that they would get 10,000 votes in the State. Now they boldly say they have 25,000 followers and will get all their votes. Clearly the Republican party is back of the scheme. No doubt many Third-party people do not know this, but the fact is yet plain.

The people of Vance county desire the Seaboard system to build a railway from Henderson to Nash county.

There was a rather curious offence in the Superior Court of Gaston county this week. Two negro thieves were convicted and given long terms in the penitentiary. A negro preacher named Montgomery, as sentence was passed, whistled long and loudly his surprise. Judge Gillner at once had the preacher brought before the bar for contempt and fined him for contempt of court.

DOCKERY.

In some parts of the State the Republicans appear to have circulated a report that they abandon all hope of electing Dockery Governor, and will devote all their energies to carrying the Legislature. At headquarters here, however, this statement is not made. They there assert that Dockery will be elected by 8,000 majority, and that Harrison will get 11,000 votes in the State. Meanwhile hard work is being done to carry the Legislature. Money is being spent freely with that view. The Republicans hope to be in a position to elect a senator to succeed Ransom, and they also hope to get Dockery through.

Rapid work is being done on the Chowan and Southern railroad. The contract for the great iron bridge across the Roanoke river has been let and preparations for building the stone piers are in progress. On both sides of the river hundreds of laborers are grading. In the next six months a great amount of work is to be done as orders have been given
stone piers are in progress. On sides of the river hundreds of laborers are grading. In the next six months a great amount of work is to be done as orders have been given to lose no time.

FARMERS' ALLIANCE.

The Farmers' Alliance members, who now number nearly 70,000, certainly stand together closely. They have remarkably accurate and speedy means of disseminating information. They aid each other in all possible ways. Their unity of effort will be of special help to them next year, when times are sure to be hard. The alliance hopes soon to have agents in each county to look after all its business matters—to see that good prices are obtained, that the members get the benefit of wholesale prices for articles purchased, &c.

Hog-cholera is very prevalent in Person county. Tobacco is being used as a preventive in this always-dreaded disease, which has done so much damage in this State this season. It is said that tobacco is a valuable remedy.

Some cases of glanders in horses are reported in the Piedmont section, but these are not numerous.

CRIME.

The question has come up as to whether there is an increase or decrease of crime in the State. It may be positively answered that there is a decrease. There has been much less crime in 1886-'87-'88 than in the years from 1879 to 1886. There is a notable falling off in the number of capital crimes particularly. Of this fact there is no question.

In Rutberford county a one-armed ex-Confederate is the Democratic candidate for treasurer, while his opponent on the Republican ticket is a one-legged ex-Confederate veteran. Each man is sure of victory, he claims.

The Farmers' Alliance desires to get better terms for its tobacco, and some of the suballiances think the action of the Morehead Tobacco Convention has made matters worse instead of better. It is therefore proposed to hold a meeting of alliance men at Durham on the 13th of November for the purpose of discussing the best means of disposing of tobacco, the meeting to be composed of dele-

tobacco, the meeting to be composed of delegates from each sub-alliance in every tobacco-growing county, and also any sub-alliance in the tobacco-growing section of Virginia.

NOTES.

The Asheville graded schools open to-morrow. They are established by a special vote and appropriation by the people of the enterprising mountain metropolis.

The track of the Georgia, Carolina and Northern railroad is now completed to Chester, and trains will in a few days begin to run.

The colored fair at Goldsboro', which closed yesterday, was a success in point of attendance as in other respects.

The Carthage people are exceedingly angry. Night before last some unknown person cut down the big Cleveland-Fowle flag which was recently raised there.

W. H. Hardon, of Brooks, has invented something in the way of a rat trap which will probably revolutionize the rat catching business. It consists of an upright circular piece, resting on a wooden base, which is raised and set with a trigger so as to fall with the slightest pressure upon the base. This always catches at least one rat. Then there is a fierely balanced trap door in the main body of the trap which can catch the rats as fast as they can walk in it. This door is fixed at an angle of about forty-five degrees, and is so nicely balanced that as soon as the rat crosses the pivot upon which it is balanced, in he goes into the trap, the door at once regaining its first position. There is no end to the number of rats this trap can catch.

Glen Waters, a Constitution reporter, was slapped in the face at Atlanta Tuesday night, by Patrolman West, on account of an article in Tuesday's Constitution. Monday night West was told by a little negro boy that several persons were engaged in a fight in the next block, and, without investigating the affair, he telephoned for help from headquarters, and had several of the mounted force dispatched to the scene simply to find the patrolman himself looking for the belligerents. Waters published the facts as they were, and the police spent Tuesday in guaying West. Chief Connolly told him if such a thing occurred again he would suspend him. When Waters went to headquarters Tuesday night, West walked up to him and slapped him in the face. Waters knocked him down in return, and Chief Connolly has suspended him until his case comes up before the commission.

On Monday night of last week the house of Mr. Bryan, at Raleigh, Meriwether county, was entered and a trunk taken from it. After the trunk was carried a short distance from the house, it was broken open and the contents, which consisted of tobacco, a pistol and $25 or $30 in money, were taken therefrom and the trunk left. As soon as the news was made known to Officers Moreland and Jarrell they went to work and soon arrested the supposed guilty parties, who were Henry Williams and Bill Parkman, both colored. Officer Moreland, knowing that Parkman was in very feeble health, deputised three other men to help guard the prisoners all night, and to give him (Parkman), a better chance to get up bondsmen the next morning. While Moreland was eating supper a party of fifteen or twenty men came up, well armed, and took the prisoners from the guards. On seeing the crowd, the alarm was given, and as Moreland started out of his house he was covered with two shot guns in the hands of two masked men, so he said. The prisoners were taken toward Cane creek and were seen no more till next morning. The body of Parkman was found in the swamp, near where the railroad crosses the creek, in a badly mangled condition. His head and face were badly beaten up, and his feet and legs were badly burned. In a gully not far from where the body was found were coal and ashes, and one side of the gully was perfectly smooth, as though some one had dragged up and down the embankment. It is supposed by all who saw it that the lynchers dragged Parkman up and down the embankment until they were satisfied, and took him to the bank of the creek, where they left him. Williams hasn't been seen since, and it is not known whether he escaped, or what became of him.

At Atlanta, Friday, a prominent citizen of Clayton county stated that the recent action of the mass meeting voiced exactly the opposite views of the Democrats of Clayton. He says the meeting was only attended by a small clique in Jonesboro. It is proposed to have another mass meeting, not with a view of trying to rescind the resolutions passed at the regular called meeting, but to show to the people of the State the true sentiment of the Democracy of Clayton county on the tariff question.

At Atlanta, it is reported upon good authority, that Gen. Clinton B. Fiske, of New Jersey, whose bank account runs up into the millions, has written his Georgia pet, Evangelist Small, to spend whatever may be necessary in his campaign work in Georgia. It is stated that as a starter Gen. Fiske has authorized the Evangelist to draw on him for $10,000 for his work. It is understood that by the aid of "grit, grace and greenbacks" the Evangelist proposes to take his little tent and speak in every county in Georgia before his New Jersey boss is snowed under in the November election.

A day or so ago Frank Benson, of Macon, received a box of eggs from Round Oak, on the Covington and Macon railroad. On the reverse side of the lid of the box he found a sentence written in pencil. This sentence was written on the piece of wood in July, 1879, by one of the clerks of Bailey & Schaffer, a firm then in existence, and referred in a playful way to both members of the firm. The singular part of it is that Mr. Benson was a clerk in the store at the time, and now, after nine years, it comes to him, and from a section of country then remote from any railroad and which he knows nothing about.

Lithonia New Era: Mr. Charles Venable is in New York on a business visit. We understand there will be a contract of 40,000,000 or more blocks for paving the streets of that city let, and we hope our granite men will succeed in securing the contract. There is no granite in the State equal to ours, and some cities will use no other. Granite can be shipped from this place to New York for from $8 to $10 a car less than to Cincinnati, which city is almost entirely supplied with Lithonia granite. It will be a "big
be shipped from this place to New York for from $8 to $10 a car less than to Cincinnati, which city is almost entirely supplied with Lithonia granite. It will be a "big thing" for our granite men and our town if this contract is secured, and we have no doubt but that it will be.

Penitentiary Guard Turner went to Hampton after the prisoners sentenced to the penitentiary, seven in all. While going across the mountain two of them slipped the handcuffs off and jumped out and ran to the woods. Mr. Turner was sitting in front of the hack, and did not see them or hear them until they had gotten to the woods. He could not leave the others, and consequently they got away very nicely. The country is being searched, and in all probability they will be caught. Mr. Turner offers a reward of $25 for them. Their names are Tom Patillo and Tom Marsh, sent for two and ten years.

At Athens, Friday, Charlie Cooper was telephoned to come to the residence of J. A. Fowler, to attend a horse afflicted with an acute case of hydrophobia. Mr. Cooper, who is an expert veterinary surgeon, discovered the diseased horse in a pitifiable condition. He had bitten at his stalls and the adjacent fences until his teeth had been torn from their sockets and with bleeding gums he still threatened the advances of Mr. Fowler and the surgeon. Before either could approach him, the horse had died. Mr. Cooper is of the opinion that the horse died of hydrophobia, superinduced by the bite of a mad dog or poisonous snake.

Lieut. Col. Wolff, of an Indiana regiment of the United States army, was killed at the battle of Richmond, Ky., in 1862. His sword fell into possession of Dr. John L. Branch, of the Confederate army, brother of Capt. W. H. Branch, of Greenesboro. The sword is of regulation pattern, leather-covered scabbard with brass mounting. The blade is fuely embellished and the hilt has an inlaid pearl shield with the word "Union" engraved upon it. It is twenty-six years since the gallant Federal Lieutenant Colonel relaxed this sword from his dying grasp, and it has been in the possession of a Confederate surgeon ever since. Dr. John L. Branch is now a resident of Cedartown, Ga., having, like Capt. Branch, survived the perils and privations of the war. It is not known what Indiana regiment Lieut. Col. Wolff was connected with, nor are his initials remembered, if they had been known.

Henry Williams, one of the negroes reported lynched near Raleigh, is not dead, and is now in Greenville jail. He was discovered a short distance from Woodbury Wednesday. He would run at the approach of a white man, and for some time was afraid of his own race. He was finally caught and carried to Greenville by about thirty-five armed negroes. He shows signs of having been beaten badly. He says that he knows every one concerned in the affair, and says that there were sixteen of them. He tells how he escaped, and says that after the party had killed William Parkman they were fired into, and all ran but one, and he knocked him down. Another rumor is that they left him for dead, and after they had left him he crawled into neck-deep water, and remained there nearly all night. His not being dead, however, throws new light on the matter, and some startling developments will be made, it is thought, in a few days.

An Incendiar's Fate.
NAH Ga Feb 10 About
SAVANNAH, Ga., Feb. 10.—About a fortnight ago a fire occurred at Johnston's Station, on the Savannah, Florida and Western railway. James Chapman lost a store, and the railway company's warehouse was burned, along with several other buildings. It was suspected that the fire was started by an incendiary, and Wednesday a negro was arrested on suspicion. He was given a preliminary hearing, and confessed. While the deputy sheriff was on the way to Hinesville jail he was surprised by a crowd of fifteen men, who took the prisoner away from him. The negro was carried into the woods, and it is supposed that he was hanged or burned.

Events of a Week in the Sunny Southland.
EXCITEMENT IN FAYETTEVILLE. TENN.
GEORGIA.
GEORGIA.

The most horrible and revolting crime ever committed in Cherokee county has just come to light, the consequences of which blast the life of a young and pretty girl. Henry Brownlee, colored, has been arrested on the charge of seduction and is now in jail. Great excitement prevails and it is feared that an outraged citizenry may do violence to the negro.

The girl is about 16 years of age, and resides on the Etowah river, four miles from this place, with her grandmother. The girl's grandfather, some two years ago, paid Henry Brownlee out of the chaingang, and the prisoner had since then been living on the place. He is a mulatto, 39 years old, and has a wife and nine children. Brownlee has not lived with his family for some time, has figured in the courts quite extensively, and has never borne a good reputation. He appears confident of coming out all right, denying the seduction. He waived a preliminary hearing and went to jail. He will be tried at Cherokee superior court, which meets three weeks hence. Colonel C. D. Maddox and Captain H. W. Newman will assist in the prosecution of the case.

William, alias John, Love, colored, was arrested Sunday afternoon, at Savannah, for the murder of Mamie Tompkins.

Last week the body of a colored woman was found in the river. It was decomposed, and was not identified before burial. Some colored people gave Captain W. D. Dixon, coroner, some information a day or two later, which led him to believe that the woman had been murdered and thrown into the river. He went quietly to work, and Sunday had a warrant issued by Magistrate Molina for Love's arrest.

Love works on the steamer Katie. He was asked if he knew where Mamie Tompkins was, and he said that he did not. He was not accused of the murder, but was sent to jail for safe keeping. The Tompkins woman has not been seen since the night of January 8th, and it is said on that night Love was with her, and he is the last person who was with her, so far as has been learned. The case is being worked up by the coroner. The clews so far obtained point directly to Love as the murderer of the woman.

Recently a house and warehouse were destroyed by fire in Hinesville, and all the circumstances pointed to its being the work of an incendiary. The people have been greatly wrought up in consequence. Intelligence received here states that a negro was arrested there Tuesday on the charge of burning the houses aforesaid. He is said to have confessed the deed, and implicated several in the crime. After a preliminary investigation, he was committed to jail in Hinesville. That night a band of armed men overpowered the deputy sheriff, who had the prisoner in charge, and carrying him off to the woods shot him to death. Great excitement prevails in that section.

The American Newspaper Publishers' Association began its annual session at Indianapolis on the 8th.

The Michigan Grand Lodge A. O. U. W., in session on the 8th at Detroit, adopted legislation prohibiting the admission to membership of habitual drunkards and those engaged in the manufacture or sale of intoxicating beverages.

Advices of the 8th say that John Clark, wife and five children died near Leavenworth, Kan., from drinking water from a well near which hogs dying of cholera were buried.

Mr. A. J. Snell, a well-known citizen and millionaire of Chicago, was murdered by a burglar in his residence on the West side about two o'clock on the morning of the 8th.

John Williams, of Delaware, O., accidentally struck his son with an axe on the 8th while splitting wood, killing the boy instantly.

The British steamships Algitha, Lufra and Darien, all bound from England for Philadelphia, were given up as lost on the 8th with their crews, numbering eighty men.

On the 8th two car-loads of goods, believed to have been stolen from Baltimore & Ohio freight cars, were seized in the house of John Britain at Pittsburgh, Pa.

Officials at Yankton, D. T., were on the 8th sending out official denials of the reports that one thousand lives were lost in the Territory in the late blizzard.

Interest in the gold-mining enterprises north of Ishpeming, Mich., on the 8th was increased by rich developments.

A NEGEO arrested at Hinesville, Ga., on the charge of setting fire to several houses, was taken from jail on the 8th by a mob and riddled with bullets.

J. L. Hudson's mammoth clothing store at Cleveland, O., was damaged by fire on the 8th to the extent of $100,000.

CASHIER EDWARDS, of the Cincinnati Metropolitan National Bank, said on the 8th that after all claims were paid there would be $820,000 left for the stockholders.

In the United States Court at Fort Smith, Ark, on the 9th Judge Parker sentenced Owen D. Hill, George Moss, Jeff Hilderbrand, Emanuel Patterson, Richard Sutherland, Jack Crow and William Alexander to be hanged on April 27 for murder.

The sixty-second anniversary of the birthday of the late Senator Logan was commemorated on the 9th by the dedication of a memorial tablet in the Metropolitan Methodist Episcopal Church in Washington which the Senator was in the habit of attending.

The Builders' National Association at its annual session on the 9th in Cincinnati elected J. L. Stevens, of Philadelphia, president.

Four dwellings at Kutztown, Pa., were burned on the 9th, John Hopp, his daughter, aged fifteen years, and his son, aged nine years, perishing in the flames.

JOHN JANAUSCHEK, a farmer living near New Prague, Minn., killed his wife on the 9th, fatally wounded his ten-year-old daughter and killed himself. A quarrel over money was the cause.

THOMAS STEVENS and his wife, of West Gardiner, Me., were placed in an insane asylum on the 9th. Their hallucination was that their house was overrun with monkeys.

At Indianapo's on the 9th William M. Singerly was elected president of the State N newspaper Publishers' Association.

The American Horticultural Society, in annual session on the 9th at Riverside, Cal., elected Parker Earl, of Cobden, Ill., President.

Clement A. Day was hanged on the 9th at Utica, N. Y. He was convicted of the murder of his mistress, Johanna Ross Crow, of whom he was insanely jealous.

LIBERTY TO HAVE A HANGING.
William Macon Sentenced for the Murder of John Spain.
Murder of John Spain.

Liberty county will have its first hanging since the war on Jan. 17. William Macon was convicted in Liberty county superior court this week of the murder of John Spain at Joslyn, thirty-five miles south of Savannah, about two months ago, and was sentenced to be hanged at Hinesville Jan. 17.

The murder grew out of a quarrel over a game of cards. Macon became enraged, and drawing a pistol, shot Spain in the breast, killing him instantly. Both men were colored. There were a number of witnesses of the shooting. Macon escaped and went to Darien, where he was captured a week or two afterward and was taken to Hinesville for trial. There is little doubt that he will hang, as no motion was made in his behalf. The hanging will be the first that has taken place in Liberty county since the war. The last person hanged there was a slave.

The Liberty county court adjourned Wednesday night. Judge Adams, Solicitor General Fraser and Messrs. Lester, Erwin, Meldrim and Osborne returned yesterday morning. The criminal docket was a heavy one. George Washington, William Fields and Julius McLary were convicted of arson and sentenced to the penitentiary for life. Washington was the negro who set fire to the Savannah, Florida and Western railway warehouse and Chapman's store, at Johnson's station nearly a year ago. He escaped after the fire, but was captured and was reported to have been lynched. The report proved untrue, and he was afterward run down by the officers. Fields and McLary were his accomplices.

John James and Joseph Green were convicted of burglary and were sentenced to the penitentiary, James for four years, and Green for five years.

Stewart Johnson was sentenced to six months on the chain-gang for assault and battery.

Alfred Herrington, who shot his sister and little niece at Hinesville last month, was indicted for murder. His case will come up at the next term of court. There were no acquittals on the criminal side of the court. Only two civil cases were tried.

The McIntosh superior court will convene on Monday. Judge Adams, Solicitor General Fraser, Messrs. Lester and Meldrim, and a number of other attorneys will leave for Darien to-morrow morning. The court is expected to be in session about three days. Three murder cases are on the docket.

Judge Adams will convene the December term of the superior court here Monday, Dec. 3. The criminal docket will have no less than five killing cases for the grand jury to pass upon:

Smith, for the shooting of Rustin.

Westcott, for the shooting of a colored thief.

Weidner, for the killing of a negro who assaulted him with a club.

Pinckney (colored), for the murder of Ben Hartley (colored).

Silvers, the Portugese, for the shooting of Fate Nelson (colored).

The civil docket will be very large. It will not be fully made up by Clerk Carr until to-morrow.

Narrow Escape of a Chinese Thief From Being Lynched.

[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

IRVINGTON (via Niles), May 25th.—This morning a one-eyed Chinese burglar entered the house of Mr. Henion at his ranch, a mile or two below Warm Springs, and stole $80. Mr. Henion's son noticed the burglar's departure, and calling his father overtook and searched the thief, who it appears had hidden the money in a barrel of water, where it was afterwards found. While Mr. Henion was engaged in placing the burglar under arrest, it is reported that a number of determined persons secured a rope, put it around the Chinaman's neck and elevated him several feet from the ground. Mr. Henion finally succeeded in getting the Chinaman away alive, and then handed him over to the Constable, who locked him up.

DOUBLE LYNCHING.
Puss Kirkpatrick Hanged From a Tree and Her Husband Shot Dead by the Same Crowd—The Woman Acused of Incendiarism.

GALLATIN, TENN., April 19.—One of the most sensational tragedies in the history of this county was enacted last night, about twelve o'clock, a few miles from town. It was the lynching of a negro woman named Puss Kirkpatrick, and the shooting fatally of her husband Isaac. The woman was charged with incendiarism. Jim McCollough, while walking along a country road at an early hour, saw some distance ahead what he supposed to be a woman in her night-dress hiding behind a tree, and in his close scrutiny of so unusual a sight he almost stumbled over the body of Isaac Kirkpatrick, the husband, lying beside the road. Upon reaching the tree the ghastly truth burst upon him. The woman was hanging dead, her foot almost on the ground. He hurriedly reported the fact in town. A coroner and jury of inquest repaired to the spot, reporting that the woman came to her death by strangulation and the husband by a pistol-shot wound by parties unknown. The husband was not suspected of complicity in house-burning, and the theory of his killing is that he discovered the identity of some of the lynching party, and was shot to avoid exposure.

GEORGIA.

An opera house is to be built at Waycross.

Georgia's plurality for Cleveland will be nearer 35,000 than 25,000.

Several of Carrollton's mercantile houses were draped in bunting election day.

Williams Bros., grocers of Bainbridge, have failed for something like $4,000, though with assets ample to cover all their liabilities.
