Gov.-elect F. P. Fleming and party, of Florida, came up to Thomasville on the passenger train from Monticello Wednesday, en route east.

Hon. C. F. Crisp is very proud of his vote of last Tuesday. Two years ago he only received something over 1,700 as a vote of the district, but this time his majority will be 5,000.

Messrs. Hawkes and Blalock are out of the race for solicitor general of the South-western judicial circuit. Col. C. B. Hudson, the present incumbent, is now the only candidate for the position.

A. K. Clark, who purchased, last winter, a half interest in the Americus ice works from Mr. Bye, has sold his interest to Bascom Myrick and W. C. Gray. The firm is now Sims, Myrick & Gray.

The boys of Blakely were ready with their cannon and fireworks to celebrate a democratic victory, but the bad news from New York cast a damper over their spirits, and not a solitary gun was fired.

There has been a wonderful decrease in crime in Macon county during the present year. Last year the sheriff made over sixty arrests for various crimes, and up to date this year there has been only eighteen.

The Central hotel, at Rome, after a short career under Capt. W. T. Dozier, has been closed. The largest bills against the hotel were held by Thomas Fahy and M. G. McDonald. There are also several other creditors.

On a half acre of average land, Fletcher Edwards of Hart county made 800 pounds seed cotton with the rows six feet wide. Used 175 pounds of guano. On one-fourth of an acre he made 22½ bushels of corn. This is good farming.

Hen. F. B. Hodges of Hartwell says he has been sowing wheat for twenty years, and has never failed to reap a fair harvest for the amount planted. Carefully selected seed, thorough soaking in blue-stone, and proper cultivation, are the secrets of his success.

The steamer Laureens, which left her wharf at Dublin, Tuesday morning, bound for Mount Vernon, struck a snag and was sunk near Ring Jaw, about ten miles below Dublin, on the same day. The steamer was loaded with brick, which were to be used in the erection of Montgomery county's jail.

Since there is complaint by the people of the lower part of Oglethorpe county that the Lexington Terminal cuts up their road to Crawford, the citizens of Crawford are contemplating opening a new road from that place to intersect with the Lexington and Elberton road a few miles out of Lexington.

Tuesday was regular sale day at Oglethorpe, and a great deal of property changed hands. The Jordan place was sold to Mrs. E. Joiner at $1,550. The Reynolds place was bid in at $1,546 by B. F. Martin. The old Miles Taylor place on Whitewater creek was sold to C. E. Ogburn of Butler for $140.

At Elberton a business combination has been formed between T. M. Swift, W. M. Wilcox and B. B. Braswell. Messrs. Wilcox & Braswell will close out their present business by Jan. 1, when the new firm of Swift, Wilcox & Braswell will commence business at the stand now occupied by Swift Bros.

Porter Stocks of Atlanta received a note warning him to leave the city on account of an interest he took in an effort to find a negro republican who fired a pistol shot in the streets. The note bore the names of several leading negro republicans. It develops that they did not sign it, and the whole affair is probably a hoax.

Nathan Stewart, a young man about 20 years of age, and one of the B. V. & E. victims, had his left arm amputated in Ellaville on Wednesday. His arm was broken in two places. At last accounts he was not doing very well, but was not dangerously ill. Mostly all of the parties that were injured by the run-off, are improving, no others have died, and all are now out of danger.

A homicide occurred at Temperance on Saturday night last, in which Boss Fletcher (colored) was the victim, meeting his death at the hands of a sable brother, Oliver Wilcox. The murder was the result of an old feud of some years' standing, having its origin in some family quarrel, and was accomplished by the aid of a trusty shotgun filled with buckshot. The murderer fled to the swamp, and is at large.

While a large crowd was assembled about a light on the square at Jefferson last Tuesday night rejoicing over the election returns, a man with several sets of plow gear hanging about him, rushed through the darkness in the direction of the crowd hallooing "Whoa!" causing a general stampede. Large ones ran over the small ones, sober ones over the drunken ones, until the supposed runaway horse had been stopped.

At Albany, Margaret Mitchell went to the house of another negro woman named Nettie Rhodes, on Thursday night, and calling her to the door, attacked her with a knife. She cut off a piece of Nettie's nose and cut a gash in each cheek and another across her upper lip in less time than it takes to tell about it. Nettie's wounds are not dangerous, but are very painful and will disfigure her face for life. Margaret was arrested.

Montezuma Record: An effort is to be made to incorporate Barrowville and Mitchellville in the northwestern part of Macon county. Unless there is a town to incorporate we do not see how it can be incorporated. It is said that the object is to sell whisky, and that it bodes no good to the community where these proposed towns are to be located. The farmers in the neighborhood are very much opposed to it and will do all in their power to prevent it.

At Gainesville Friday night Jack Hemphill (colored), was arrested for attempting an outrage on a white girl of 12 years, and placed in the lock-up. A crowd gathered and started to lynch him. The marshal beat the crowd to the lock-up, took the prisoner and spirited him away. In-

james-semmes-halls-station-1888-01-24.A2:
MRS. JEFFREYS-LEWIS INVISIBLE. "La Belle Russe" Not Performed at the Windsor Theatre Last Night. Miss Jeffreys-Lewis was to have appeared in "La Belle Russe" in the Windsor Theatre last night, but the curtain was not raised. Mr. Frank B. Murtha, the manager, came before the house and announced that Miss Jeffreys-Lewis was too ill to appear. He dismissed the audience, and the money was refunded at the box office. SHE WAS STEALING THE PLAY.
A Woman Turned Out of a Theatre While Taking Short Hand Notes of the Drama.

BALTIMORE, Jan. 24.—During to-night's performance of "The Gladiator" by Robert Downing at the Holliday Street Theatre, attention was attracted by a fashionably dressed woman who was taking stenogaaphic notes of the play. Manager Joseph H. Mack caused her to stop. A member of the company explained to the audience that the woman, who is said to be a Pittsburgh actress named Desmond, was attempting to steal the play, and she was greeted with a storm of hisses as she confusedly left the house. Manager Mack said that several attempts had been made to steal the play, which is the property of Mr. Downing.

The Families of the Anarchists.

CHICAGO, Jan. 24.—The Pioneer Aid and Support Association has decided to fix the weekly payments to the families of the hanged Anarchists at $8 to each of the widows, and $2 for each child where there are two children, and $1 for the third child in the case of Mrs. Fischer. It appears that the families are better off now, financially, than they ever were while the husbands and fathers were alive, and as their circumstances bettered, so did their wants increase. Mrs. Parsons recently bought a gold watch, for which she paid $65. Some time later she complained she had no money to pay rent. She got the money from the committee.

A Point Blank Shot at a Policeman.

Policeman Fred Cortlander of the Oak street station heard pistol shots yesterday on James street. Running in the direction from which the sounds proceeded, he found a wild-looking Italian with a smoking revolver in his hand. He spoke to him, and attempted to take the weapon from the Italian's hand. The latter, muttering some unintelligible jargon, drew back and fired point blank at the officer. The shot missed, and the policeman threw himself upon the foreigner and disarmed him. When taken to the station house the prisoner described himself as Pasquale Peri, aged 30, of 63 James street. It is thought that he is insane.

Banker Bergamial's Will Filed.

The will of Emiliano P. Bergamini, the Italian banker, who had an office in Centre street, and whose depositors since his death last month have been mpatiently looking for their money, was filed for probate yesterday. The testator gives the house and lot on Alexander avenue, where he lived, to his widow, and of the residue of the estate one half is to go to the widow and the remaining half is to be divided equally between the three daughters, Mary, Rachel, and Theresa, share and share alike. The son gets no money. The widow is appointed executrix.

Agostino Trifano, a creditor, has filed an objection to the granting of letters testamentary to the widow.

Fay Knocked Out in Short Order.

CLEVELAND, Jan. 24.—Sam Eaton, 118 pounds, and Jay Fay of Indianapolis, 119½ pounds, fought to a finish for a $100 purse in the Cleveland Gymnasium tonight. Four-ounce gloves and Queensberry rules were used. It was a quick, savage fight. Eaton rushed his man after half a minute's sparring, and soon got him fighting wild. Eaton swung on Fay's head and neck ten times with either hand, knocking him down three times, and on the third knock down Fay stayed down, completely knocked out. Time, 2:28.

A Deputy Sheriff Killed by a Negro.

TUSCALOOSA, Ala., Jan. 24.—Deputy Sheriff Antrey was shot and instantly killed this morning, at Hall's Station, by a negro named James Semmes, for whose arrest he had a warrant. As Antrey and his assistant approached Semmes's house, Semmes fired a gun through a crack of the door and put a full charge of buckshot into Antrey's neck and chest. The negro then rushed out, knocked the other officer down, and made his escape. A posse is in hot pursuit.

Mrs. Langtry's Palace Car.

WILMINGTON. Del., Jan. 24.—Mrs. Langtry, accompanied by President Mann of the Mann Boudoir Car Company, arrived here this afternoon and inspected the work now being done on her new car by the Harlan & Hollingsworth Company. The car will cost about $40,000, and will be one of the finest ever turned out in this city. It will be sixty-seven feet long, and will be completed in about one week. Mrs. Langtry returned to New York again this afternoon.
james-semmes-halls-station-1888-01-24.A6:
CONDENSED TELEGRAMS.
Rear Admiral Clark H. Wells, retired, died Saturday morning at his residence in Washington.

The postoffice at Neosha Falls, Kas., was burglarized Saturday night, and $125 in money and stamps taken. Two registered letters, contents unknown, were rifled.

The dwelling of Dennis Clifford, five miles from Tawas City, Mich., was burned and Clifford and his wife perished in the flames. They were an old couple of very dissolute habits.

The Pacific Railroad Company Saturday gave a hearing to Mr. Peckham, the General manager of the English interests represented before the committee by Mr. Brotherton, of London.

The heating apparatus in the directors' car on the Delaware & Hudson railroad at Troy, N. Y., exploded Saturday morning and seriously injured the colored porter. The interior of the car was completely wrecked.

The cable in the Southside loop of the North Chicago City Railway, was successfully laid last night. It took less than four hours to complete the job. This week the cable will be swung on Clark and Wells street.

Nearly 500 carpet weavers, representing most of the shops in the northern part of Philadelphia, met Friday night in Temperance Hall and voted to continue the strike at the manufactories at which the men are now out.

The Illinois Miners' Convention has adopted the report of the Legislative Committee, which recommends that the Legislature pass a law to secure semi-monthly payment of wages to employes. There is a contest over the offices.

At Milwaukee, while workmen were engaged in lifting a water heater at the foundry of E. P. Allis & Co., it broke away from the tackle and fell to the floor, killing James Dwyer instantly and fatally injuring Thomas Hickey.

Upon application of Butler, Stillman & Hubbard, Judge Andrews, of the New York Supreme Court, has issued several attachments against the property of James W. Vaile & Co., of Milwaukee, Wis. The firm has attachable assets in the National Park Bank.

Eight cows suffering from pleuro-pneumonia were killed Friday in Hudson county, N. J., by order of Dr. Demard, of the Department of Agriculture. Twenty-two cows out of a herd of 138 have also been ordered killed, and it is believed that the whole herd will have to be slaughtered.

The Surveyors and Engineers' Association of Illinois has approved Senator Cullom's bill requiring a portion of the engineers upon public works to be selected outside of the army. The State delegate to the National Convention of Engineers was instructed to labor for an endorsement of the measure.

The negro, Jim Seams, who shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Autrey on Tuesday night, was captured Friday in the Big Sandy neighborhood, about twenty-five miles south of Tuscdorea, Ala., after a desperate battle with the Sheriff's posse. He was shot several times, but not fatally. There is considerable talk of lynching.

Henry Pretre was burned to death in his barn near Tyler, Minn., Thursday night. The bodies of ten horses, seventeen cattle and twenty hogs were also found in the debris. The circumstances of Pretre's death will probably never be known. The fire is supposed to have originated from a lantern, remains of which were found in the ruins.

The trial of Pasqual Riccis, for the murder of Anthony Mattes, at Hazelton, a few months ago, was ended Friday night, the jury's verdict being "Not guilty." The prisoner was released. Riccis is an ignorant Italian, and when the verdict was given he did not know what it meant until the District Attorney motioned him to leave the court room. His wife proudly marched her husband out of the room.

The Civil Service Commissioners were before the House Committee on Reform in the Civil Service, Saturday, and discussed in an informal way various questions connected with the civil service rules and the administration of the law. Representative Crane's bill to create a retired list in the civil service was taken up by the committee, and after a short debate it was decided to be inexpedient and an adverse report was ordered upon it.

Noah Drew, the confederate who turned informer on Barney, Swinney, the Wabash railway robber, says a scheme to rob Norton Brothers' bank at Missouri City was under consideration and being planned by Swinney last fall. The plan was for him and Swinney to overpower the cashier, S. D. Brady, some night while he was going to or from his boarding house, and force him to go to the bank and open the safe, but the train robbery superseded the idea.
james-semmes-halls-station-1888-01-24.A7:
DURING THE WEEK.
The Week's Synopsis of General and Local News
CONDENSED FOR OUR WEEKLY FRIENDS
Tuesday, January 24.—M. & E. Solomon, tobacco dealers of New York, have failed, with liabilities of $613,000...A large fire occurred in Philadelphia, destroying property to the amount of $1,500,-000...A railroad accident occurred on the Salem branch of the Delaware and Hudson road, which resulted in the serious injury of sixteen passengers. Four of them will die. Two of the passenger cars went over an embankment and turned over three times...The Patapseo river at Baltimore is frozen over, which has stopped navigation except to the largest steamers...Three prisoners, all that were in the jail at Murfreesboro, N. C., escaped. They were out in the corridor and picked a hole in the wall with a common poker...Floyd county will be dry on March 31st, the people having voted out whisky on July 19th last. The saloons in Rome are closing up now as fast as their licenses expire, and the last one expires on the 31st of March...Charley Johnson and Jim Anderson, two negroes, engaged in a deadly combat with knives, in which the former was seriously and it is thought fatally stabbed by the latter, in Augusta...J. A. Smith's ginhouse and press, four miles from Washington, Ga., was destroyed by fire. The ginhouse had not been used since Christmas. It was near midday when the fire occurred, and the ginhouse was near his dwelling. Therein lies a mystery which Mr. Smith would like to have explained away..... "Grandma" Garfield, mother of the late President James A. Garfield, died at her residence in Mentor, Ohio, and her remains were carried to Cleveland and placed in the receiving vault at Lakeview beside those of her son, the president.

Wednesday, January 25.—Colonel Charles William Moulton, of New York, died at the Arno house from apoplexy. Colonel Moulton was born in Cayuhoga county, Ohio, December 16, 1830. His widow is the youngest sister of General and Hon. John Sherman. He was the father of four children, all of whom are married and well established in life. Deputy Sheriff Autry was killed near Maxwell's station, Ala., while endeavoring to arrest Jim Starnes, colored, a noted desperado. A large posse of white men are securing the country for him, and if he is caught he will be strung up. It is thought that the damage from the large fire in Philadelphia will reach the enormous sum of $2,000,000. The farmers of Beardsly, Miam., becoming desperate from the cold weather and not being able to procure fuel have torn down the railroad's snow fences and hauled them away. They have also wrecked several cars and carried them off. Chancelor P. H. Meill, of the State university at Athens, is dead. His illness was of over a month's duration and was occasioned by overwork, which, combined with his age, made his recovery at all times doubtful. His funeral occurred Friday. There was a jail delivery at Kingston, Tenn., in which Ben Williams, a murderer, and Lawrence Huffman, a notorious criminal, made their escape...Superintendent George Maston, of the limestone quarries of Youngstown, Ohio, placed twenty-five sticks of dynamite on a stove to thaw, when the treacherous stuff exploded, killing him and two Italian laborers instantly.

Thursday, January 26.—Isaac N. Stanley, paying teller of the National Bank of Commerce, at Cleveland, appropriated to his own use, and skipped o the Ohio penitentiary for five years...During a regular revolver fusilade at a dance at York, S. C., Jim Beam, of Shelby, was instantly killed by being shot through the heart by some one of the party.

A large fire occurred in O. G. King's shoe store, Newark, N. J., destroying the building and contents, causing a loss of $150,000...A can of dynamite exploded at a dynamite factory in Jenkington, Pa., instantly killing four men...The celebrated trotting stallion, Happy Medium, valued at $53,000, died in Louisville, Ky...In a quarrel over the ownership of a shovel, on the Kansas City railroad, near Birmingham, Jim Johnson, colored, drove a pocket knife to the hilt in Jim Douglas, killing him instantly...Charles G. Minnigerode, a prominent man of Alexandria, Va., committed suicide by shooting himself through the head with a pistol...The Buffalo, N. Y., Rubber company has failed with liabilities of $51,000...The William Penn Coal company at Shenandoah, Pa., has started up its colliery
Friday, January 27.—Half the population of Bainbridge, Ohio, have been indicted for stealing coal. Among the number that the detectives have arrested, are the city marshal, a hotel proprietor, and a Presbyterian preacher. The amount of the peculations may be imagined when it is known that, although the whole village uses coal, yet there has not been a single car assigned to a single resident this winter....The court of appeals has decided that priests of France are entitled to enter into the married state....A young man by the name of Oscar F. Knox committed suicide in Columbus by shooting himself through the head with a pistol. Letters on his person showed that he was engaged to a daughter of one of the most prominent citizens of Troy, Ala. It is thought that financial embarrassment was the cause of the deed....Reddick Peacock, a young man, fell between two freight cars of the Florida Railway and Navigation company, at Chattahooche, Fla., and was crushed to death....The Macon and Covington railroad, which has had so much trouble, financially, since it commenced building, is now an assured success. Alexander Brown & Sons, of Baltimore, have taken hold of the enterprise, and it will be pushed to completion as fast as money and energy can do it.....John Wilson, a wealthy bachelor of Montgomery, Alabama, who died Friday, left his entire fortune of $75,000 to the orphans' home and the institution for deaf, dumb and blind children, in Montgomery.....A passenger train collided with a freight train, seventeen miles east of La Harradura, Cuba, instantly killing both engineers and firemen of the two trains.

No one knows better than those who have used Carter's Little Liver Pills what relief they have given when taken for dyspepsia, dizziness, pain in the side, constipation, disor- ed stomach, &c. Try them.
james-semmes-halls-station-1888-01-24.A8:
He Had Killed His Man.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala, January 28.—[Special.] Jim Seams, the negro who killed Deputy Sheriff Autry, of Tuscaloosa county, last Tuesday, was brought to this city for safe keeping. An effort to lynch him was made at Tuscaloosa, and the sheriff brought him here under a strong guard. The negro talked freely about the crime today, and said he guessed he would be suspended where he could kick at the United States, but it was all right, as he had killed his man.
james-semmes-halls-station-1888-01-24.A10:
SOUTHLAND DOTTINGS.
INTERESTING NEWS ITEMS FOR BUSY PEOPLE.
The Social, Religious and Temperance World-Projected Enterprises-Marriages, Fires, Deaths. Etc.
Chancellor P. H. Mell, of the University at Athens, Ga., is dead.

The grand jury at New Orleans, La., has decided that keno is not gambling within the meaning of the statute.

Hon. John T. Allen, ex-State Treasurer of Texas, died at Houston, aged 30. He bequeathed $300,000 to the city for an industrial school for boys.

A bottle of corn whiskey taken from a drunken man in Atlanta, Ga., while on the mantlepiece of the police station, exploded with the noise of a small cannon.

Stenographer Barnes asked for $600 for reporting the Woolfolk murder case at Macon, Ga., and Judge Gustin allowed the bill. There were 300,000 words put in the record.

Deputy Sheriff J. M. Autry was shot and instantly killed near Tuscaloosa, Ala., while arresting Jim Semmes, a negro. The negro fired from his house just as he reached it.

The jail of Edgecombe county, North Carolina, at Tarboro, and the old Steele Creek Presbyterian church in Mecklenburg county, North Carolina, were destroyed by fire.

Rev. J. S. Dill, who was called to the pastorate of the Central Baptist Church at Atlanta, Ga., and also to that of the Baptist Church of Goldsboro, N. C., has accepted the latter call.

The court house of Mobile county, Ala., was destroyed by fire. A defective flue set fire to the roof and the flames spread slowly and gave time to save the records. The building was valued at $50,000.

While the fast train on the Georgia road was approaching Augusta, some miscreants, when the cars were about two miles from the city, threw rocks which smashed several windows. No one was hurt.

Rev. Sam Jones, the revivalist, spoke "To Men Only" at Kansas City, Mo. The attendance was 6,000, and the collection for Jones' personal benefit amounted to $3,500. He spoke that night to an audience of 7,000.

The celebrated trotting stallion, Happy Medium, valued at $40,000, died at Lexington, Ky. He was foaled in 1863. Thirty-nine of his get have records of 2:30, or lower. He was of Ned by General W. T. Withers.

"Hands up; I am a detective!" were the words used by Albert Knott, a young colored man who had summoned Fred. Patrick, of Atlanta, Ga., to the front door. With his hands out, Patrick captured the bogus detective.

J. M. Frazier, who was for years treasurer of the Mobile & Georgia Railroad company, left Columbus, Ga., for Mexico to accept the position of auditor of accounts of the construction company of the Mexican National railway.

It having been announced that the printers who recently struck on the Courier-Journal, of Louisville, Ky., proposed starting an opposition paper, W. N. Haldeman, proprietor of the Courier-Journal, tendered the strikers full associated press dispatches six months free of charge.

Central railroad engine, No. 29, Engineer Greagor, run over J. B. Brinson, a young white man, at Tennille, Ga., and cut off both his legs just below the knee. Brinson is a train hand on the W. & T., and was in the discharge of his duties when he was struck by the engine, which he did not see, as he had his back to it. He died.

Cold weather has at last closed Patapsco River with ice, and navigation is stopped to Baltimore, Md., except to larger class local steamers and a few smaller craft which get up in tow. Both state and city ice boats are at work, and thus far have succeeded in breaking the ice from that city to open water in Chesapeake Bay.

Charles G. Minnigerode, a prominent citizen of Alexandria, Va., in the railroad supply business, committed suicide at his residence by shooting himself in the head with a pistol. He was a son of Rev. Dr. Minnigerode, of Richmond, Va., was at one time a Confederate soldier and served on Gen. Fitzhugh Lee's staff. He leaves a wife and eight children.

Goldthwaite Graham, a well known citizen, for many years deputy sheriff of Montgomery, Ala., committed suicide. The deceased had been drinking and remarked to his son: "I'm going to kill myself. Old man Workman went by the laudanum route, and I'll do the same." He was noted for courage and integrity, and when not drinking was a very estimable man.

Murphy Phillips, indicted for rape: Jack Chapman, charged with the murder of Monroe Bynum, and a negro named Jones under a jail sentence—the only three prisoners in the Murfreesboro, Tenn., jail escaped. The jail is constructed after the usual manner, with an inside cage surrounded by a corridor. At the time of the escape the prisoners were out in this corridor, and, by the use of a common steve poker, they dug a hole through the brick wall of the jail.

The man who was secured by the Montgomery, Ala., police, confessed to the captain of police that he was Reuben Barrows and the fugitive his brother Jim.

jean-pierre-salet-ville-platte-prairie-1.A1:
RIDDLED WITH BULLETS.
Negroes of Incendiary Proclivi ties Killed by a Mob.
ties Killed by a Mob. OPELOUSAS, La., Sept. 17.—Yestermorning, at Ville Platte Prairie, a crowd of armed men rode to the houses of two negroes named Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere and, after leading them a short distance away, riddled them with buckshot, killing them both instantly. The killing is supposed to have been brought about by incendiary language recently used by these two negroes. The affair created intense excitement in the neighborhood where it occurred.
jean-pierre-salet-ville-platte-prairie-1.A2:
Shot for Incendiary Language.
OPELONSAS, La., Sept. 18. At Ville Platte Prairie a crowd of armed men went to the huts of two negroes named Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere, and took them to the woods, where they shot them to death. Incendiary language on the part of these negroes is said to be the cause of the killing, which has caused intense excitement in the neighborhood where it occurred.
jean-pierre-salet-ville-platte-prairie-1.A3:
GENERAL NEWS.
The farm buildings of George F. Wolecott, at North Conway, N. H., burned yesterday. Twelve cattle perished in the flames. Loss, $1,500; insurance, $400.

The case against the alleged dynamite conspirators, John H. Ronek, Frank Capek, Rudolf Sevic and Frank C. Heleboun, who are charged with a plot to murder Judges Gary and Grinnell, Police Inspector Bonfield and others, who were connected with the trial of August Spies and his comrades, was called in Judge Tutthill's court at Chicago yesterday. On application of the prisoners' counsel, the hearing in the four cases was postponed till the October term of court.

Teemer, O'Connor, Gaudaur, Ross, Bubear, Lee, Hamm, Plaisted and others, are enlisted for a conspirators for a six days' race at Madison Square Garden, New York, using a new invention consisting of a carriage propelled by a rowing apparatus.

Wm. Bohan, of Rockaway, N. Y., who gouged both his wife's eyes has been found guilty of mayhem. The penalty is from 5 to 15 years' imprisonment. His wife refused to testify.

The chiefs of the Sioux tribes at Standing Rock, Dakota, are rejoiced at the thought that the commissioners now treating with the Indians for the opening of the reservation will endeavor to have them visit Washington. Sitting Bull and Red Cloud were the leaders several months ago in a movement to have a delegation of chiefs visit Washington, and hold a personal interview with President Cleveland.

Gen. Adam E. King says it will not be sur, prising if Mr. Blaine makes up his mind after he leaves Michigan, to go to the Pacific slope. The invitations from the California people are very pressing, and they are putting forth every effort to induce their old friend to go there. General King says that Mr. Blaine is in excellent spirits, and delighted to be engaged in active campaign work again.

As an express train was rounding a curve near Indianapolis Sunday night, the trucks of a passenger coach mounted the switch and the car was thrown on its side. The coach was crowded with passengers, six of whom were severely injured and a number slightly bruised.

The tide guage at San Francisco Sunday recorded several irregular traces of an earthquake transmitted throughout the Pacific ocean. Professor Davidson says the waves travelled at the rate of 400 miles an hour. Wherever the earthquake had taken place it must have occurred from 6 to 18 hours before it was registered on the California coast.

Dr. H. S. Tanner, who became famous about eight years ago by fasting forty days in Clarendon hall, New York city, has just arrived in Chicago from New Mexico. He is apparently in perfect health, and his girth
about eight years ago by fasting forty days in Clarendon hall, New York city, has just arrived in Chicago from New Mexico. He is apparently in perfect health, and his girth is such as to suggest anything but abstinence from food. About the last news from the doctor, previous to his arrival, was that he was in New Mexico, living there on a purely vegetable diet. He says that he has been in Mexico for four years, pursuing investigations into the subject of suspended animation, or counterfeit death. He is convinced that large numbers of people are annually buried alive all over the world.

Henry George created a sensation in Philadelphia Saturday night. He spoke at the Academy of Music at the first grand rally of the campaign organized by the Democratic city committee. To the surprise of his audience and to the consternation of the Democrats, he boldly refuted President Cleveland's letter of acceptance, proclaimed himself an absolute free trader, and said that the re-election of President Cleveland meant the overthrow of protection.

Isaac W. Sulloway, the lumber dealer and prominent citizen, of Kingston, N. H., who was injured last week by being thrown from his carriage died Saturday from the effects of the injury.

Mr. G. W. Wilson who accompanied Mrs. Proctor on her journey north thinks Prof. Proctor died of a species of billious fever common in Florida and which resembles yellow fever. It is not contagious.

Great consternation prevails in Leadville, Colorado, over the opening of all the gambling dens after being closed for nearly five months. An order to that effect was issued Saturday by the mayor so as to pay off a bonded debt. It is thought that over $60,000 changed hands yesterday. Each den is required to pay $200 per month as a license fee.

Two negroes were shot to death by white men at Ville Platte Prairie, La., Sunday. Incendiation language used by the negroes is supposed to have been the cause.

The Chicago police have arrested a gang of small boys, whose ages range from 8 to 13 years, and who have committed burglaries attributed to experienced criminals.

Mojave Indians recently burned to death a young squaw, believing that she was a witch and responsible for an epidemic in the tribe. The sickness is believed to be typhoid fever, of a malignant type.

The opening of the Augusta, Ga., national exposition has been postponed from October 10th to November 3rd, to close December 15th. The reasons given are floods and yellow fever.

At twelve o'clock last night the switchmen in the Central yards at Ashland, Wis., went
on a strike. They want $2.25 and $2.50 per
day.
jean-pierre-salet-ville-platte-prairie-1.A11:
POINTED PARAGRAPHS.
Spicy Manner.

Joseph Link, died of lockjaw at Hopkinsville, Ky.

Findlay will dedicate her new court house October 31. Cost $200,000.

Harry Hall, aged seventeen, of Gargo, Ind., was accidentally shot by a companion.

The circuit court at Louisville commenced its fall term with fifteen murderers on the docket.

The first triennial congress of American physicians and surgeons is in session at Washington, D. C.

Stonecutters on the new court house at Columbia City, Ind., are on a strike because one was discharged.

The National Association of ex-Prisoners of War will live over their old time sufferings in Indianapolis.

Charles A. Pillsbury & Company, the Minneapolis millers, divided $40,000 profits among their employes.

The case of Mrs. Garrett, charged with murdering her two imbecile stepdaughters, is in progress at Medina, O.

Work has been resumed at Brown & Company's rolling mill, Pittsburg, the strikers going back at the old wages.

Hon. Sobieski Brady, secretary of state of West Virginia from 1876 to 1880, died at Wheeling, aged seventy-three.

Joseph Thomas, a miner employed in Burton's new mine near North Lawrence, O., was crushed to instant death by a fall of siate.

James Stole, a Wabash brakeman, was fatally injured at Wabash, Ind., while coupling the advertising car of Wallace's circus to his train.

Miscreants attempted to cast reflections upon a Prohibition meeting at Liberty, Ind., by unfurling rebel flags. The flags were promptly hauled down.

Jean Pierre Salet and another negro named Didacre were shot and killed at Platte Prairie, La., by a mob who objected to language used by the negroes.

Indiana is reported to be ablaze with political enthusiasm from lake to river, and the aforesaid boundaries are expected to get there later in the campaign.

Twenty-four Swedish girls arrived in New York Monday from Europe, under contract to marry men whom they knew only through correspondence and photographs.

The city council of Ripley, O., has appointed Col. O. Edwards, mayor pro tem., and removed F. F. Shaw, who has been on a continual spree since his election.

Indianapolis gas fitters kicked themselves out of the working harness on a question of 30 per cent. advance in wages and a reduction of work from ten hours to nine.

James McCann, aged twenty-eight, ran away from home in Williamsport, Pa., when but eight years old. He has returned to his family, after an absence of twenty years.

I. S. Pruitt fatally shot his wife and her lawyer and tried to kill himself in a 'squire's office at Kokomo, Ind. He became enraged because his wife had applied for a divorce.

Lewis Weddin, the man shot at Falmouth, Ky., Sunday, is still alive, with chances of recovery against him. John Hardin, who did the shooting, was held in $500 bond for trial.

Body of Abe Wilson, colored, was found shot and stabbed on the railroad near Mt. Sterling, Ky. The cautious chronicler reports that he is supposed to have been murdered.

At Canton, O., Miss Lucinda Gonder was walking with her betrothed, George McCurdy, when he fell dead at her side with hemorrhage of the lungs. The shock made her seriously ill.

In the Springfield, O., opera houses the audiences sit on their feet to keep them from being gnawed by the rats that sport at will over the floor during the performances. So says the local press.

At Portsmouth, O., Albert Gims, a six-year-old lad, while endeavoring to loosen a knot with a pair of scissors, the latter slipped, and piercing the ball of his right eye, destroyed the sight instantly.

Col. Henry B. Hubbard, an old and leading citizen of Wheeling, W. Va., who succeeded Col. Thoburn in command of the First West Virginia infantry when the latter was killed, died, aged seventy-two.

Congressman Dingley, of Maine, offered a resolution requesting the president to inform the house if American fishermen are denied any of their rights in Canadian waters, and when and where these rights were interfered with.

Weak minded man named Iverson, residing in Trinity county, California, blew his wife's brains out, took down the Bible and read a few chapters, and then scattered his own brains about. The babe was found playing in its parent's blood.

FRANK CORFREY and Miss Minnie Taffly were drowned on the 14th in the Schuylkill river at Philadelphia by the overturning of their row boat.

During the seven days ended on the 14th there were 124 business failures in the United States, against 157 the previous seven days. The total of failures in the United States January 1 to date is 7,007, against 6,675 in 1887.

The Roanoke river was on the 14th reported to have risen thirty-seven feet above high-water mark, flooding North Hampton and Halifax counties, N. C., destroying the entire corn and cotton crops in the lowlands, at an estimated loss of $500,006, drowning cattle, tearing houses from their foundations, and, it was feared, causing much loss of human life.

MRS. ELIZABETH LANGLIER and her five-year-old daughter, of Boston, were burned to death on the 14th by the upsetting of a kerosene lamp.

Fritz Sheen, a German farmer living near Hillsboro, Ill., died on the 14th after forty-eight hours' illness, and the doctors pronounced his case one of genuine Asiatic cholera.

At Winfield, O., on the 14th Richard Jones, while sick with typhoid fever, cut his throat in the presence of his wife and mother because they would not permit his children to see him.

While the paying teller of the Third National Bank of Buffalo, N. Y., was at lunch on the 14th a sneak-thief purloined a package containing $2,049.

Charles L. BODENDIECK, a pronounced Anarchist, was caught manufacturing bombs in Chicago on the 14th.

At Hampden Park, Springfield, Mass., on the 14th Johnston paced a quarter of a mile in 2914 seconds, beating all previous records for that distance.

ALEXANDER GOLDENSEN was hanged on the 14th at San Francisco for the murder of Mamie Kelly, a fourteen-year-old school girl, because she refused to accept his attention, and Dock Dangan, a negro, was hanged at Columbus, S. C., for the murder of William F. Coxe, a white boy.

A fire on the 14th at Washburn, Wis., wiped out the entire business section, destroying thirty buildings at a loss of $150,000, small insurance.

Forty three new cases and twelve deaths was the yellow fever record at Jacksonville, Fla., for the twenty-four hours ended on the 14th. Total number of cases to date, 830; total number of deaths to date, 116.

A man named Wise was lynched on the 14th in the Turtle mountain district of Dakota for horse-stealing.

CHARLES KLEIN, a night watchman at Fort Wayne, Ind., in a rage of jealousy against his wife, shot her fatally on the 14th and then killed himself.

Heavy frost in the section surrounding Mason City, Iowa, had on the 14th killed the grass and damaged corn severely, reducing the average acreage, it was estimated, by twelve bushels.

YELLOW FEVER broke out on the 14th at Hendersonville, N. C., among the refugees from Jacksonville.

At twenty-six leading clearing-houses in the United States the exchanges during the week ended on the 15th aggregated 1988,650,593,against $806,557,143 the previous week. As compared with the corresponding week of 1887 the increase amounted to 5.1 per cent.

By the upsetting of a boat on the 14th at Cary, Ill., Walter Graham and his two sisters, Maria and Sarah, were drowned. Their home was in Chicago.

SEVENTY workmen were overcome by coal gas on the 15th in the Hoosac tunnel near North Adams, Mass., and it was with great difficulty they were saved.

JOHN SPILINEK, of Omaha, Neb., a Bonemian tailor, in a fit of temporary insanity on the 16th fatally shot his wife and then killed himself.

FIVE employes who entered into a conspiracy and robbed the New York wholesale house in which they worked were on the 15th sentenced to Sing Sing for five years each.

W. D. Cox was on the 15th arrested at Marshall, Mo., for killing William Neece at Carroll, Ill., in 1877.

FIFTY-six buildings in the business portion of Florence, Wis., were destroyed by fire on the 15th.

While in a drunken rage on the 15th Andrew Ruhl, a farmer living near Manchester, Mo., visited the house of Fred Fink, a neighbor, shot him and his sister Minnie fatally, and then returned home and killed himself.

The official bulletin for the twenty-four hours ended on the 16th showed seventy-four new cases of yellow fever at Jacksonville and eight deaths. This made the total number of cases to date 295 and the total number of deaths 126.

Sherman Fabrier (colored) was lynched on the 15th at Whiteville, N. C., for assaulting an aged white woman.

A wind story in Washington on the 16th unroofed several buildings and uprooted many trees.

Ole Johnson, a Sweedish farmer living near Nebraska City, Neb., made a bet with Hans Erickson of his wife against a fifty-five dollar cow that Harrison would be elected President. The bet was declared to be a bona fide one, Mrs. Johnson agreeing to the wager.

A fire on the 15th at Spokane Falls, M. T., destroyed property valued at $100,000.

The oldest daughter of Byrd Smith, of Devine Station, Tex., attempted to start a fire on the 15th with kerosene oil, when the can exploded, scattering the burning oil over the girl and her two sisters and her baby brother, all of whom were burned to death.

The flood in the Savannah river had on the 16th covered the rice plantations near Savannah, Ga., and the rice crop was destroyed.

The discovery of rich gold mines at Bonanza Creek, M. T., was reported on the 15th.

On the 15th Mrs. Snell, widow of Amos J. Snell, the Chicago millionaire who was murdered in his house in February last, offered a reward of $20,000 for the capture of William B. Tascott, the supposed murderer.

The supply of wheat in sight in this country on the 17th was 300,000 bushels larger than a year ago, amounting to 31,378,431 bushels.

Incendiaries started a fire on the 17th at Paducah, Ky., which destroyed property valued at $200,000.

At Mount Sterling, Ky., on the 17th a young man named Bowen shot and killed a man named Estis and mortally wounded his two sons in a quarrel over working a road.

Charles A. Pillsbury & Co., Minneapolis millers, on the 17th divided $40,000 among their employes, in pursuance of a profit-sharing plan.

Yellow fever made its appearance on the 17th at Gainesville, Fla., six persons being stricken down.

The picking department of the New Albany (Ind.) woolen and cotton mills was burned on the 17th, and eight hundred operators were thrown out of employment.

A Brutal Crime.
A St. Martiusville special of the 17th inst., to the Times-Democrat, says:

News reached here this morning of one of the most cowardly crimes that ever was committed in this parish. Friday night, at about 11 o'clock, in the vicinity of Breaux Bridge, a gang of four or five parties, some of them so far unknown, whipped a black man, criminally assaulted one black woman and killed another. The particulars gathered from the mother of the dead woman are about as follows:

"On Friday night the gang called at the door of the woman's house and knocked, saying that it was the sheriff. She opened the door and recognized one of the parties, Sam Polk. She shut the door on them. They then fired through the door several shots, one of them taking effect in the woman's abdomen, and she died next morning."

The coroner's inquest revealed the fact that she bore seven months' twins, one of them having the ball through his head. The man Polk was recognized as having engaged in the three crimes. His hat was also found at the door of the cabin. He was not found when search was made for him.

The white people are indignant and very much excited. Warrants have been issued against Polk and three other parties suspected to have participated in the crimes. The white people will see that the colored people are protected and justice done.

Baby Carriages, at Albert's. Double Murder in St. Landry.

An Opelousas special, of the 17th inst., to the N. O. Picayune, says:

"Yesterday morning, at Ville Platte prairie, a crowd of armed men rode to the house of two negroes named Jean Pierre-Salet and Sidairo, and after leading them a short distance, riddled them with buckshot, killing both men instantly. This killing is supposed to have been brought about by the incendiary language recently used by these two negroes. The affair created intense excitement in the neighborhood where it occured.

Princess Letitia Bonaparte, who has just married her uncle, the Duke of Aosta, can amuse herself by calculating the odd relationship which she has entered into. She will be at the same time the daughter and sister-in-law of her own mother; niece and sister-in-law of the King of Italy, and cousin and mother-in-law of the duke's children by his former marriage. She will also be the aunt of Princess Amelia d'Orleans, the present Duchess of Braganza. The duke is not far behind, for he will be the son-in-law of his sister and of his brother-in-law, also brother-in-law of his nephews and nephew of his brother and of his sister.

THE CLEVELAND GAZETTE is the oldest, and has the largest bona fide circulation of any Newspaper in the interest of the Colored People, published in the State of Ohio, and comparison with any will immediately establish its rank as one of the NEWSIEST AND BEST in the country.

OUR CHAMBERSBURG, Pa., Findlay, O., and several other letters arrived a day late this week and hence their non-appearance in this issue. It is useless to mail correspondence any week later than Tuesday.

THE THIRD ANNUAL Fair of the (colored) Industrial and State Fair Association of Arkansas will be held in Pine Bluff, Ark., October 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13. Prof. J. C. Corbin is president of the association, Mr. Wiley Jones, treasurer, and S. J. Hollensworth, secretary. THE GAZETTE acknowledges the receipt of courtesies.

AS AN ENCOURAGEMENT to our youth we wish to give the following: Edward Byrd, of Ashland, O., recently went to Carthage, Mo., to stand an examination for a position as teacher in the "colored" school of that place. His standing was one hundred per cent in twelve and ninety-nine per cent in the thirteenth study in which he was examined. It is hardly necessary to add that he was given a position.

GENERAL LEGITIME, who is announced as the new President of Hayti, in place of Salomon deposed, is one of the two officials whom the latter sent out of the country in the early part of June with a present of $5,000 and six months' salary each. He is a mulatto who had always claimed to uphold the interests of the black party, but his fidelity in this respect has been somewhat questioned, and altogether the outlook for a quiet submission to his rule is not yet reassuring. The mulattoes and the blacks are still arrayed against each other in Hayti.

SOME SOUTHERN Democrat ought to send the Springfield, O., Buckeye club a leather medal. If the Republicans wish to lose this fall in Ohio, all they have to do is to tolerate such organizations as the Buckeye club. At this rate it will not be long until we will be obliged to call upon the Republican party of Ohio, to pass an Ely-Arnett bill to wipe out the discrimination on account of color being practiced in the party ranks by hypocrites claiming to be Republicans. Attorney Newberry is more of a gentleman and a better Republican, than any of the scamps in the Buckeye club who black-balled him Monday night.

OPELOUSAS, La.—At Ville Platte Prairie a crowd of armed men recently rode to the house of two Negroes, Jean Pierre Salet and Didears, and after leading them a short distance away, riddled them with buckshot, killing them instantly. The tragedy is supposed to have been brought about by incendiary language recently used by these Negroes.—Ex.

It is a matter of regret that we are so situated in the South that we are unable to help ourselves and are compelled to take everything put upon us—insult, abuse, outrage of the foulest kind—all for no other reason than that of color. The solution of the Negro problem is slow work, and at times discouraging. But we must be firm and resolute and undaunted. We must fight it out if it takes a generation to do it. Violence, intimidation, fraud and murder must cease. The present system of bulldozing must be stopped.

NOTWITHSTANDING the many drawbacks, the Jubilee of Freedom held upon the Centennial grounds in Columbus, O., last Saturday, was a grand success. Bishop Arnett's oration, Rev. James Poindexter's opening address, J. Madison Bell's "Ode to Freedom," Miss Hallie Q. Brown's readings, Prof. John F. Ransom's solo work and chorus directing, the Schubert Club's chorus work, and the Excelsior Reed and Brass Band's rendition of overtures, medleys and numerous selections, as well as its accompaniment of H. C. Smith's cornet solo, were all what they should be, delighting an audience of nearly 5,000 persons, at least one-third of whom were whites. The affair was a credit to the race and the participants have every reason to feel proud.

T. E. BURTON, Esq., the Republican Congressional nominee of this, the Twenty-first Ohio district, is a young man who, by his ability as a scholar and a student, has made for himself a leading place in the legal profession of Ohio. He is a graduate and was for some years a tutor at Oberlin college, where, by his association with colored students and colored residents, he became greatly interested in the race. To-day few men have a better acquaintance with the leading colored men of the country than Mr. Burten. As a finished orator he is among the best in Ohio, as was illustrated by his masterly speech in reply to Judge Blandin's free trade address at Music Hall recently. There is no doubt of his election, this being a Republican district. Mr. Burton, as a candidate for Congress, will add strength to the Republican ticket.

STATE SCHOOL COMMISSIONER TAPPAN has received a letter from J. A. Wilcox, superintendent of the public schools at Bainbridge, O., stating that he was ordered by the board of education to deny colored children admission to the schools, and asking what

he should do under the circumstances. Commissioner Tappan sent the following reply:

"You have no right to deny admission to any child merely on account of color. If the board of education insist on your doing so, they ought as individuals to guarantee you against all damages that may be recovered. Unless they do so with a good and sufficient bond of indemnity, I advise you to refuse to obey them. Your advice to admit the children was good. I do not advise you to deny the children, but if you do so be sure that you are fully indemnified."

Mr. Tappan counsels well. The duty of the colored residents of Bainbridge is made clear by his reply. The law is upon our side. Let them be prepared when necessary to appeal to it and secure damages in every case where one of their children is refused. If Mr. Wilcox is instructed to refuse colored children admittance and guaranteed indemnification by the board of education, let our people in Bainbridge prosecute Wilcox to the fullest extent of the law and secure the heaviest damages possible. If it must be done, why teach the trash that they can not and shall not withhold from us a single right the Constitution of the United States and the law of Ohio grants us as law-abiding American citizens. FIGHT THEM! If help is needed, call upon our people throughout Ohio and we know there are hundreds who will gladly respond. We rise or fall together and must help one another.

Talk about the rebellion in Haytfl, but where on earth can there be found worse state of affairs than reigns in parts of Louisiana now. Hundreds of innocent people are shot down for no other cause than that they desire their rights. Part of Louisiana is now in the hands of outlaws, murderers, thieves, cutthroats, assassins, and these scourges of humanity are Anglo Saxon white men. In the jungles of Africa among the Cannibals can not be found a worse sort of incarnate devils. Yet the newspapers edited by Christian gentlemen and the pulpits where Christ ought to be preached in dorser and encourage those murderers. What will become of this world if there is a God?

The damage to North Carolina cotton by floods is estimated at fifteen per cent.

The dumping of four hundred yellow fever refugees at Hendersonville, N. C., has caused much uneasiness in Charleston, S. C., as quite a number of Charlestonians have summer homes in that neighborhood.

The cotton factors of Savannah, Ga., have organized a pool to fight the Bagging Trust by importing the covering of last year's cotton and using it in place of syndicate bagging. Samples of old covering have been secured and the plan is pronounced practicable. Since the organization of the pool, syndicate bagging has been offered at one-quarter to one-half cent less than quotations.

Two men named Steele and Mockabee, both drunk, boarded a train at Mt. Sterling, Ky., a few days since and fought all the way to Stepstone, where the conductor, for the safety of those in his charge, put the men off and told them to fight it out. They drew pistols and exchanged five shots each. The fifth shot from Steele's pistol passed through Mockabee's brain, killing him instantly. They were cousins. After the killing Steele boarded the train and proceeded home, the train having waited until the duel was over.

At a special election recently the citizens of Augusta, Ga., voted an extra levy of one per cent., to repair the damages to the city caused by the recent floods.

J. B. Bobb, a prominent citizen of Trenton, Ky., while engaged in a mill, a few days ago, had one of his hands cut off with a circular saw. His suffering was so great that there was fear of look jaw.

The survivors of the Jones and Green families of Hancock County, who have been at war since last February, were placed on trial at Sneedville, Tenn., for murder. Every citizen going into the town was searched. Fifty special deputies were standing guard about the courthouse.

The jury in the case of ex-Secretary of State Will A. Strong, of Louisiana, charged with embezzling about $3,500 from the State, agreed upon a verdict. The sheriff went out to call the Attorney-General, and Strong walked out behind him, attracting no attention. He was declared guilty, but is not to be found.

Louis Hill, a negro fugitive from Union County, Miss., was arrested near Memphis, Tenn., recently, by the sheriff of Union County, who came upon him accidentally. Five years ago Hill resolved to get rid of his wife in order to wed a dusky belle who had enslaved him, and tried to poison her by boiling a moccasin snake's head in her coffee.

A partly-constructed bridge over a ravine in the southern part of Paducah, Ky., gave way a few days ago, and five carpenters—W. F. Brown, J. L. House, H. Palien, Robertson and Roberts—were severely hurt by falling twenty-five feet. John Bachman, who was standing on the bridge watching the men at work, was caught between the timbers and fatally injured, both legs being broken and his head crushed.

The negroes of Tuscaloosa, Ala., are in a terrible fright and meet every night to pray for deliverance from the voodoo. Their meetings often last all night. Flora Baker, a respectable colored woman, owned two horses. A few days since in ese suddenly became sick and died a few hours later. Flora said they had been voodooed and had their stomachs opened. In the stomach of one was found a green snake eight inches long, while the stomach of the other one contained two small lizards. The negroes of the town at once became greatly alarmed, fearing some great harm would come to them through the unknown and mysterious voodoo.

M. V. Ingram, of Clarksville, Tenn., has issued a call for a meeting of the tobacco planters of the State, to be held in Clarksville on the 20th inst., to take action on the proposition to head off the Regie monopolies and secure full value for the very large crop of tobacco now being housed. The planters will be asked to sign an agreement pledging themselves not to plant any tobacco next year, on condition that a general organization of planters is effected to this end before the 1st of February next.

A fight occurred between George Whitt (white) and a colored laborer at Gadsden, Ala., a few nights ago. Whitt and his friends fired on five negroes from ambush, killing two and wounding the three others. Later in the night negroes armed themselves, and a regular battle between the two parties followed. Several are reported killed and wounded.

There was a strange stew in a church in Burke County, N. C., recently. People who had occasion to enter the building were horrified at seeing a dead man lying on the floor, and beside him a bottle of liquor. An investigation of the case was at once begun, and a most disgraceful state of affairs was brought to light. The dead man was Horace Cardwell, and, in company with two other abandoned fellows, John Mitchell and Columbus Mitchell, he had gone to the church to have a drunken spree. The three had purchased five quarts of brandy, and in a night drank it all save half a pint. When daylight came the Mitchells left. Cardwell lay unconscious on the floor. He never awoke, and was found horribly swollen and distorted. The men had lighted the lamps in the church and had a regular orgy.

joe-joiner-hulto-1888-10-15.A1: A TEXAS LYNCHING.—Joe Joiner, a negro, attempted to assault S. W. Wolsey's twelve-year-old daughter, near Hutto, Texas, Sunday evening. He was frustrated in his attempt by the screams of the child and her little sister, and attempted to make his escape by mounting a horse and leaving. A posse was soon gathered and started in pursuit of him. He was overtaken 6 miles from Hutto, and was shot through the shoulder before being captured. The posse returned with him to Hutto, and at 11 o'clock at night he was hanged to a tree by unknown parties.

A Negro Lynched.
TAYLOR, Tex., Oct. 16.—Joe Joiner, a negro, was lynched at Hulto, near here, yesterday. Joiner attempted an assault upon a 12 year old white girl, and was arrested. On the road to the jail a mob of masked men seized the prisoner and hanged him.

Special Telegram to the Statesman.

ROUND ROCK, October 16.—The 10-year-old daughter of Mr. Woolsey, of Hutto, was criminally assaulted by a negro named Joe Joyner. Her sister, hearing the screams of the little girl, came to her rescue. The rape fiend fled. He stole a horse, mounted it and put out in the direction of Round Rock. He was overtaken and arrested near this place. Subsequently a mob of masked men took him from the officers and, carrying him to the scene of the crime, hanged him to a tree.

TELEGRAPHIC SUMMARY.
HIGHLAND, Ill., Oct. 16.—The boiler of a traction engine exploded last evening on a farm near here, resulting in instant death of the owner of the engine, and seriously injuring 4 other men.

TAYLOR, Texas, Oct. 16 —Joe Joiner, a negro, was lynched at Hulto, near here, yesterday. Joiner attempted an assault upon a 12 years old white girl, and was arrested by the sheriff. On the road to the jail a mob of masked men seized the prisoner and hanged him to a tree.

ST. ALBANS, Vt., Oct. 17.—Horace Ellsworth's house and barn in East Fletcher were burned yesterday with all the hay and grain in the barn. Some farm machinery was also destroyed. Although the two buildings were some distance apart they were both found on fire at the same time.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 13.—At Johnson City, 100 miles east of this city, 14 guests of Smith's hotel are reported to have been poisoned by something eaten at supper. Three have died and several others it is feared cannot recover. It is believed that the poison was administered intentionally by some one unfriendly to the proprietor.

JESSUP, Ga., Oct. 16.—In January, 1886, Robert J. Smith of this city was murdered by Lewis Edwards, colored, who was sentenced to life imprisonment. His attorney secured a new trial and the case was to have begun yesterday. Sunday night the sheriff brought Edwards here, and at 3 o'clock Monday morning a party of masked men entered the jail and shot him dead.

WILKES BARRE, Penn., Oct. 16.—Another terrible accident occurred on the Lehigh Valley Railroad this morning. A construction train was unloading ties at the Tamand siding, near Lost Creek, on the Pottsville branch, when a fast Pennsylvania freight came along and dashed into the construction cars. Of the 40 Hungarians who were at work unloading ties, 6 were killed outright, and 26 injured. A brakeman on the Pennsylvania train was killed outright. Twenty of the freight cars were wrecked. It was 3 hours before help could be procured and during that time the injured lost so much blood that it is feared many of them will die.

NEW YORK, Oct. 11.—There was another large fire this morning in Greenpoint, which will result in a damage of $200,000, besides the injuring of several brave firemen. From what can be learned the fire broke out early this morning on board the steamer Navis, which was lying at the wharf of Pennsylvania and Scranton Coal Co., at the foot of North Tenth St. The flames then extended to other vessels and although three alarms were sent out to which the firemen quickly responded, the fire spread with surprising rapidity, communicating from the vessels to the pier, and from there to shipping department and buildings of the Standard Oil Works. Three vessels and the steamer Navis were all partially burned. An explosion of an oil well severely burned 6 firemen, besides injuring some of them otherwise. There were about 5,000 barrels of oil burned.

QUINCY, Ill., Oct. 11.—A grand stand was erected here yesterday to accommodate 5,000 people who were to witness the display of fireworks, "The Bombardment of Alexandria." The amphitheatre was crowded with people, and probably not less than 6,000 were massed upon the seats. Scarcely had the first rocket been fired when the supports at the west end of the structure gave away, the 800 feet of seats sidled over and the vast multitude were hurled upon the ground and buried in the mass of lumber which fell upon them. The air was filled with the cries and moans of the injured, while the panic stricken sought escape from the debris. With the descent of the platform the electric lights, which were to light the grounds, but which were extinguished to aid the display, were incapacitated for service and the darkness of the scene added to its terrors. As the lights from the pyrotechnics lighted up the place the able bodied sought their friends, while the more humane began the work of aiding the injured. Some say that fully 500 people were hurt, and this is probably true, but 150 will doubtless include those who were injured at all seriously.

WILKESBARRE, Penn., Oct 11.—Throughout the night the depot was throughed by hundreds of persons suffering untold agony over the uncertainty, the railroad people refusing to give any information regarding the accident.

The throng was loud in its denunciation of the company for refusing this information and causing needless suffering. Many persons wanted to go to the scene of the disaster, and endeavored to charter a locomotive, but the favor could not be obtained. After waiting from 10 to 3 in the morning many persons took the south bound train, which passed here at 3:10, and went to the scene of the accident.

It was there learned that the third section of the excursion train had stood on the track a few hundred yards from Mud Run, waiting for sections ahead to get out of the way. A flagman some say, had been sent back with a lantern to guard the train from the rear. Suddenly the passengers on the platform saw a train approaching at a high rate of speed. Several saw the danger and jumped and escaped. There was a frightful crash and the engine plunged her full length into the train. The shock drove the rear car through the next one for two-thirds its length, and the second car was forced into the third. Not a single person escaped from the rear car. The second was crowded with maimed and bleeding bodies, and the third had but few passengers who escaped. When the steam and smoke cleared from the rear car its awful sights were revealed. The timbers were crushed and wrenched, while on all sides hung mangled bodies and limbs. The few bodies which were not mangled, were burned and scalded by the steam, and little remained in the car which bore human semblance.

When the shock of the crash had subsided, the uninjured began to do what could be done for their unfortunate companions. The St. Francis Pioneer Corps, who were on the train, plied with zeal the broad axes which were meant for holiday occasions. They were but little adapted to the work and were soon useless. To free the bodies in the rear car the train men attached a locomotive to the wrecked engine and started to pull it from the wreck. The first movement of the shattered wreck brought from the wounded such awful cries that friends ordered the engineer to desist on pain of his life. The few houses about the spot were thrown open to the suffering, and bonfires lighted to aid the work of relief.

The passengers give many different accounts of the probable cause of the accident, some attributing it to the negligence of the flag man in not going back with the red light, others saying the fourth section which ran into the third had no air brakes. The latest figures give the skilled at 55 and the injured at 40. The scenes at the depot when the trains with the dead and wounded were expected were heartrending in the extreme. Several hundred persons assembled, and it was pitiful to see the parents looking for their children. and husbands for their wives and friends for friends.

LATER NEWS.
JOHN WATERS was stoned to death at Pittsfield, Mass., by a party of drunken men whose orgies he and his wife had interrupted.

WHILE Mrs. William Morgan, of Donaldson, Penn., was sitting in her dining-room nursing her infant her six-year-old son picked up a shotgun and discharged it. The entire charge entered the head, face, breast and shoulders of the unfortunate woman and the back and head of the infant, fatally wounding them.

The non-fulfilment of the full terms of his agreement by Yerkes, the Chicago street railroad man, has led to a renewal of the street disturbances and of the strike.

A DECISION has been rendered by Judge Sawyer in the United States Circuit Court, San Francisco, upon two test cases under the recent Chinese Exclusion act. The Court affirms the constitutionality of the act, and holds that all Chinese now in the San Francisco harbor, as well as those on the way from China, must be sent back.

PRESIDENT CLEVELAND has approved the act authorizing the establishment of life-saving stations along the coast.

MRS. ADA M. BETTINGER, of Lincoln, Neb., has been admitted to practice before the United States Supreme Court, being the third woman accorded this privilege.

A CONSPIRACY against the Dutch residents in Java has been discovered at Madion. Forty-two of the ringleaders in the movement were arrested, and eleven others who refused to surrender were killed.

Forty thousand copies of Dr. Mackenzie's book on Emperor Frederick's case have been seized at Leipsic by the police. The book is not allowed to be sold in Berlin. The police have seized copies exposed for sale at book stores in Berlin.

The French Chamber of Deputies has assembled, and Premier Floquet introduced his bill to revise the Constitution.

Fire resulting from an explosion of gas destroyed the Cameron Colliery at Shamokin, Penn., entailing a loss of $75,000.

A FRESHET in the Penobscot River has caused great damage to pulp mills and paper factories. Bangor, Me., has been partially under water, and the damage to machinery and buildings is enormous.

Joseph Joiner was lynched by citizens, indignant at his career of crime, on his way to jail at Hulto, Texas.

Lewis Edwards, a colored murderer, was shot dead by a party of masked men who broke into the jail at Jessup, Ga.

Hon. John Wentworth, better known as 'Long John,' a wealthy citizen and a amous pioneer of Chicago, has died of old age.

The Senate has confirmed the following nominations: Harry E. Shields, to be Receiver of Public Moneys at Seattle, Washington Territory; George S. Duryee, to be United States Attorney for the District of New Jersey, and James A. Moore, to be United States Marshal for Nevada.

LORD MOUNT TEMPLE, a wealthy and famous Englishman, is dead. He was seventy-seven years of age and leaves no heir.

THE German Emperor, accompanied by King Humbert of Italy and the Duke d'Aosta visited Naples, and was enthusiastically received by the populace.

A COURIER has arrived from the Congo (Africa) Free State bringing details of the death of Major Barttelot, who was killed by a porter in the Stanley relief expedition in revenge for ill-treatment. The murderer was placed under arrest and has since been hanged.

The New York club has 70 games to its credit, and Chicago 65.
Pretty Hattie B. Flack of St. Louis eloped with and married a negro.
Walter Grantham and his two sisters were drowned in Fox river.
The steam barge St. Joseph was burned while shooting the St. Clair rapid.
There are reports out that Professor Proctor did not die of yellow fever.
Dr. Tanner believes he can hibernate, in bear style, for months, without food or drink.
Dominick McCaffrey says he has $5,000 backing him to fight either Kilrain or Mitchell.
St. Louis leads in the American Association games with 75 games, against 69 for Brooklyn.
Lelia Farrell, an attractive burlesque actress has sued Nat Goodwin for $10,000 for breach of promise.
Mrs. Cleveland has been presented with a fine Russian staghound. Some one may yet send her an elephant.
Haggin's Firenzi won a grand mile and an eighth race at Coney Island on Saturday, with 125 pounds up, in 1:56—1:56².
Sixty-nine men were overcome by gas in a railroad tunnel in Massachusetts and narrowly escaped being run over by a train.
A Quincy, Ill., man who violated the fishing law, was arrested while going to church, although he carried a shotgun to defend himself.
John L. Sullivan, the pugilist, is lying critically ill at Trenton Cottage, Crescent Beach. He is suffering from a very severe attack of gastric fever.
An attempt was made by a mob of 300 at Pittsburg to break down the doors of the lock-up at Rochester, Pa., and lynch John Nicoli, an Italian charged with assaulting two little girls.

A terrific explosion occurred on Saturday at the National Milling Company's mill in Cleveland. There were eighteen people in the mill at the time. Seven men are unaccounted for, and it is feared three are still in the ruins. The mill took fire from the explosion and was entirely destroyed. Peter Giarmann perished in the flames. Four others were severely burned and bruised.

FOREIGN.

The Czar and Czarian decline to see Queen Natalie.

The Socialists will hold an International Congress.

The relations between the powers are as sensitive as ever.

The shortage of the French wheat crop is estimated at 100,000,000 hectoliters.

Premier Mercier has caused a sensation by raising the cry, "Quebec for the French!"

It is said that Mr. Langtry will not now oppose the granting of a divorce to the "Jersey Lilly."

Striking workmen were charged by the military at Pierre Bouffierre, France, and seven persons were wounded.

The Porte's protest against the Italian annexation of Massowah was a surprise to the Central European powers.

Several important changes in the Salisbury Ministry are undoubtedly pending. The change will probably include the displacement of Hon. W. H. Smith, First Lord of the Treasury, and Home Secretary Matthews.

Advices from Samoa state that the natives have rebelled on account of the attempt of Herr Branders, a German official, to induce them to confirm the name of Malietoa upon Tamasese; also because taxation is excessive.

PACIFIC COAST.

The Santa Maria Fair is ended.

Rain fell in many towns in the State on Saturday.

Orland has voted in favor of issuing irrigation bonds.

The loss by the Spokane Falls fire will reach $100,000.

Major Glenn died at Willows from the effects of a fall.

Political conventions and many meetings were held on Saturday.

John McGuire, a Mexican war veteran, died suddenly at Santa Rosa.

The telegraph office at San Pablo was struck by lightning on Saturday.

The residence and soda factory of George W. Madison, of Red Bluff, was burned on Saturday.

Bernard Conway, convicted of murder in the second degree at Mariposa, has been sent to Folsom for ten years.

Two burglars were discovered in Dr. J. W. Goodwin's residence at Pomona, and one was shot, though both made their escape.

The delegates to the Sovereign Grand Lodge of Odd Fellows at Los Angeles arrived on Saturday, and were received with typical California hospitality.

T. E. Beck, the witness and perhaps accomplice after the fact in the case of the murder of Henderson by Lee Sykes in Shasta county, who escaped a short time ago from the Tehama County Jail, has been recaptured.

B. F. Neah, of Neah City, Or., was accidentally shot near that place by his companion, George Archibald, who mistook him for an animal. Deceased was a highly respected citizen. He leaves a wife and several children.

John Payne met a dreadful death in Pine canyon, near Fillmore, Utah, on the 5th. He was taking home a load of lumber, and in some way, by the slipping or breaking of the brake rope, he was thrown under the wagon, the wheels passing over him, crushing the skull and breaking the bones of his body. The horses took the load home, and search was made for Payne and his dead body found in the road. He probably died instantly.

Mr. Carlisle has been re-nominated to Congress from the Sixth Kentucky district.

An incendiary fire, at Paducah, Ky. caused a loss of $200,000, half covered by insurance.

Dr. B. Brawble of Cincinnati has purchased Libby Prison at public auction for $11,000.

Keely states that it will take $100,-000 to put his motor in such a condition that it would operate.

The German-Australian steamship company has been founded at Hamburg, with a capital of 4,000,000 marks.

It is estimated that over two thousand speeches are being delivered every night now throughout Hoosierdom.

The bill to create an executive department of agriculture stands at the head of the Senate calendar as unfinished business.

The international literary and artistic congress at Venice has declined to authorize that copyright shall include the right of translation.

The business portion of Florence, Wis., was wiped out by fire Friday afternoon. Fifty-six buildings were, burned. No particulars. Loss, $75,000.

At a caucus of the Democratic members of the House held a few days ago it was decided that the House should not initiate an adjournment resolution.

The news of the spreading of yellow fever at Decatur, Alatama, is confirmed. There is great excitement there and people are fleeing. The stores are all closing up.

The Chronicle's Berlin correspondent says that Prince Bismarck has asked Emperor William's permission to resign, but that it is unlikely that any change will be made at present.

An attempt was made by a mob of 300 Saturday night to break down the doors of the lock-up at Rochester, Pa., and lynch John Nicoli, an Italian charged with assaulting two little girls.

Spokane Falls, Washington Territory, has just been visited by another fire, which destroyed about $35,000 worth of property. The insurance is about $15,000. There is every reason to suspect that these frequent fires are the results of incendiaries.

The Calumet and Hecla company offers $20,000 reward for information leading to the conviction of the persons who set fire to Hecla shaft No. 1 in the sixteenth level last November. This shows that the fire is at last conceded to be of incendiary origin.
R. F. Seymour, who says he is from Chicago, in daylight stole five packages of money from two New York banks, the aggregate being $11,700. After he had fired three shots at the officers who chased him, he was caught. All the money save $2,000 was recovered.

Rear Admiral Kimberly, commanding the Pacific station, telegraphs to the secretary of the navy from San Francisco that he has sent word to the commander of the United States steamer Nipsic, at Calao, to proceed at once to Samoa for the protection of American interests.

A wholesale haul of horse thieves was made Tuesday night by Deputy Sheriff Rogers of Crook county, who captured five of the gentry near Sundance. They had in their possession a band of horses, some stolen from Dundy county, Nebraska, ranchmen and others as indicated by the brands from Kansas and Texas.

News received from the South Seas shows there was heavy fighting on the Marquesa group before the natives allowed the French to hoist their flag and take possession. Two hundred French warriors and several thousand natives were killed. The natives retreated to the mountains, from whence it will be difficult to dislodge them.

A heavy fire is reported at Spokane Falls, Washington Territory, which destroyed a whole business block, doing damage amounting to $100,000 and but partially insured. During the progress of the fire an explosion occurred, but no one was injured. For some time it looked as if all the business portion of the town would be destroyed.

A special from Paola, Kansas, says a ghastly discovery was made at the Fort Scott & Memphis depot to-day. Last Tuesday a mysterious box was left there by a well dressed man, who asked to have it checked to Fontana, Kansas. By some mishap the box was broken and a skeleton exposed to view. The mysterious stranger promptly fled.

John Murphy, deputy postmaster of Artesian City, Meade county, Kansas, was arrested Monday on the charge of robbing the United States Express Company of $10,100. The robbery was committed at Greenville, Ohio, a year ago. Murphy was a driver for the company. He confessed his guilt and returned $8,000 of the stolen money. He is now on his way to Ohio.

A Jacksonville dispatch of the 18th says: "We have had a bright, sunshine but delusive day, in which the pestilence has seemed to do its worst. It has been the most terrible in our history. The record of new cases is 156 for the 24 hours ending at 8 p. m. This includes some 35 cases reported by the medical bureau just after the official reports closed. The death roll is twenty."
