The question of woman suffrage in Washington Territory came up recently before Judge Nash at Spokane Falls on a test case. The Judge delivered a lengthy opinion last Friday in which he decided the act of the Legislature extending franchise to women unconstitutional.

Joe Bateright, a negro aged 22 years, was sold under hammer at Marshall, Mo., last Friday afternoon at the courthouse steps for vagrancy, the purchaser taking possession of him for six months. The highest price bid was $6.50. There were several other small bids. A large crowd witnessed the sale.

The residence of Rev. Wm. Mackay, Waldron, Ark., was destroyed by fire on Tuesday of last week. His brother-in-law, John Smith, was arrested on the charge of arson and placed in jail. Public sentiment ran high against him as he was taken from the jail and twice strung up, but taken down again when cooler counsel prevailed and taken back to jail.

The House committee on elections has heard all the arguments in the Smalls-Elliott contested election case from the Seventh South Carolina district, but will not attempt to dispose of it until the Sullivan-Felton contest from California is disposed of, and which is set for a hearing to-morrow.

Professor Chambers, of North Carolina,

Professor Chambers, of North Carolina, addressed the House committee on education last Friday in favor of a bill creating a commission to inquire into, and report upon the material and mental progress of the colored race since 1865. The committee took up the consideration of the Blair educational bill, but only succeeded in making a few changes in phraseology, the point of action not being reached.

In respect of patronage the position of postmaster general is now the most important in the Cabinet. The 50,000 postmasters who are responsible for their appointment to the chief of the department, are supplemented by an immense number of clerks who serve at Washington, on the railroads and as examiners and inspectors all over the country, and the postmaster general is to the people at large almost as influential a man as the President himself.

In 1890 will end the term of 100 years during which the cities of Boston and Philadelphia have each enjoyed the revenue from a bequest of $5,000 made by Benjamin Franklin. The money was to be loaned out to young married artificers, and the trust has been executed, although the lapse of a century requires a new disposition of the funds. It is significant that while in Boston the $5,000 has grown to nearly $328,000, in Philadelphia the $5,-000 has become only $70,000.

Mr. Jefferson Davis is not often epigrammatic, but in his letter to the ladies of the Monumental Association of Mississippi, there is a phrase that is sure to live. Speaking of the fact that the monument which was begun at Jackson on Friday is the first to be raised by Mississippi to her sons, Mr. Davis says that the omission cannot be ascribed to the absence of meritorious claims to such consideration, for "Mississippians have neither been of the war party in peace, nor of the peace party in war." This is better than "invincible in peace, invisible in war" with which the public has become familiar.

— A destructive cyclone swept over Brownton, Texas, 25 miles east of Bonham, last Thursday evening, destroying the Methodist, Baptist and Congregational churches and eight dwellings. One building was carried across a railroad track and crushed. Amanda Willis (colored), who had taken refuge inside, was instantly killed. Eight persons, including the sheriff and county recorder, were fatally injured. The damage will exceeded $12,000. The path of the storm was three hundred yards wide and everything within those limits, crops, fences, barns, outhouses and trees, was swept away. A terrible rain, hail and lightning storm followed.

— On Wednesday last, the supreme court of Missouri received the mandate of the United States supreme court in the case of Hugh Brooks, alias Maxwell, the Englishman convicted of the sensational Southern hotel murder. Court adjourned without fixing the date for the execution. It will not convene again until June 4, when the date for the execution will be named, and the mandate forwarded to the sheriff of the county. Maxwell was not much affected when he was informed that the State court would in a few days dispose of his case forever. His trans-Atlantic friends are working hard on Secretary Bayard, Minister Phelps, Minister West and Governor Moorehouse. A half dozen different petitions are in circulation, but the signatures are few.

— Of all the incidents connected with the recent floods out West, perhaps none was more thrilling than that related of the father who "was on the levee working with other farmers when the embankment gave way. Mounting his horse he had a mad race with the advancing waters for his home, where his three little children were sleeping. Reaching there just as the water struck the house, he placed the children in a wagon and started for the bluffs. The rapidly advancing flood floated the wagon box from the wheels and two of the children were drowned, Johnson saying himself and his little daughter. The child is all he has left of a happy home and a farm af 200 acres." This pathetic story from real life might furnish the theme for a companion poem to Miss Ingelow's well known "High-tide on the coast of Lincolnshire."

— Judge Speer, of the United States district court, in a case heard before him at Macon, Ga., last week, holds that decoy letters sent out to catch postal officials are not such letters as the law contemplates when it punishes those who tamper with them. The case arose out of the trial of Rudolph Dennicke, a route agent on the Central Railroad between Macon and Atlanta. The number of letters tampered with on that run was so large that a strict watch was instituted. A decoy letter addressed to an imaginary person in Atlanta was mailed in Macon. At Barnesville, half way along the route, a postoffice inspector entered the car, arrested Dennicke, and found the letter, with the seal broken, upon his person. The trial of the case has excited much interest. When the evidence was all in, Judge Speer ordered the jury to bring in a verdict of not guilty, as the bogus character of the letter affected the entire proceeding. This will break up a very common practice among the post-office detectives.

— A few years ago leprosy was considered one of the impossible diseases in this land. It was held to be a peculiar development of unsanitary conditions incident to long past ages. It was, to be sure, known that in Africa, and possibly among the Chinese, leprosy still lingered. But now it has fairly located itself in America, and is one more evil that may reach enormous proportions. Dr. Allen, in the New York Medical Journal, concludes: " (1) Leprosy has existed in this country to some extent for twenty years; (2) the tendency is for the disease to increase, not only from immigration, but from sporadic cases; (3) it is a contagious disease, and may also be transmitted from parent to offspring; (4) transmission takes place in some case by inoculation; (5) segregation has been proved to be the only sure means of freeing a country from its ravages; (6) it is the duty of the Government to establish leprosy hospitals or isolated settlements for the treatment of the afflicted."

— At Helena, Ark., there is a wonderful colored man named Mack Hamilton, who has been making a show of himself on the streets of that town. His appetite is always in good order, and for a dime he will eat enough to convince the most skeptical that there is no trick about it. ITEMS OF INTEREST.

RUSSELL SAGE once lost a wallet containing $44,000, and a clergyman found and restored it.

It is said there is a single county of Iowa that raises more wheat each year than all the New England States.

A cat belonging to W. C. Strickhouser, who lives near Gettysburg, Pa., killed a blacksnake three and one-half feet long the other day.

The skeleton of six men who must have been giants were unearthed the other day, along with much pottery, in a big mound near Kankakee, Ill.

The class of 1877, Harvard, will place in Memorial Hall two beautiful windows, one representing Charlemagne, and the other Sir Thomas Moore.

EVERY MEMBER of the Blake family at Canton, O., who has died in the last twenty years, has dreamed of falling into a well about two weeks before death came.

EUROPE has a new coin. It is the coin of the present German Emperor, and bears his profile. The die was actually prepared in the life time of the last Emperor.

JOHN SMITH, of Waldron, Ark., who was arrested on a charge of setting fire to his brother-in-law's house, was taken from jail twice by an excited crowd of citizens.

"BETSY," a noted performing elephant, died last week on the street in Richmond, Va., while en route to the train. Pneumonia caught in the blizzard is supposed to have caused his untimely end at the early age of 93.

CHRIS AHERNNS, who has just died near Clinton, Ia., was nearly 7 feet high, and wore a coat 70 inches about the chest and 80 about the waist. His weight was within a fraction of 400 pounds, and a special coffin had to be made for him in Chicago."

CARRIAGES containing a wedding party on their way to the preacher's house, at Plymouth, Luzerne county, Pennsylvania, the other day, ran over and killed a little girl. The whole party were arrested, and the marriage did not take place.

The floor of an old building occupied as a saloon in Woonsocket, R. I., was taken up recently and eight bottles of fine old whisky were discovered. The bottles were covered with mold and had every appearance of having lain there for years.

AMERICAN ENTERPRISE is felt at Hermosand, Sweden, which has just been provided with the most northern electric light station in the world. The lights there are lighted at 2:30 o'clock in the afternoon, and put out at 12:15 o'clock at night.

THERE was a snow bank two feet deep and half a block long in Frankfort street, New York, last Saturday. It was formed by snow taken from beneath the arches of the New York anchorage of the Brooklyn bridge. This is the last of the big blizzard.

THE British Legation in Washington has been taught that the horse has some rights in this country which even titled Englishmen must respect. Last week a member of the legation had his horses tails docked in the English fashion, and was fined $250 in each case.

One of the most remarkable mechanical changes of the day is the setting aside of steel and the readoption of iron for some of the most important parts of locomotives on many railroads. It is only comparatively a few years since the change was made on most roads from iron to steel.

THE Queen of England's grandson, George "Collars and Cuff," is irreverent. He was dancing at a ball recently with a pretty but plebeian partner when his brother called him to account. "You can go and hum 'God Save Grandmother,'" was his retort. "I'll dance with whom I please."

SAN DIEGO, CAL., is soon to have an orphans' home for both sexes, combined with an educational and technical school. The endowment amounts to $2,000,000, and was subscribed by four citizens of San Diego. The city has also given 100 acres of land, which is estimated to be worth nearly $1,000,000.

A REMARKABLE FREAK of nature, a mare known as the "Oregon Beauty," was recently on exhibition in Louisville. Her color is a sorrel, and that of the mane, tail and forelock a creamy tint. The mane is ten feet in length, the forelock four feet, while the tail sweeps the ground. Although the mare is eight years of age, the mane and tail are of only four years' growth, having grown an average of two feet a year during that time.

ITALIAN OPERA, so often said to have outlived its time in England, is once more in full swing at Covent Garden, London, under Mr. Augustus Harris. There is nothing remarkable about it, either musically or dramatically. Old operas are given with singers who are not new. But society has been good enough once more to show interest in the matter, and the first night saw the house full of fashionable ladies in full dress and diamonds, quite in the olden style. There are four operas weekly, and each performance has been thronged. Indeed, every good box in the house was subscribed for in advance.

THE OUED RIR', now becoming one of the most prosperous regions of Algeria, is a great oasis in the Sahara. It overlies a vast subterranean water reservoir from two and one-half to eight miles wide, which is a distance of some seventy-eight miles from north to south, is now tapped by about 114 French spouting wells and 492 native ones, with a total discharge of 63,425 gallons of water per minute. The Ouer RIR' has nearly 530,000 palm trees in bearing condition, and an annual date production of more than $500,000. The population, which, like the productive land, has more than doubled in thirty years, is about 13,000, distributed through thirty-one centers.

BENNETTSVILLE, IND., has an electrical man named Henry Lurgeman, who becomes so highly charged when a storm is approaching that flies which happen to light upon him drop to the floor dead, while such things as small particles of iron or steel cling to his fingers. It is alleged during a recent storm he drew the blade of a case knife between his fore finger and thumb, so thoroughly magnetizing it that heavy iron articles could easily be raised with it. When placed in a dark room thousands of tiny sparks are emitted from his body, and his eyes shine as brightly as incandescent lights. He claims that he feels no inconvenience from his peculiar gift, but will go near no moving locomotive or heavy iron body for fear of being drawn against it and killed.

VERY Few PEOPLE have any idea of the vast areas of government land held by alien landholders in the United States. The largest tract, 4,500,000 acres, is held by the Holland Company, of New Mexico. An English syndicate holds 3,000,000 acres in Texas, Sir Edward Reid and a syndicate in Florida owns 2,000,000 acres; 1,800,000 acres belong to an English syndicate in Mississippi, 1,750,000 to the Marquis of Tweedale, 1,300,000 to the Phillips-Marshall Company, of London, and 1,600,000 acres to a German syndicate. These comprise the larger landowners. There are, however, a score or more of persons and syndicates owning less than 750,000 acres. The grand total foots up to 20,747,000 acres of government land held by aliens in the United States.

CHICAGO Aug 1—A dispatch from Bir-
CHICAGO, Aug. 1.—A dispatch from Birmingham, Ala., says the telegraph operator at Bacton, who arrived there last night, gave meager details of a tragedy in Bibb county. For some time a gang of moonshiners have been operating around the coal mines and railroad camps in that neighborhood. They defied arrest, and the last United States deputy marshal who visited that section was run out and ordered never to return. Last Sunday the gang waylaid and murdered a prominent citizen of the county for his money.

HUNTING THEM DOWN.

This aroused such excitement that a posse was organized to hunt the outlaws. They were soon found, and after an exchange of shots the moonshiners took refuge in an old drift of the Brierfield coal mines. A posse of citizens determined to starve them to death if they would not come out and surrender. Monday night one of the moonshiners made a bold dash for liberty, was shot at by the posse and fell dead. The rest are in the mines and the posse is standing guard.

STILL IN THE SHAFT.

MONTGOMERY, ALA., Aug. 1.—The moonshiners reported yesterday as being besieged by citizens in the Bibb county coal mining shaft, are still under a heavy guard. Deputy marshals have gone to the scene of siege and propose to take the prisoners dead or alive. It turns out that this gang is the same one that called Mr. Lawley from his house about a week ago and killed him. Lawley had given information to revenue officers.

The officers were guided and assisted by Jack Lowley, a prominent citizen of Bibb county. Last Sunday night Lowley was called to his gate and was shot dead and robbed by Snyder, Ray, Hickey and the negro. This aroused the citizens and the moonshiners were driven into the drift and one of them killed. They being well armed the citizens' posse decided on the starvation plan.

Night before last a large party of masked men went to the jail at Plymouth and took therefrom three negroes charged with murder. The lynchers carried the negroes, whose names were John Blount, Matthew Blount, and Patterson Spruill, to a point some half a mile from the jail and, after tying them to trees, shot them to death. The murder with which they were charged was that of Edward Dawman, a travelling jeweller, who was passing through the neighborhood of Cresswell, Washington county. He was decoyed into some dense woods by four negroes on the afternoon of December 23d last. While the negroes were walking along with him one, with an axe, slipped up behind him and crushed his skull. Another blow was given, and then Dawman lay dead, with both temples broken, back of head crushed in, and a shoulder broken. The murderers dug a hole and hastily put him in it. They only partially covered the body, and a negro who was driving through the woods saw his knees sticking out of the shallow pit. The murderers were arrested Christmas day. One of them gave evidence which betrayed the three who were hanged. There was great excitement about the crime, and precautions were taken to prevent a lynching or disturbance, for lynching was expected at any moment. Vigilance had in the past ten days been relaxed.

CRIMES AND CRIMINALS
A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money.
HIDING OUT FROM THE LYNCHERS.
RALEIGH, N. C., January 28.—[Special.]—News has been received here of a terrible lynching at the town of Plymouth, the county seat of Washington county, night before last. The mob, composed mainly of mounted men, marched to the jail and took therefrom Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount, all colored. The doomed men were taken to a piece of woods a mile from town, and were tied to trees. The lynchers then opened fire upon them with all sorts of weapons, from Winchester rifles to shotguns, and did not cease firing till all the men were dead and riddled with bullets and shot. This lynching is the result of a very brutal murder which was committed in the afternoon of the 23d of last December. While a man named Ed. Dawman, an itinerant jeweler, was passing through the country near the town of Creswell, four negroes, three of whom were those lynched, met him and presently knocked him in the head, robbed him and threw the body in a shallow pit, where a teamster discovered it, seeing the knees sticking above the ground. Christmas day all four men were arrested. One confessed the crime. All were taken to jail at Plymouth. Violence was feared, as public feeling ran very high, and special precautions were taken. The people in the section where the murder was committed, which is some miles from Plymouth, were particularly stirred up, and it is probable that they were the lynching party. Everything was conducted quietly and with system. The men would have been tried for their lives at the spring term of court. The evidence against them was regarded as conclusive. It is the first lynching in the state in many months.

A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money.

Corpus Christi, Texas, January 23.—[Special.]—News reached this city last night that Jake Stafford, a German, was murdered and robbed near Collins, Texas, this county. Stafford was a peaceable man, and engaged in the sheep business.

Last Thursday, at three o'clock, he left Collins for his home, some few miles in the country. His wife became alarmed by his not coming that night. A search was begun in the morning, and his body was found Saturday, in a water hole, with three bullet holes in it, one through the body and two through the head. Stafford only had nine dollars on his person before starting home. No money or valuables were found on him, thus proving that robbery was the cause of his death.

Santosear Salizar, a Mexican of bad character, was arrested on suspicion, and rumor reached here this morning that Salizar was hung last night by a mob.

The Plymouth massacre or lynching is one of those atrocious deeds which can find apologists nowhere. It was a deed done in cold blood without the ordinary provocations which sometimes justify popular violence. There was no pretense that justice would not be meted out to the guilty; the murder though an atrocious one, did not involve as a victim one who drew to his character or associations the fury of popular vengeance. That vengeance could patiently await the course of the law. There is only one crime for the punishment of which lynch law is excusable. In this Plymouth case, the lynchers were murderers, and if detected, should be punished as such.

WHITE MEN SHOULD THINK.

The District of Columbia, though it has no vote, is allowed to send delegates to the National Republican convention which names the candidates of that party for President and Vice-President. In the District, as elsewhere in the South, the negroes constitute the bulk of the Republican party. The other day a convention was held in Washington to select delegates to the next National Republican convention. The negroes, representing both Blaine and Sherman, raised such a row that the police had to interfere, and the convention adjourned without choosing delegates. In a communication to the National Republican Fred Douglass, a negro leader, says:

"I hardly need say in this I was sorely disappointed and greatly humiliated. The proceedings of that convention far transcended in treachery, baseness, brutality and violence any description which I have seen in the most malignant of the papers which have noticed it."

And yet the delegates chosen by this people may decide who shall be the candidate of the party for the high office of President of this great country, and who, through such agencies as such and their allies may put in operation may be declared to be elected.

Do white men of this country want their government controlled by such elements and such agencies.

And yet it is just such that Republicans say shall again have control of not only the nation, but of the Southern States. If this party has any hopes whatever of again getting control of the State of North Carolina it is through votes three-fourths of which will be cast by this same ignorant, irresponsible negro. In their demand that the present system of county government be repealed it is with the knowledge that the tax assessing, tax collecting and tax spending control of nearly one-third the counties of this State will again pass into the hands of negroes. While the negroes in these counties pay no taxes, comparatively, they are to be entrusted with the assessment of the property of white people, the levying and collection and expending of taxes. Can white men think of such propositions with patience or indifference?

The Raleigh Index Appeal correspondent says: R. G. Dunn, a wealthy resident of this city, has made public an offer to furnish free of charge for rent, any reasonable number of acres of land, in Wake county, for two years, to any person known to be a practical tobacco grower, who will agree to plant and raise a crop on the same. He also agrees to furnish all the necessary timber for barn building, &c. Of course none other but a reliable person in all particulars will be selected. It is an opportunity rarely presented, and no doubt a number of offers will be made.

The supreme court has just made public a decision which may be of service to the legal profession and which to some extent puts a check to the almost innumerable cases appealed from the lower courts. It decides that the only ground on which an application to the supreme court for a new trial below can be based in the discovery of such new evidence as was proper to be heard below, and the supreme court will not interfere because of irregularities occurring in the trial below, its jurisdiction as a court of appeal for the correction of errors not extending to such cases.

The question of what shall be done with the governor's mansion, now in an unfinished condition, will come before the next legislature, and there is a great diversity of opinion concerning it. It is evident that the building is of too grand proportions, and planned in too extravagant a style to suit the meagre salary of $3,000 per annum, now allowed the governor. It was rumord last spring that the Baptist denomination of the state desired to buy it and remodel the building for a female school, but the board of public buildings did not feel authorized to sell it, withou

legislative sanction. It is hardly probable, in the present financial condition of the state, that either party will brave public opinion so far as to vote a sufficient sum for its completion, and it will either stand for some years in its present unfinished condition or be used for some other department of the state government. The general tendency of opinion is that it should be turned over to the judicial department, and that the building just finished for the supreme court be devoted entirely to the state library and museum. This is a good idea and will, in all probability, be carried out by the general assembly.

C., Jan. 27.—Lynch law ran riot here last night, and this morning the people were horrified to find that three negro prisoners had been taken from the county jail by a crowd of masked men, conveyed to a piece of woods on the outskirts of town, tied to trees and shot to death. This morning their bodies were found in the position in which the lynchers left them, securely bound to the trees and riddled with bullets. The lynching party gathered at the jail shortly before midnight and demanded that the jailer should deliver to them Jack Blount his brother Matthew Blount and Patterson Spruitt, who had been charged with the murder of John Dawson, a peddler, of Creswell, in this state. The jailer refused but was overpowered and was was forced to permit the men to be taken away.

When the woods were reached, the victims begged pityously for mercy, but no attention was paid to their outeries, except the stern reply that they would be given a moment to pray. Then the lynchers, who were variously armed with shotguns, muskets and pistols, began their bloody work and fired volley after volley until the prisoners were dead. Matthew Blount, one of the three victims, was a preacher of some local notoriety and had previously lost an arm.

The crime for which the three men were thus summarily made to suffer occurred on Jan. 1. On that day John Dawson, the peddler whom they were supposed to have murdered, was walking down the country road on his way to the house of a neighboring farmer. Patterson Spruitt happened to pass by in his cart, and when Dawson asked for a ride he consented and the two drove some distance. Before they reached the end of their journey they came up with the two Blounts. The three negroes determined to rob Dawson and murder him. They overpowered him, carried him off to a secluded spot, choked him to death and then endeavored to hide his body, on which they found only one dollar as the reward of their crime. They were arrested and Spruitt made a confession that Preacher Blount had committed the murder and the other brother had stripped the dead man's person of the money.

HAPPY MEDIUM, a famous stallion, died on the 25th near Lexington, Ky. He was twenty-four years old and valued at $40,-000.

I. M. PRIBIL, of Chicago, a wholesale dealer in guns and cutlery, failed on the 26th for $100,000.

On the 26th Grant Martin, aged fifteen years, and Grace Silvers, aged thirteen years, were married at Fairmount, Ill., with the consent of the parents of each.

C. C. BRADLEY was on the 26th sold under the vagrant law, for a term of six months, to William McClanahan, of Milan, Mo., for thirty-five cents.

Two WORKMEN named McDermott and Fowler fell to the bottom of the hot-air oven of the Floodwood furnace at Athens, O., on the 26th, and were baked to death.

While miners were boring for coal on the 26th near Carmi, Ill., oil was struck at a depth of 1,121 feet which was gushing to the surface at the rate of over fifty barrels an hour.

TEN tons of Texas cotton seed were shipped on the 26th from Galveston, Tex., to Zanzibar, Africa, where cotton-growing will be tried.

DYNAMITE explosion on the 26th at the Carbon Limestone Company's quarries, ten miles from Youngstown, O., killed three men.

On the 26th the Republicans of the Eleventh Michigan Congressional district, in convention at Ishpeming, nominated Henry W. Seymour, of Sault Ste. Marie, to succeed the late Seth C. Moffatt.

At St. Paul a street-car cable train be came unmanageable on the 27th, and when descending a bill the cars shot downward at great speed, ran off the track and were smashed to pieces. Three persons were fatally injured and fourteen were badly hurt.

On the 29th C. B. Hitchcock and wife were found murdered on their farm in Los Angeles County, Cal. Robbery was the motive.

C. P. MAYSEY, one of the best-known men in Western Arkansas, was shot and killed on the 27th in Golden City by Oscar Coulter, the outcome of a quarrel of six year's standing.

Masked men took three negro prisoners from the jail at Plymouth, N. C., on the 27th and shot them to death.

Business was resumed on the 27th by the San Francisco Bridge Company, which assigned recently, with liabilities of $400,000.

HENRY PRETRE, of Tyler, Minn., was burned to death in his barn on the 27th, and ten horses, seventeen cattle and twenty hogs were also cremated.

The Chamber of Commerce building at Peoria, was burned on the 29th, Loss, $150,000.

On the 28th Frederick Auschlag, a young German of Los Angeles, Cal., confessed to the recent murder of Charles B. Hitchcock and wife, near Garden Grove, Cal.

MRS. BRIDGET NIHILL died on the 28th at Hudson, Ill., aged one hundred years.

On the Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee road an express train was derailed on the 28th at Durand, Mich., and one passenger was fatally and six others were badly injured.

The thermometer on the 28th registered four degrees below zero. Winchester, Va.

A colored man named Ben Edwards, who assaulted Catherine Hayes, a white girl, was taken from jail at Amite City, La., on the 29th and lynched.

DENNIS CLIFFORD's house at Tawas City, Mich., was burned on the 28th, and Clifford and his wife, an aged couple, perished in the flames.

In the trial of the election-workers at Indianapolis, Ind., the jury returned a verdict on the 28th finding Simon Coy and W. F. A. Bernhamer guilty.
DEMOCRATS of the Eleventh Congressional district of Michigan on the 28 h met at Marquette and nominated Burtley Breen, of Menominee, to succeed the late Seth C. Moffatt. The Prohibitionists met the same day at Ishpeming and nominated S. S. Steel, of Schoolcraft.
A FIRE destroyed the printing and bindery establishment of H. W. Rokker at Springfield, Ill., on the 28th. Loss, $100,-000.

JUDGE LYNCH.
A FEARFUL CRIME COMMITTED AT PLYMOUTH, N. C.
Some two or three weeks since, as stated before in this paper, a clock peddler was found murdered, in Washington county, near Creswell, N. C. Three negroes by the names of Jack Blount, Mathew Blount and Patterson Spruill, were charged with the crime and arrested and taken to the jail at Plymouth, N. C., to await the action of the Superior Court.

On Thursday night, January 26th, about mid-night, they were taken from the jail, by a gang of masked men, carried about one mile from Plymouth, lashed to trees and riddled with bullets. When found, the morning afterwards, we hear, the clothes of one of them was on fire, supposed to have caught from the powder when shot.

It is also reported that lynching was talked of for some time.

MUNCIE, Ind., Nov. 9.—Tuesday evening some person, supposed to be a woman, fired through the window at Mrs. James Wright, at her residence in this city. The ball grazed her head, inflicting only a slight wound, but the lady was prostrated with fear. No cause can be assigned for the shooting.

NEW LEXINGTON, O., Nov. 9.—Lee Burrell and his mistress, Mel Green, both colored, were arrested at Chauncey, Tuesday night, charged with the murder of Pete Donnelly, at Corning. Sheriff Brunner foiled a lynching party by bringing his prisoner here. Both deny their guilt.

Body of a Missitg Man Found With Skull Frac- tured
Corning, O., Nov. 5.—The body of Peter Donnelly, who has been missing for two weeks past, was found Saturday afternoon on a small island in Sunday creek, near the southern corporation line. The body was lying on the face and was almost entirely covered with sand and mud. There seems to be a considerable mystery connected with the case, and it is pretty generally supposed that there has been some foul play, as on examination it was found that his skull was fractured in two places. A colored man by the name of Burrough was arrested at Chauncy, Saturday, who is thought to know something of the affair. A cononer's inquest was held last night, the deceison being that he was murdered by some unknown person. More arrests are expected to follow soon. Donnelly was a single man, much respected, and was in the employ of the K. & O. More arrests are expected to follow soon. Tuppins, hearing the report, accosted the Corning marshal at this place and told him that the Negroes of Rendville demanded justice for one of their race, and if they lynched this man he would bring a multitude of Negroes and tear the town up; that we were tired of being killed and no law to protect us, and that if the law would not protect us we would protect ourselves. A Murder at Winamac.
WINAMAC, Sept. 13.—[Special.]—Joseph W Robinson of Francisville, Ind., a contractor for the drilling of gas and oil wells, was shot and instantly killed here this evening by Mike Reinhart, a barber of this place. Robinson and others of Francisville were here attending court. This evening just at dusk, when making ready to go home, Robinson and others stepped in Deutsch's saloon at the corner of Main and Logan-sts. to get a glass of beer, and while in the act of lighting a cigar Reinhart came in. Robinson seeing him proposed making friends as he was intending to leave town and there had been some trouble between them. Reinhart replied "All right." With this he stepped up to Robinson, drew his pistol, thrust it behind his ear and shot him. Robinson fell into the arms of a friend and then to the floor, expiring without uttering a word. After the shooting Reinhart ran from the saloon to the western limits of the town. When next seen he was endeavoring to board the cars for Logansport. Failing in this he ran to his shop, entering by the rear entrance. Here he changed his hat and coat and attempted to hide by crawling under a stairway. He was discovered and gave himself up without a struggle, begging protection of the authorities from the infuriated crowd. Excitement is now running high and threats of mob violence is made, but a better council will probably prevail and he be given a trial. The sheriff's posse now guards the jail, fearing an attack from friends of the dead man. Robinson was a highly respected citizen of Francisville, thirty-five years old. Reinhart is a local tough.

— The Washington correspondent of the New York World says: A movement is on foot among Southern capitalists to secure a good grade of English colonists. A Southern capitalist told me that he belonged to a syndicate which was offering inducements to English manufacturers to come to the best districts of the South with their entire plants. — The cotton crop of the United States for the year ended September 1, 1888, as compiled by the Financial Chronicle, amounted to 7,017,707 bales against 6,513,662 bales in 1887, and 6,550,215 bales for 1886. Of the crop of 1888 there was exported 4,638,981 bales, while spinners took 2,230,294 bales, leaving a stock on hand of 181,225 bales. — A man near Fayettville, Tenn., built a fire one cool morning, lately, and in a little while saw a pair of big black feet drop down the chimney. A little search revealed a colored neighbor of bad reputation stuck fast in it, and upon being released, said that, owing the householder ten cents, he had come to pay it, and finding doors and windows last, chose this mode of entrance; but as his shoes and an axe were left outside, his tale was not credited and he was sent off to jail.

—J. W. Robinson, a prominent and wealthy oil contractor of Lima, Ohio, was shot down and murdered in cold blood last Friday night by Michael Rhinehart. They were in friendly conversation. Rhinehart was promptly arrested and barely escaped being lynched before the sheriff could get him to jail. The sheriff then summoned a strong guard of men and placed them in position to guard against any lynching. The murdered man stood high in society and leaves a widow and two children. He has many friends who swear they will avenge his death.

—As an illustration of progress in Central Asia, it may be mentioned that while, a few years ago, the traveler was likely to be killed by the natives, he is now in greater danger of being smashed up in a railroad accident. A train on the Trans-Caspian Road was upset a few weeks ago near Samarcand, and five people were killed. They happened to be train hands and Europeans, but had they been Mohammedan pilgrims, who now employ this modern method of expediting their journey to Mecca, there might have been a great cry against this infidel invention for killing off the faithful.

—Just before dawn last Saturday morning, an explosion of flour dust occurred in the brick flour mill of the M. B. Clark Company in Cleveland, Ohio, blowing off the roof, shattering the walls and setting fire to the whole inside of the building. Eighteen men were in the building and all were injured by being blown against the walls and machinery. Four were seriously hurt and taken to the hospital; two, unable to escape, perished in the burning building. The rest escaped. The building was entirely destroyed. Loss, $90,000. The explosion was caused by the spontaneous combustion of flour dust.

A rather remarkable lawsuit is in progress in what is known as the "Northern Neck" of Virginia, which involves the ownership of both the Rappahannock and Potomac rivers, with their tributaries and immense fish and oyster interests. The Marshalls, heirs and descendants of Lord Fairfax claim the entire control of these rivers under the original grant made to Lord Fairfax by the Crown of England, which includes the river on the charter track. It is not generally thought that there is any validity to their claim, but they have retained able counsel and are pushing the matter. They have purchased from the descendants of Lord Calvert their interest in the Potomac on the Maryland side.

The following dispatch is from Ottawa, Ontario, under date of Friday last: Late advices from the northwest report great suffering and many deaths from starvation among the Indians of the Canadian Northwest Territory. From the Peace river district several cases of cannibalism are reported, where, to save their own lives, heads of families have killed and eaten their children. Last season Parliament voted the sum of $354,000 for supplies for the destitute treaty Indians by the Northwest, but from what has been learned dishonest agents who were entrusted with its disbursement have appropriated the greater portion of the grant. Gabriel Dumont, Riel's lieutenant, has again been attempting to stir bad feelings among the Indians, with, it is said, a considerable degree of success.

— Says a correspondent of the Albany Argus: A gentleman told me recently of a strange experience related by a friend of his. It was during the battle of Gettysburg that his friend, just before entering the action, took his canteen from his shoulder and hid it in a crevice in the rock. Then came the fiery hail of shot and shell that swept down regiments like fields of wheat before the reaper. At the close of the battle the soldier forgot all about the canteen, nor did it ever occur to him again until he visited the field at the late reunion. Then it flashed through his mind, and after a few minutes' search he found it where he had left it on that momentous day. It seemed scarcely credible that it could have been overlooked during the minute explorations of the field ever since the war, but the gentleman who related the incident is of unimpeachable veracity.

MINOR NEWS ITEMS. For Week Ended November 20
At midnight, November 30, the canals in the State of New York will be closed.

Major J. B. Thomas was on Saturday ap pointed governor of the Dayton (O.) Soldiers' Home.

The statistics of agrarian outrages in Ireland during the last quarter places the number at 173.

Major Henry Farnsworth, Assistant Inspector-General, died Monday forenoon at Fortress Monroe.

Lindauer Brothers & Co., wholesale clothing dealers in Chicago, failed on Friday for $400,000.

Gray Easton, 17 years old, was cut completely in two by a circular saw on Thursday in Columbus, O.

Several buildings at Little Rock, Ark., were destroyed by fire on Saturday, causing a loss of $100,000.

The annual convention of the National Electric Association will be held in Chicago February 19 next.

Grass on the ranges in the vicinity of Albuquerque, N. M., is short and a hard winter on cattle is expected.

James M. Dougherty, who has been following Mary Anderson about the country, has been pronounced insane.

A negro who assaulted a young white girl near Donaldsville, La., was captured on Thursday and hanged by a mob.

Three little girls while crossing a railroad bridge on Thursday at Circleville, O., were struck by an engine and killed.

Samuel R. Bullock, a water-works contractor of New York, failed on Saturday, with liabilities amounting to $3,500,000.

Judge Winfield decided at Marion, Ind., Monday that ex-County Treasurer Henry Beaver owes Huntington County $14,110.

The Industrial Leader, the organ of the Knights of Labor in Dubuque, Ia., has been discontinued because of lack of support.

The report that five men had been lynched by "Bald-Knobbers" in Christian County, Mo., was on Friday pronounced false.

In a fit of insanity the son of Porterfield Brooke, a farmer near Staunton, Va., shot and killed his father and then committed suicide.

The trustees of Columbia College, in New York, have sanctioned the request for an annex to the college, which shall be for women.

Mike Reinhart was convicted on Saturday of the murder of Joseph Robinson at Winnamac, Ind., and sentenced to life imprisonment.

John Hodell, a native of Switzerland, confined in the State prison at Weathersfield, Conn., on a life sentence, killed himself Monday.

A heavy fall of snow, the first of the season, was reported on Monday from points in Northern Illinois, Indiana and Western Iowa.

Mrs. Henry Jones died suddenly on Friday at Bridgeport, Conn., aged 90 years. She was the daughter of Noah Webster, of dictionary fame.

The famous Doris mansion at St. Louis, lately utilized as a public resort, was burned Monday morning. The insurance is about $25,000.

Wilson Arnold (colored) was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Miss., on Monday and lynched for the murder of Captain Robert Johnson.

The Woman's congress closed its sessions at Detroit on Friday after the election of officers. Mrs. Julia Ward Howe was re-elected president.

Sheep belonging to C. J. Myers, living near Cincinnati, O., died of hydrophobia Friday, three weeks after they had been bitten by a dog.

A bill granting the right of suffrage to women was defeated in the Vermont House of Representatives on Thursday by a vote of 192 to 37.

Frank, the 5-year-old son of William Mason, of Terre Haute, Ind., who was bitten by a dog a few weeks ago, died of hydrophobia on Monday.

Rear-Admiral Charles H. Baldwin (retired) died in New York on Saturday. He was born in that city in September, 1822, and entered the service early.

The treasurer of Indiana filed his annual report on Monday, showing that the total domestic debt of the State was $383,783, and the foreign debt was $6,770,668.

Oscar Carmichael, a convict at Sunnyside, Ga., who escaped after killing a guard, was surrounded at his wife's house on Monday and riddled with bullets.

Fritz Anschlag, who was to have been hanged at Garden Grove, Cal., for the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, of Illinois, committed suicide on Thursday.

The Christian World, a London journal of immense circulation and influence, and hitherto stoutly advocating Unionist principles, has been converted to home rule.

At the Dudley poor-house in London a woman named Sarah Wright, who had been a pauper for thirty years, died on Sunday at the advanced age of 110 years.

Mlle. Gaudart, a French governess in the family of Mr. Bonnell, at Youngstown, O., committed suicide Monday by jumping from a window, fifty feet to the pavement below.

William Davis, of Damascus, Md., committed suicide on Saturday through worry over his mother's illness. The news of his death proved such a shock to the mother that she died in a few minutes.

CITIZENS OF RYE FORM A BODY GUARD.
BLOODSUED, PISTOL SHOTS AND RIOT IN A CAMP OF ITALIAN LABORERS.
BLOODSHED, PISTOL SHOTS AND RIOT IN A CAMP OF ITALIAN LABORERS.

The village of Harrison, on the New-York, New-Haven and Hartford Railway, was on Sunday night the scene of a desperate affray which may possibly result in the death of one or more of the persons concerned in it. For some time there have been in the neighborhood Harrison, West Chester and Rye, large gangs of Italians, employed as laborers on the roads. At night they gather in their shanties along the sides of the roads, where they form themselves into little colonies. Of late a good deal of rivalry and ill-feeling has sprung up between the different gangs, and considerable disturbance has been the result.

On Sunday evening, July 8, Gactano Gamardelli, who keeps a liquor store at Westchester, swaggered into the Harrison encampment and threatened to "let daylight" into any man who dared to come within six feet of him. Louis Conventi, proprietor of one of the "shanties," approached Gamardelli, who attempted to draw his revolver, but, being seized from behind, was disarmed and driven away, leaving his hat, stick and pistol behind. On last Sunday night, between 11 and 12, he again appeared at the camp, this time accompanied by Napoleon Emgalias Cabello. Gamardelli asked a man named Lorenzo Veritto where Conventi was, and, receiving no satisfactory reply, drew a six-chambered revolver and fired at Veritto, inflicting a wound in the eye.

CLUBBED WITH A SHOT GUN.

Gamardelli and Ems then walked on until they met Angelo Gleiss, of whom they inquired about Conventi. Gleiss being unable to afford the required information, Ems clubbed him over the head with the butt end of a shotgun he carried in carried in his hand, fracturing the skull. Gamardelli then went to the shanty occupied by Conventi, and having learned that Conventi was asleep, went to the door of the latter's bunk and called upon him to surrender. Receiving no reply, he clambered up over the partition which separates Conventi's bunk from the rest of those in the shanty, and fired his revolver at the sleeper, the bullet crashing into the woodwork an inch above the pillow. Conventi then opened his floor, and Gamardelli, holding a pistol to his head, demanded $10 as the price of his life. The money was paid over and Gamardelli and Ems then fled, firing one or two farewell shots among the confused and only half-awakened crowd.

Police Constable Samuel Graham, of Rye, at half-past 4 yesterday morning, was called out of bed by an Italian, who informed him that a robbery had been committed at Harrison, and added that Gamardelli and Ems had last been seen, scurrying off in the direction of Rye. Graham went across to the station, and there learned that the Italians had gone on to Mamaroneck. He reached Mamaroneck just as a train with the culprits on board was moving off. Springing on board, Graham handed a pistol to the brakeman, and directed him to fire at the Italians if they offered any resistance. He handeuffed his prisoners and took them to Justice Downing's office at Rye.

A CROWD OF WOULD-BE LYNCHERS.

In the meantime news of the arrest reached the Harrison camp, and a body of Italians, numbering about three hundred, armed with guns, revolvers and knives, marched to Justice Downing's office, where they yelled and shouted for the surrender of the desperados, that they might lynch them. Ems grinned at and taunted the crowd, but Gamardelli was completely cowed. With ashen face and trembling lips he fell on his knees and besought his captors to remove him to a place of safety. Justice Henderson, of Portchester, who now arrived, dispatched a messenger for a reinforcement of police from his district, but meanwhile some of the citizens of Rye armed themselves with pistols and formed a bodyguard for Gamardelli and Ems, who were taken off in a wagon to White Plains Prison. Graham repeatedly charged the crowd and contrived to keep them at bay. Gleiss is in a dangerous condition, but Veretto's injury is slight. Gamardelli and Ems, who decline to say anything in reply to the charge, will be brought up for examination to-morrow.

New York, July 17.—For some time past there have been in the neighborhood of Harrison, Westchester, and Rye, large gangs of Italians employed on the railroad. A good deal of rivalry and ill-feeling has sprung up between the different gangs, and disturbances have been frequent. On Sunday evening, July 8, Gaetano Gamardelli, who keeps a liquor store at Westchester, staggered into the Harrison encampment and threatened violence to a number of his fellow-countrymen there. He was finally disarmed and driven away.

Last Sunday evening he reappeared, accompanied by Napoleon Emgolios Cabello. The two men used their pistols, and shot several of the Harrison Italians, who were mostly asleep. The two then fled, but were afterward arrested at Mamaroneck and taken to a justice's office at Rye. The news of the arrests reaching the Harrison camp, a body of Italians, numbering about 300, armed with guns, revolvers, and knives, marched to the justice's office where they yelled and shouted for the surrender of the desperadoes that they might be lynched. It was with the greatest difficulty that the constables, assisted by an armed posse of citizens of Rye, succeeded in safely getting the two prisoners to the White Plains prison. They will have a hearing to day.

RAILROADERS RIOTOUS.
A Mob of 300 Italians Attempt the Lynching of Two Murderers.

NEW YORK, July 18.--For some time past there have been in the neighborhood of Harrison, West Chester and Rye large gangs of Italians employed on the railways. A great deal of ill feeling existed between two of the gangs which culminated in bloodshed and almost a lynching. A tough from one of the camps was driven out of the other, but later he returned with a companion, when the laborers were asleep, and shot several of them. The murderers were arrested. It was with the greatest difficulty that the constable, assisted by an armed posse of citizens of Rye, succeeded in getting the prisoners to the White Plains prison, a mob of about 300 Italians attempting to capture the desperadoes to lynch them.

Wolverines Thirst for the Blood. of a Ravisher in Hoc in Chicago. CHICAGO, Oct. 18.—Deputy Sheriff Shaley, of Grand Rapids, Mich., is around the central police station today, and is sorely in need of advice. "If I take the villain back to Grand Rapids he will be lynched before I can get him safely locked up," he says. "The whole town is up in arms, and if they knew I had him there would be 10,000 people at the depot when I got in." The man whose blood the citizens of Grand Rapids are said to be thirsting for is R. H. Kreuger. He was arrested here this morning on a telegram from Grand Rapids saying that he had been guilty of outraging twelve-year-old Louisa McKay. He was en route to Portland, Ore.

Arrested on a Terrible Charge.
Arrested on a Terrible Charge.
CHICAGO, Oct. 19.—A. H. Kruger, a respectable-looking man of 30 years, was arrested yesterday morning as he was about to take a train for Portland, Ore. Kruger was from Grand Rapids, Mich., where he is charged with a horrible crime. Several days ago it is said he took Louisa McKay, a 12-year-old girl, out riding in a buggy, and in a secluded place in the suburbs of Grand Rapids he basely assaulted her. The child is not expected to recover.

Kinney's Disreputable Methods to Injure Colonel Bishop. The following letters were received by the
Colonel Bishop.

The following letters were received by the TELEGRAM-HERALD yesterday:
To the Editor of the TELEGRAM-HERALD.

The article published in this morning's Democrat signed by H. R. Kruger, No. 86 Sherman-st., Chicago, Ill., is wholly unwarranted and calculated to prejudice some against our present Sheriff, Bishop, who are not familiar with the facts. Knowing what I says to be true, and many of his former friends are willing to testify to it no man received better treatment under a similar charge than said Kruger, which was given and granted by request of his friends, and Democrats at that. As to his money and effects, we have no proof except his word, which would not now be accepted by his most intimate friends, as he has proved himself unworthy before his statement was published; but it is known that he did receive, outside his attorney's fee, more than he had, and that his money was all paid to him after his release. His friends would advise Kruger to keep a strict watch over himself or he may visit Grand Rapids for a longer period than he desired for the language used openly against a certain party here. Signed, JUSTICE.

PARIS, May 1.—The municipal authorities of Rochefort gave a banquet in honor of President Carnot last evening. The President started from Rochefort for Paris this morning. A crowd gathered at the station, where he took the train, and greeted him with hearty acclamation.

M. Raynal, member of the chamber of deputies, in a speech at Bordeaux, defended the parliamentary regime, and advocated the retention of the senate and the presidency. He declared that the moderate republicans would support the cabinet. The ministry, he said, pursued a business policy and energetically opposed Boulangerism. A republican League of Action has been instituted, of which M. Laguerere is president.

The Arkansas Labor Party.

WHAT THE PLATFORM DEMANDS—THE NOMINEE FOR SECRETARY OF STATE DECLINES.

LITTLE ROCK, ARK., May 1.—The platform adopted by the labor party last night endorses the national platform of February, 1887, on land, transportation, money, income tax, and Chinese labor; favors the reforms demanded by the Agricultural Wheel, the Farmers' National Alliance, and the Knights of Labor; favors taxing all lands held for speculative purpose to full value; favors the consolidating of state and national elections; favors national aid to education; legislation for subjection of trusts, railroads, and all other corporations to state control, and the establishing of a labor and agricultural bureau. Before adjournment Poyner, who was nominated for secretary of state, telegraphed from Clarksville declining to accept.

A Stage Robber Captured.

SANTA ROSA, CAL., May 1.—A German named Joseph Frye was arrested near here last evening on suspicion of being one of the men who robbed the stage coach near Cloverdale last Saturday. He has made a confession, stating that he was one of the robbers, but was led to the deed by his brother-in-law, Eugene Preus, who lived in San Francisco. Frye says that after they had robbed the stage and were overtaken by the officers, he wished to surrender, but Preus said he would rather die. Preus then turned and fired, killing Constable Crigley. The men with the constable returned the fire, shooting Frye in the arm. Frye says nothing about the other robber who was killed by the officer, and it is not known whether or not it was Preus.

Asking the Amarchists' Release.

THEIR FRIENDS PREPARING A PETITION TO PRESENT TO GOV. OGLESBY.

CHICAGO, May 1.—A local paper says: A petition to Gov. Oglesby for the pardon of Anarchists Fielden, Schwab and Neebe has been circulating the last few days among the socialists, anarchists and radical laborites of this city. It is said to have received thousands of signatures. It is intended to submit it soon to a mass meeting of workingmen for ratification. Adon Butler Defeats J. F. Dormer.

A COLLAR-AND-ELBOW WRESTLING MATCH AT CHICAGO.

CHICAGO, May 1.—The collar-and-elbow wrestling match for the light weight championship of America and $500 between Adon Butler, of Chicago, and J. F. Dormer, of Shamokin, Pa., was won last night by Butler. The winner stripped at 135 pounds, while Dormer had the advantage of 3 pounds. Butler won in two straight falls. In the first Dormer was downed five times before Butler scored the four points demanded by Ed. James' rules. Time, seven minutes and twenty-five seconds. In the second fall Dormer broke his hold, and the referee declared the match won by Butler. Time of second fall 7 minutes and 12 seconds.

Two Railroad Workmen Killed.

ELKO, NEV., May 1.—A locomotive ran into a hand-car 18 miles east of Elko last night. Two section men were killed and three seriously wounded. The engine ran into a car while turning a curve.

A Drunkard's Double Crime.

FATALLY BEATS HIS WIFE FOR REFUSING HIM MONEY AND ATTEMPTS SUICIDE.

CHICAGO, May 1.—Wm. Wilmer, who for some time has been out of work and drinking heavily, on the retusal last night of his wife to furnish more money to use in buying liquor, crept up to her bedside where she was sleeping and dealt her a blow on the head with a hammer. Her screams attracted the neighbors. Before help arrived he threw her to the floor and inflicted several more blows. He then ran into a back room and slashed himself across the abdomen with a razor and fell to the floor. When officers arrived both husband and wife were apparently near death. They were removed to the county hospital. It is believed that the injuries to both will be fatal.

Lynched for Criminal Assault.

NEW ORLEANS, May 1.—A special to the Picayune from Vicksburg says: Jim Harris, colored, who criminally assaulted Mrs. M. Simmons, here, Sunday night, was lynched last night. Harris refused to confess to the last. It is said that he had two accomplices, but he would tell nothing.

A Prize Fight Prevented.

ELIZABETH, N. J., May 1.—The prize-night which was to have taken place in Linden township at midnight last night, between Frank Moore, of Elizabeth, and Thomas Lane, of Boston, was prevented by the arrival on the scene of Chief of Police Austin and a squad of men from Elizabeth. Seventy-five sporting men and the principals were on the grounds and were dispersed.

The Seventeenth Illinois District.

JOHN J. BROWN NOMINATED FOR CONGRESS BY THE REPUBLICANS, AND GREESH DELEGATES CHOSEN.

VANDALLA, ILL., May 1.—The republican congressional convention of the seventeenth Illinois district nominated John J. Brown for Congress. Benson Wood, of Eflingham, and R. T. Higgins, of Vandalia, were chosen delegates to the national convention. They go uninstructed, but both favor Judge Gresham.

The Braddock Strike a P failure.

PROBABILITY THAT IT WILL BE DECLARED OF.

PITTSBURG, May 1.—The rail, blooming, and converting departments, at the Edgar Thomson Steelworks, have not yet been started up, but the machinery is in operation, and everything points to a resumption in these departments at any hour. A large number of men applied for work this morning, including some of the striking Knights of Labor. The impression is growing among the people of Braddock that the strikers are about convinced that the company will be able to operate the works without their assistance, and it would cause very little surprise if they would declare the strike off at the meeting this afternoon. The only hitch now seems to be the signing of the ironclad agreement. The strikers say they are willing to accept a reduction, but will not consent to the disruption of their organization.

A terrible tragedy occurred at Jackson on Tuesday last, by which Gen. Wirt Adams, postmaster, and John H. Martin, editor of the New Mississippian, lost their lives. Martin had published Gen. Adams in personal squibs in his paper. On Tuesday they met on President street, and after a few words both drew pistols and began firing. All the shells in Martin's pistol were exploded, and in Gen. Adams' three were exploded and another gave evidence of having been snapped upon, but failed to fire. Gen. Adams was shot through the heart and died immediately. DOMESTIC

The public-debt statement on the 1st showed the total debt to be $1,706,833,376; cash in treasury, $110,244,969; debt less cash in treasury, $1,181,652,855. Decrease during April, $9,235,300. Decrease since June 30, 1887, $97,795,881.

NEAR Alliance, O., Peter Whitefeather, a retired farmer, aged sixty-five years, was killed by a horse's kick on the 1st.

LEWIS W. McGLAUFLIN, a heavy San Francisco grain dealer, failed on the 1st for $100,000, with the Bank of Nevada as his largest creditor.

OF 586 applicants for liquor licenses at Philadelphia on the 1st 389 were refused licenses.

A PETITION to Governor Oglesby for the pardon of Anarchists Fielden, Schwab and Neebe was in circulation in Chicago on the 1st.

During the forty-eight hours ended at noon on the 1st nearly ten thousand immigrants were landed at Castle Garden, New York.

The general conference of the Methodist Episcopal church began in New York on the 1st, Bishop Bowman presiding.

JIM HARRIS (colored), who assaulted Mrs. Simmons at Vicksburg, Miss., was lynched on the 1st.

In Pittsburgh, Pa., 502 out of 727 saloons closed up on the 1st, when the Brooks Liquor law went into effect.

WILLIAM G. DUTTENHOFER, tax-collector of Columbia borough, Pa., was on the 1st adjudged a defaulter in the sum of $6,000.

At Jackson, Miss., on the 1st General Wir t Adams, the postmaster, and John Martin, editor of the New Mississippian, fought a duel in the street, both being killed.
Twenty houses were burned on the 1st at Trenton, Ky.

The great strike of the engineers and firemen of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy railroad system, which was inaugurated February 26, was on the 1st said to have been officially declared lost.

The surface buildings of the Eclipse mine at Little Cottonwood, U. T., were burned on the 2d. Loss, $100,000.

The total log-cut of the Duluth (Minn.) district during the past season was 270,000,-000 feet.

A fire on the 2d destroyed Conrad Ziegler's slaughter-house and fifty head of cattle at Allegheny City, Pa.

The address of the Methodist Bishops, read at the general conference in New York on the 2d, showed that in four years 450,000 souls had been brought into the church and the membership increased from 1,769,534 to 2,093,935. The Bishops are opposed to high license and in favor of total prohibition of the liquor traffic.

General Martin Beem, a prominent Chicago lawyer, committed suicide by shooting himself on the 2d at Stanton, Neb., where he was visiting. Family troubles were the cause.

At Helena, M. T., on the 2d John T. Rand killed his wife and child and himself.

Two children of Farmer Henry Rincho, near Canton, O., were burned to death on the 2d.

George Martin, a miner, who shot and killed Deputy Marshal Kelly at Warrior, Ala., was lynched by a mob on the 2d.

Six consecutive days of rain were reported on the 2d from Mason City and other Iowa points.

The little hamlet of McIntyre, Pa., was wiped out by fire on the 2d.

It was reported on the 2d that a mail pouch on the Northern Central road had been robbed near Baltimore of $10,000 in registered letters.

A storm of wind on the 3d demolished a two-story store building at Lacoma, Ia., burying in the debris and killing farmer Leonard Wilson. Several houses were unroofed.

Allan O. Meyers was convicted on the 3d at Columbus, O., of contempt of court in publishing objectionable articles during the tally-sheet forgery cases, and was fined $200 and sentenced to three months' imprisonment.

Theodore F. Dwight, Librarian of the State Department at Washington, tendered his resignation on the 3d, and it was accepted.

The first convention of the National Pure Food Association was held in New York on the 3d.

The strike of the Edgar Thomson steel works at Braddock, Pa., was declared off by the Knights of Labor on the 3d, the men resuming work at the old rates.

MURDER IN WALLINGFORD.
Stephen Anthony Shot and Instantly Killed By His Son-in-Law-Domestic Troubles the Cause of the Tragedy.
Stephen Anthony Shot and Instantly Killed By His Son-in-Law—Domestic Troubles the Cause of the Tragedy.

Wallingford has again come to the front with a murder. It is not a mystery like the famous shoe-box case, but simply a brutal homicide. Stephen Anthony, who resides on Colony street in Wallingford, was shot by his son-in-law, Solon Jenkins, yester-day afternoon about 6 o'clock.

Jenkins and his wife, who is a daughter of Anthony, have not been living with each other for some time. Jenkins is a dissolute character and hard drinker. He had been maltreating his wife and her father advised her to leave him and live at her old home. Jenkins had made several unsuccessful attempts to see his wife and children, his father-in-law refusing him admission to the house.

He drank hard yesterday and went to his father-in-law's house bent upon seeing his children at any cost. He knocked at the rear door, which was opened by Anthony. Jenkins drew his revolver and shot his father-in-law the very instant he opened the door. Anthony died immediately.

Anthony's son hearing the report of the pistol rushed out of the house and had a hand-to-hand encounter with Jenkins, whom he overpowered after a hard struggle. He bound him with ropes and delivered him to the custody of Officer Reilly.

The murder was premeditated. Jenkins is a tinner by trade and has been boarding at No 22 Orange street, New Haven. He took an afternoon train for Wallingford and on the train he met Henry Allen of Wallingford. Jenkins told Allen that he was going to see his children and if the old man (meaning Anthony) refused to let him in he would shoot him. He showed Allen the revolver.

After reaching Wallingford Jenkins went to the house twice or three times, but no one was home only the mother-in-law. She did not go to the door, being afraid of him. Jenkins stopped in several places near by and would occasionally vary it by walking up and down the street, evidently waiting for Mr Anthony, who would come home soon from the factory.
Jenkins evidently missed him and then returned to the house. In going up the steps leading to the door Jenkins tumbled around and Mr Anthony hearing the noise opened the door. Without a word of warning Jenkins pointed the revolver at him and fired. The bullet went up Anthony's nostril, lodging in the brain.
Jenkins claimed in the lockup that Anthony shot him first and that he shot Anthony in self defense. Jenkins probably shot himself as there is a wound back of his left ear.
Jenkins broke the handcuffs while in the lockup. Officer Reilly then searched him and found a knife and 32 caliber revolver. Two chambers were empty.

RUINED BY DRINK.

WALLINGFORD, Conn., Nov. 16.—Solon G. Jenkins, formerly a prosperous merchant, but who has gone to the dogs through drink, last night shot and killed his father-in-law, Stephen Anthony, aged 60 years. WILL PROSECUTE A RAILROAD.

NEW YORK, Nov. 16.—The Herald says the interstate commerce commission will probably take a hand in in the west bound freight rate war and prosecute the roads which have been secretly cutting rates in violation of law. The Pennsylvania Co., is believed to be the chief offender.

SOME DIDN'T LET GO.

CHAMBERLIN, Dak., Nov. 16.—In February, 1885, president Arthur issued a proclamation declaring Crow creek, Winnebego reservation open for settlement, and a large number of people flocked to the lands. Soon after president Cleveland's inauguration he withdrew the lands from market and ordered all the settlers off. Many left, but a large number are still living on the lands, and are circulating a petition asking that the lands be again thrown open to settlement and that they be allowed to perfect their titles.

AN INTERESTING WITNESS.

LONDON, Nov. 16.—The proceedings in the Parnell commission to-day were made interesting by the appearance on the witness stand of Lady Mountmorris, whose husband was murdered at Cloubar county, Galway, in 1880. Lady Mountmorris testified that a friendly feeling existed between her husband and his tenants on the Eberhall estates at Cloubar until the land league began holding meetings there. In July, 1880, her husband obtained a writ of ejectment against a tenant. In the following September, while witness was in Scotland, her husband was shot. When she went to Ireland to attend the funeral she heard that the men refused to assist in putting the coffin in the house. Witness left Eberhall in October. While on her way to the steamer people laughed and hooted at her, and stones were thrown at her eight-year-old son. Her husband received threatening notices only after the league meetings had been held. Sir Charles Russell, counsel for parties, was proceeding in the cross examination of Lady Mountmorris upon the exact dates of the league meetings alluded to, when witness fainted and would have fallen to the floor, had not the court officer caught her. Sir Charles therenupon intimated that he would not proceed with the cross examination.
stephen-anthony-wallingford-1888-11-15.A3:
JENKINS BOUND OVER.
He Accuses His Wife of Being Unfaithful—The Murder of His Father-in-Law Premeditated—A Candidate For the Scaffold.

Solon G. Jenkins, who so cold-bloodedly murdered his father-in-law, Stephen Anthony, in Wallingford, Thursday evening, was yesterday afternoon brought before Judge Hubbard in the Borough court. He was defended by Hall Brothers.

Jenkins was bound over to the Superior court.

The crime was premeditated, as shown by the evidence. He went from this city to Wallingford, and on the train told Henry Allen, a Wallingford man, that he was going to kill Anthony, at the same time flourishing a revolver.

It seems that a noise was heard by Mrs. Anthony at the back door. Her husband went to see what it was. It was dark. Just as he called to his wife and said no one was there, the fatal shot was fired.

Another shot was fired. The murderer attempted to take his own life, but the ball grazed the ear.

Several years ago Jenkins was a prosperous merchant in Wallingford. He was a tinner by trade and a good workman. He kept a stove store, and for a time made money, but he began to drink excessively, neglecting his business and was at length closed up by the sheriff. Since that time he has worked in Hartford, Meriden and New Haven. A few days ago he secured a job in Wallingford, but did not keep it long.

Jenkins in his defense tells a rambling story. He says his wife has made several attempts to poison him. He also charges that his wife has been unfaithful to him and was intimate with a policeman named Willis. On Wednesday of this week he wrote a letter to the chief of police in Hartford accusing one of the officers of the force with being intimate with his wife.

The wife is now in Hartford. She denies the charges and says she could not live with him. Her father gave her and her three daughters, aged 13, 10 and 7 respectively, a home.

It is certain that Jenkins and his wife frequently quarrelled.

JENKINS THE MURDERER.
JENKINS THE MURDERER.

The Warning Letter—The Murdered Man's Death Wound—The Murderer's Wife.

Solon G. Jenkins, who murdered his father-in-law in Wallingford, is lodged in the New Haven county jail. The most startling thing about the testimony was a warning letter received at the Anthony home on the morning of the murder. Miss Lizzle Anthony, daughter of the murdered man, swore positively that the handwriting on the postal card was that of the murderer, Solon Jenkins. It was dated at New York, addressed to his wife, Mrs. Fanny Jenkins, Wallingford, Conn., and read as follows:

You and someone else has played the last scheme. I will play the next racket if it takes five years. I know where your shop is located if you have moved to Pearl street. I know you both. I shall go prepared to work it if it takes plenty of help.

The card was not signed, and had evidently been posted on the train, bearing the mark of the Springfield & Boston railroad postoffice. This card will go far toward proving that the act was premeditated, it is believed.

SHOT THROUGH THE LUNGS.

Another peculiar phase of the case was the very peculiar and at the same time simple blunder made by the doctors in their superficial examination of the murdered man's wounds. Blood was found issuing from the dead man's nose and mouth and no other point was noticed to have been disturbed. It was announced and published by all that the bullet entered the nostril, without making the slightest abrasion, and entered the brain, causing almost instantaneous death. The post-mortem examination was going on until a late hour on Friday, and before it had finished an official was responsible for the statement that the superficial examination had, he understood, been borne out by the later one. But when the coroner came in to make his report he announced that the ball had entered the right shoulder, glanced down and through both lungs and lodged in the outer wall of the left lung. Over a pint and a half of blood was taken out of the lungs, as well as the bullet, which was found to fit the revolver which was found with Jenkins in the grape arbor immediately after the shooting. The reason why this wound was not discovered Thursday night was that the blood all came from the lungs to the nose and mouth, attracting attention to the former organ. SUICIDE OF A MURDERER IN HIS CELL.
New Haven, Dec. 20 (Special).—Solon Calthoun Jenkins hanged himself at the New-Haven County Jail between 2 and 6 o'clock this morning. He was awaiting trial in the Superior Court for murdering his wife's father, Stephen Anthony, on the morning of November 15, at Wallingford. In early life Jenkins was an exemplary man, but domestic troubles caused him to drink, and finally his wife left him and petitioned for a divorce. This act seemed to make Jenkins wild and on the evening of the murder he started out to kill his wife and all her family. His father-in-law was first met, and before he could finish his fiendish work he was overpowered and locked up. Jenkins left several communications stating that he committed suicide to save the State expense.
