GEORGIA.
From the Lincolnton, Ga., News.

At a church in an adjoining county on Sunday morning just before preaching, a crowd of farmers were seated in the shade of a large oak discussing matters relative to their noble avocation. By some hook or crook, the credit system was introduced and fully discussed by all, save one old gentleman who kept "mum." He was noted far and wide as being one of the most eccentric fellows in all the land and his comrades prevailed on him for his views.

"Well men," he said, "I'll tell you what I think about it in a mighty short time. I'll give you my personal experience. Last year I was living with you as you remember. Well I went up to W—— and found a man willing to run me. I tell you I lived high. He actually fed me—furnished my clothes, fed my stock—supplied me with tobacco; and would you believe it, really let me have sugar and coffee and shoes—everything and nary a time did he cheap "money" to me. Thus it went on during the spring, summer and early fall. Oh, I rolled in clover. But when the leaves begun to turn and about the time for the autumnal equinox to come on, a genuine commercial cyclone struck me and scattered corn, cotton, potatoes, wheat, oats, mules, horses, cows, calves, pigs—lock, stock and barrel—and bore it away. It went away in wagons. Yes, sir, he run me in the spring and summer and everlastingly galloped me in the fall. Run me out of the county. From now henceforth and forever I don't want no more running in mine—a fox trot will do me. If the merchant is satisfied I am."

From the Walker County, Ga., Messenger.

A gentleman whose word is undoubted for truth, reports that, while squirrel hunting the other evening on the ridge between James Garrett's and Ed Carlock's, he discovered a small hole in the ground near a bunch of hickory sprouts, and, as he thought, yellow jackets going in and coming out, but on examination he found them to be bees. After considering a short time over the matter, he concluded to make a thorough search after their whereabouts, therefore he went a short distance to a neighbor's house, procured a pick and shovel and returned, commenced digging and excavating the dirt and soon he struck honey in vast quantities. After much labor and fighting bees he succeeded in procuring several hundred pounds of honey left a considerable amount of it on the ground. He is of the opinion that the cavern extends a long distance and that it is full of sweet stuff as far as it reaches. The bees have probably been there ever since the flood, and no doubt but that Noah started the first settlement of bees in that cave.

A sensation was created at two o'clock in Augusta, Tuesday, by the report, which rapidly gained circulation, that young Frank Wheless had killed himself. A crowd of his friends soon collected before the front door of the wholesale house of Wheless & Co., on Warren block.

The lifeless body of young Wheless was found in a pool of blood in his bed in the sleepingroom above the store. A 38-calibre pistol was grasped in his right hand, one chamber of which had been discharged. The bullet had entered just above the right ear and had torn its way entirely through his head, coming out on the left side near the top. When the shot was fired Mr. W. T. Wheless, Frank's father, was in an adjoining room. He thought the shot came from downstairs, and rushed down into the store. Finding no one there, he ran out on the pavement and then back in the store, to be greeted by the shocking discovery that his son had killed himself.

A note was left asking the delivery of certain little keepsakes, but there was nothing ascribing or indicating any cause for the rash act. Frank Wheless was a popular and successful young business man, and there was nothing in the condition of his affairs to warrant his action. He attended to his duties about the store as usual in the morning. At one time he was sitting in a rocking chair, and seemed moody, drowsy and quiet. His father remarked that he seemed sleepy, and he replied, "yes, I didn't sleep well last night."

He was last seen alive by Mr. Will Harris, a young man employed in the store. His room adjoined Frank's, and they went up together to get ready for dinner. Frank sat on the bedside and moved a pillow that was lying at the foot of the bed, and placed it at the head. In doing so he exposed the pistol, which was under the pillow. He leaned over, and picking up the pistol, placed it under the pillow at the head of the bed, laid back upon it with his feet hanging over the bedside, and one resting on the floor. In this attitude Harris left him when he went out to dinner, and thus he was found when the pistol shot was heard. His pulse beat for several minutes, but death soon came. So far as his consciousness was concerned, death was instantaneous. Frank Wheless came home from Birmingham a few months ago, where he had been in the real estate business, to go into business with his father. He was a joyous, light-hearted fellow, and a good business man. The jury returned a verdict of death by a pistol shot wound from his own hands.

Americus Republican: Blackman, the doomed murderer, will not hang until late in the fall. This seems to be an accepted fact among all concerned. Judge Fort, when interviewed in regard to the appointment of a day for the execution, said that he would not call a special term of the court simply for the purpose of fixing a day, and that unless he were petitioned to do this by citizens of the county that Blackman would be resentenced at the regular term of Schley superior court in September. Pineville was treated to a regular cloudburst on Friday morning. As a small wagon, says the Marion County Patriot, with two mules, on its way to Americus, the driver of the wagon stopped his mules in the stream to let them drink. While they were drinking the rush of the water from the hills came upon them and washed mules, wagon and all under a water gate just below the road. There were three negroes in the wagon, but they got out safely after passing under the water gate, and followed the mules and wagon down the stream. One of the mules was drowned, and, strange to say, it was the one that got loose from the wagon. The other one remained hitched to the wagon, was washed across three lots of land and the wagon and mule knocked down the center pier of a new bridge which was built since the March flood. How the mule went through with all this without being killed is something remarkable, but he was gotten out alive, though badly crippled, and will never do much more service.

The Morning News published several days ago a short account about the Sycamore affair. The following fuller particulars are clipped from the Worth Local at Sumner: A week or two since Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Horkan left their home, and during their absence a negro man from an adjoining place came for water. Finding no one at the house but a little white girl about 13 years of age, who lives with the Horkans, he made insulting proposals to her. Upon the return of the Horkans she informed them. Mr. Horkan went after the negro and attacked him. He shot at him four times. The first shot was aimed directly at his forehead. The negro dodged and the ball cut his hat directly in two without striking his head. Three other shots were fired, two of them taking effect, one in the back, lodging in the region of the shoulder blade, and the other in the fleshy part of the hip. The neighbors threatened to lynch him and finish the work, but Mr. Horkan wouldn't let them touch him, but said he would give him a chance for life. He was permitted to go to Jehu Branch's place, in Irwin county (where a brother stayed and where he could receive attention), under promise if he recovered from his wounds he would leave the community and never return. It seems that this was not the first meanness he had been guilty of in the Sycamore neighborhood and over in the edge of Irwin county, and that he was generally disliked by the citizens, both white and black. Consequently, as soon as Mr. Branch learned he was on his place he sent him word that he must leave. This he did, going back to Sycamore. A day or two after his return to Sycamore he mysteriously disappeared, and it is generally supposed he was lynched, as his father says he does not know where he is, having failed to find him after diligent search. The father seems indifferent about the suspected fate of his son, and speaks of it as not at all unexpected.

Murdered by Moonshiners.
HARRISON, Ark., Feb. 13.—T. J. Patterson and Rich McMahon, while hunting in the Boston mountains, found the body of an unknown man, bareheaded and in shirt sleeves, heavily armed. There were no marks on his person to in- dicate the cause of his death. He lay near the still of Mr. Jones, where Jones was killed by Revenue Collector Frye last fall. The body is supposed to be that of a detective hunting up evidence against illicit distilling.
